## Ch. 1 — The Trail from the Seven Caves, before 1299

**A girl screaming to be killed.** In 1299 a young woman sits bound hand and foot in Culhuacan, waiting to find out what will be done to her. Her people have been destroyed. Her father begged the victorious king for a scrap of clothing to cover her torn dress, and the king looked at her, laughed, and said no — she will stay as she is.[^1]

She bears it while none of her own people can see. Then survivors start trickling in, dragged by captors or walking in to offer themselves as slaves, and she cannot bear it any longer. She asks for chalk and charcoal. Her guards allow it, perhaps amused. Bound, she struggles to mark herself in the old way, stands, and starts screaming: *Why do you not sacrifice me?* She is ready, the gods are ready, and the Culhua only shame themselves by delaying, as though they lacked the courage for it.[^2]

Some bards said the Culhua lit the pyre to shut her up. Others said her own people stepped forward and did it themselves, at her order, valuing her honour above their own lives.[^3] As the flames rose she shouted across at her enemies: *People of Culhuacan, I go to where my god lives. My people's descendants will all become great warriors, you will see.*[^2]

**What is real, and what a person is.** A death can be done correctly or incorrectly, and the correctness is public. She is not asking to be spared. She is asking to be killed properly and on time, and the delay is an insult — to her, and to the gods who are waiting. The paint is the point: she cannot free her hands but she can make her body legible as a sacrifice, and once it is legible the delay becomes the Culhua's disgrace rather than hers.

Honour survives a defeat, but only if somebody watches. She endures the exposure until her own people arrive. The audience is what turns a humiliation into a performance she controls. Noble girls were educated to be almost as stoical under duress as their brothers, so she is doing what she was trained to do.[^4]

**How you know.** The bards could not agree whether she was the chief's daughter or his elder sister, or whether her name was Shield Flower or Lily. Both were common names for noble daughters. The honest conclusion is that this was the story of more than one young woman, and that the essentials hold even where the conversation does not.[^4] Contradiction between tellings is not treated as a reason to throw the account away; it is treated as evidence about how many women this happened to.

The tellings differ on purpose, too, depending on whose people told them, whether they were written down in the first generation after the Spaniards came or the third, and whether the teller preferred a joke or a tragedy.[^5]

**The shape of time.** Two calendars run at once and you always know where you stand in both. The solar year has eighteen months of twenty days, plus five blank days at the end that everybody dreads, making 365. Alongside it runs a ceremonial count of thirteen months of twenty days — 260. On any given day you know your position in the sun's year and in the ceremonial one at the same time.[^6]

The two return to their starting point together after fifty-two solar years, and a bundle of fifty-two mattered to them the way a century matters now. Years are named by running the number thirteen through four signs: One Reed, Two Flint-knife, Three House, Four Rabbit, Five Reed, and on around.[^7] So a year is a name, and a name carries a reputation. One storyteller insisted the disaster of 1299 could not have happened in a year Two Reed as everybody else said, and must have been One Rabbit — because One Rabbit always meant catastrophe. There was even a saying, *we were really one-rabbited*, for being up a creek.[^8]

**What makes things happen.** Trouble comes from somebody the group took in. In the story every Nahua child knew, one of the more malicious gods left a foundling for the Chichimecs to find and pity and raise. His name was Huemac, Big Gift. Grown, he demanded that the neighbouring Nonohualca hand over women, and specified the buttocks be four spans wide; when they brought four and he judged them too small, they walked out in a rage. Then he tied the four to an obsidian table and sacrificed them, which is the worst thing you can do to a conquered people's women.[^9]

War followed, and it went far enough that the Chichimec leader shouted across the fighting: *Was I the one who sent for the women over whom we are fighting and making war? Let Huemac die! He made us fight!*[^10] They killed him together, and it was already too late, because too many sons on both sides were dead. So the Nonohualca left in the night, and the rest of the history is two peoples trying to find stability without the allies they had just lost.

**How people should relate.** Making alliances and deciding when to break them was the whole of political life, and they were proud of the making and guilty about the breaking. Their own stories put the worst of these crises at Tula — which was a real city, but which almost every group named as the site of its founding rupture, because *Tula* had become the word for any wandering group's first serious attempt to settle down with locals. It went badly every time.[^11]

The Mexica version has the same shape and no god in it. After Shield Flower's death the survivors are given land in exchange for servitude, and the king amuses himself with impossible tasks. Move a chinampa — a farming plot built by fencing swamp and filling it with earth, the least movable object in their world. Capture a deer without piercing its hide or breaking its bones. Defeat an enemy unarmed. They manage all three, by trickery or, in the last case, by ambush, cutting the left ears off the men they killed and bringing them back in a basket. Each time the king and his people ask each other: *who are these Mexica?*[^12]

**Where the technique lives.** In the same chapter, the borrowed weapons. The Tolteca Chichimeca are reduced to servants of a stronger people, hungry, unable to worship properly, with no weapons. They offer to run the festivities for a religious holiday. Dancing is involved; dancing requires weapons. Their leader asks permission to collect broken cast-offs for the performance and comes back to his young people in tears — the fate of the people is now in their hands.[^13]

The dialogue is the technique. *Please lend us your old weapons, some of your old shields and war clubs — not your good equipment, if you gave us that we would break it.* — *Maybe you want our good weapons?* — *No, my lord, just your old weapons that lie fallen where you throw out the ash water.* And the answer: *Fine. Ha, we don't even need our new weapons.*[^14]

A request is likelier to be granted when it visibly costs the giver nothing, and contempt is a working disguise. They do not ask to be armed; they ask for rubbish, and they raise the suspicion themselves before the owner can. Then they work night after night, gluing and sewing and repairing until the shields and spears are beautiful, while the townspeople watch them wander the patios and laugh.[^14]

**What is worth having.** Survival, earned rather than owed. Shield Flower learned, sitting by the fire, that her people deserved to survive because they loved life and fought for it — using their wits, their love and their ferocity, each as needed. Their creator would see to it, but the histories put the confidence in the people rather than in the promise: *O Tolteca, may you have confidence! Gird yourselves up, take heart!*[^15]

And pleasure, which spread further than anything else they had. What travelled out of central Mexico most easily was the town square with pyramids around it and a ball court with slanted walls on two sides. There men kept a rubber ball up with their hips until it hit the ground on the other side. Sometimes a stone ring was set on each wall, and only the best could put the ball through. Much later, under empires, some games were played to the death with the losers sacrificed — but that rare practice is not why the ball courts lasted dozens of generations. The thrill did.[^16]

**And what they chose to be proud of.** Shield Flower took more pride in coming from northern barbarians than from the corn-planting calendar-keepers her people had married into. At her death she cried out as a warrior maiden. The history she had been taught was about the wanderers, not about the people who were already living in the valley when they got there.[^17] The migrants' own weapons carried the same pride into folklore: *it is said that they had bee sting arrows, fire arrows, arrows that followed people... If it was hunting something above, they would see it come back with an eagle.*[^18]

## Ch. 2 — People of the Valley, 1350s–1450s

**A man nobody expected.** Itzcoatl's father led the Mexica for decades, but his mother was one of the palace women and nowhere near royal, so nobody expected him to be anything. His name was his alone — no one before him bore it and it was never passed on.[^19]

His mother had been a slave, a beautiful girl from Azcapotzalco who sold vegetables in the street before she was handed over to the king, probably gambled away or used to settle a debt.[^20]

**What a person is.** Your mother, not your birth order. There was no word in Nahuatl for illegitimate; there were plenty of words for kinds of union, and those settled what happened to the children, but the flat category did not exist.[^21] And a slave's child was never a slave, because the condition could not be inherited — if it were, towns would have filled with slaves in a few generations and come apart.[^22]

So Itzcoatl's mother, at her worst, still knew her son by the king would be privileged. She would never have guessed he would rule; that went to the sons of noble women from powerful towns.[^23] Then a crisis came.

The other word for a person carried a claim in it. Commoners were *macehualtin*, and the word did not simply mean common — it meant those deserving of land, and so of a place of their own in the polity.[^24]

**How people should relate.** Nobody's eldest son was waiting. There was no primogeniture, and the reason given is practical: it would have been impractical in a world that fluid, where what you needed was a highly competent leader rather than whoever came out first.[^25]

Watch what that lets a man do. Itzcoatl does not kill his dead half-brother's sons, though by custom they were the ones who should have ruled; he works with them for fourteen years.[^26] Then he and Moctezuma build something no hereditary throne can: power alternates between two family lines. Moctezuma rules and his own sons do not. He marries a daughter or favourite niece to a grandson of Itzcoatl, who is elected next. A grandchild of Moctezuma's takes a later turn, and eventually a child is born descended from all of them.[^27]

The same shape runs everywhere. Tasks were shared or handed back and forth "so that no one group would have to handle something unpleasant all the time or be accorded unlimited power all the time."[^28] And after the conquests, each altepetl went on choosing its own ruler and rotating its own duties as it always had, as long as it fought when called, worked on the roads and temples, and paid on time. One historian's summary of the whole arrangement is three words: this was no Rome. The Mexica had no interest in teaching anybody their language or drawing them into the capital.[^29]

**What makes things happen — and the machinery that keeps breaking.** Every ruler had several wives from several towns, so every throne had many claimants, and the claimants had different home villages behind them. Nobody saw this as a defect. It guaranteed an heir and it produced a clan of young men who would stand together in a crisis.[^30]

It works only while almost everyone agrees which wife is primary. Where there is real doubt, a civil war is already waiting, because factions of half-brothers by different mothers, carrying hatreds from childhood, are standing right there with different visions of the people's future.[^30] That is exactly what happened in 1426 when old Tezozomoc of Azcapotzalco died in his bed and his sons turned on each other instead of defending the family's ground.

So rearranging your marriages was how you made a political announcement. The Texcocan king started insisting his sons by his Mexica wife would inherit, and the Tepanecs did not wait for more. Hundreds of them crossed the lake at dawn in canoes ringed with bright shields, slid in silently, and killed without mercy.[^31] The bards summarised it their way — *it was said that there was war because of a concubine.*[^32]

**What is real.** The world is borrowed and the payments are open. Four worlds went dark before this one. The gods sat in the dark at Teotihuacan and somebody had to burn so the sun would rise. The confident volunteer got the heron-feather headdress; the quiet one, Nanahuatzin, got paper trinkets, reeds and pine needles. At the moment the confident man walked to the flames, took fright, turned back, tried again, and could not. The gods looked at Nanahuatzin. He shut his eyes and jumped, his flesh crackled and sizzled, and the sky went red in the east.[^33]

The priests said it plainly: *they are the ones who taught us everything. Before them, we kiss the ground, we bleed. We pay our debts to the gods.*[^34] Mostly you paid by bleeding yourself; sometimes the payment was a life; and if people stopped, the fragile world might end.[^35]

Whether the men running it believed it is left open. Some of the sharpest of them may well have known the world would not shatter like jade if nobody died. They would have concluded there was no choice anyway. The danger in the world around them was every bit as real as the danger in the cosmos they described. They had been on the other side within living memory. If they started losing wars, it would be their turn again.[^36]

**How you know.** By 1430 Itzcoatl was confident enough to order a book burning. Every old painted history that pointed to a different future — that his half-brother's sons were the ones destined to rule, or that Tenochtitlan would stay a minor town — went into a bonfire as an offering to the gods. Deerskin rolls and accordion-fold books of maguey-fibre parchment crackled and popped and went to ash.[^37] There was an old riddle: *what is the scarlet macaw leading, the raven following?* The answer is a conflagration.

The books that replaced them did the job. Under starlit skies the bards held up the new paintings, and in those the rise of Itzcoatl over Hummingbird Feather's sons looks entirely expected, and Tenochtitlan's rule over the known world looks like destiny.[^38] The performance itself kept the older discipline: they moved back and forth between the perspectives of the different parts of the altepetl, twisting the strands into one, as they said, using their own spinning metaphor.

**The shape of time.** The tribute schedule started to eat the calendar. One part of a greater altepetl might owe Texcoco, the next part might owe Tenochtitlan, one payment coming once a year in bales of cotton and another three times a year in bags of corn. Collectors arrived on time, so people had to be ready. Different villages had adopted the calendar at different moments, so one town's Year One Reed was another town's Two Rabbit — and they were now forced to try to synchronise. The counts never aligned perfectly. They began to close.[^39]

**What is worth having.** A death that somebody keeps. A young woman taken in war dips her hand in blue paint and presses it on the doorframe of the man who captured her, then walks back to the temple. The print stays in the wood for years so people remember what she gave.[^40] The warrior keeps her hair and ceremonial clothes in a reed chest in the best place in his house for the rest of his life.[^41] The watching was not a frenzy — the onlookers had fasted and stood holding sacred flowers, and it seems to have been quiet and spellbinding.[^41] Some of those who died got through it without letting their enemies see them cry. *Some, in truth, wept*, one man remembered.

**And what it cost somebody else.** A conquered chief taxed in sacrifice victims knew he would now have to make war on his neighbours constantly or send his own people's children to the stone. It was enough to make anyone think twice about resisting — and a chief who charged into a fight he would lose was called "a child."[^42] For the Huaxtecs, who fought back hard and lost anyway, the terms were worse: the allied soldiers burned the temple, killed old and young, and set out to remove every trace of that people from the earth. The story was meant as a lesson to everybody else, and it worked.[^43]

**The exception that ate a century.** Tlaxcala was too well defended and too well dug in. Early attacks stalled, so the Mexica invented the Flower Wars — scheduled combat every few years where the winners saved themselves from death — and everyone could assume Tlaxcala was being left alone on purpose as a ceremonial enemy. Nobody had to say out loud that taking it would have cost too much.[^44]

**What mothers taught.** That anybody can do good or harm and you cannot sort people into two camps on that basis. Doing good means putting your ego down and doing whatever keeps your people alive long-term. Everyone thinks about the future. And often what your situation asks of you is exactly the thing you do not want to do.[^45] Alongside: *on earth we live, we travel, along a mountain peak. Over here is an abyss, over there is an abyss. If you go this way, or that way, you will fall in. Only in the middle do we go, do we live.*[^46]

When the drought came in the 1450s and the corn failed four years running, teenagers left home so their parents would not have to feed them, and their bodies were found later on hillsides, half eaten by coyotes and vultures. In the city families sold a child to merchants heading east, where the drought was lighter and buyers were interested — telling themselves that as a slave the child would at least not starve.[^47]

## Ch. 3 — The City on the Lake, 1470–1518

**A singer at the door.** One afternoon in 1479 a young Chalcan nobleman pauses on the threshold of the Mexican king's palace, letting his eyes adjust from the glare outside to the cool dark inside. He has never been so frightened. He can tell from the looks his companions are exchanging that they think he has been summoned in to be punished — taken to one of the wooden cages the capital is famous for, then burned. *Will we all be burned to death?* they are wondering.[^48]

His name, Quecholcohuatl, means Flamingo Snake. It is a chosen name, picked to match the embroidered clothes he wears when he performs.[^48]

**The situation.** Chalco had been destroyed by the Mexica about fifteen years earlier and its royal houses disbanded. Long enough that a generation had grown up without clear memories of the war; not long enough for anyone to forget the ancient royal lines or the self-government Chalco had held for centuries. So the young men had grown restive and started saying Tenochtitlan should give them a seat at the council table and treat them as relative equals, the way it treated the valley's other powers.[^49]

**What they actually did about it.** They came to entertain the king. That is what they said. In fact they had chosen the song with a political purpose: "the Chalca Woman's Song," sung in the voice of a female prisoner of war, a concubine.[^50]

**What is assumed here, and it is the whole chapter.** Everyone in the room understands a captive woman and a conquered town to be the same figure. In ordinary marriage women were complementary to men and in no way inferior; in war the female sex genuinely suffered — a captive woman grieved not necessarily because of daily violence but because she had lost her standing as an honoured person, and could no longer take pride in her children inheriting her place and carrying the line forward. She became a nonentity socially, a sexual object with no lasting power.[^50]

So a subject polity can say a thing to its conqueror's face, in his own palace, that it could not say in a petition. It says it in a borrowed voice everyone can decode and nobody has to acknowledge. The protest is deniable by design. That is also why the singer is terrified: deniable is not the same as safe.

The song works. Axayacatl comes out from where he is with his women, lifts one foot on the dance floor and starts turning in circles, completely happy. Then he goes inside and sends for the lead performer. He takes him to bed and asks him to promise to sing only for him, then tells his wives to stand up and seat the man among them: *here has come your rival.*[^51] Men going to bed with men is treated here as one of the possibilities in a life, part of the joy of being alive, not a category a person belongs to permanently.[^52]

**How people should relate — the code everybody could read.** The reassurance sent back out to the terrified Chalcans on the patio was clothing: a cloak, loincloth and sandals embroidered with jade, all of them the king's own. Public gift-giving was a language. In another history, all a narrator has to write to establish that a ruler meant to destroy a man is *he gave him only one tilma* — one cloak.[^53] The Chalcans saw the quality of the gifts, whooped, and started teasing the ones who had predicted disaster.

The politics of the city ran on the same principle at a larger scale. No individual stood alone and no group stood alone; families made a calpolli, calpolli made an altepetl, altepetls made a greater altepetl, and harmony depended on each part doing its share. Unpleasant jobs — keeping up a temple, clearing weeds to make a port, collecting tribute for a conqueror — got rotated between the parts. So did the chieftainship between lineages, to keep resentment down. What Tenochtitlan did was formalise all of that at scale, with one addition: they would always be the head of it.[^54] The image they used for the whole was a bird. The nobles might be the head, but the commoners were the tail and the wings, and no bird flies without those.[^55]

**What a person is.** Something that can be finished or spoiled by about the age of twenty. Almost every child, boys and girls, nobles and commoners, went into a temple boarding school at about thirteen and stayed a few years, passing the worst adolescent years away from home.[^56] A girl learned the prayers for her wedding and her daily life, learned to spin and weave and embroider, and learned that she would get very little sleep for most of her adult life and must not resent it: *here is the task you are to do: be devout night and day... Do not practice the pleasure of sleep.*[^56]

A boy learned war unless he was headed for the priesthood or born into a merchant family. Training started gently — sweeping, firewood, singing in the evenings — and the violence came in by degrees. By about twenty, a man who had not made a kill or taken a captive faced a life of shame. If it became clear in training that he could not fight at all, he could be designated a burden bearer. He might spend the rest of his life paddling a canoe of water vats around the edge of the town, leaving them at the appointed places, and everyone would know why.[^57] The other end of the same scale was open. A commoner who fought well became a *quauhpilli*, an eagle lord, honorary nobleman, rich on the slaves and loot he brought home. He was often given an official position, and nobody argued about his right to it.[^57]

**What is real, and who says so.** There were no written laws, and there was a fixed law anyway — principles everyone understood, judges who set the penalties, separate officials for commoners' grievances and nobles', and a high court over both called the *tlacxitlan*, the place at the foot. Adultery was a crime punishable by stoning or strangling, defined differently by sex: a married woman could have no relations outside her marriage, a married man could, unless the woman was married too. A person in debt could sell a child into slavery, and that child kept certain protections and the right to buy their way out. In practice nobody could find a person once they had been carried east — but thousands of people held the idea of a fixed law in their heads with no written code behind it.[^58]

**How you know.** By keeping records and sending people to look. Near the palace courtyards stood storage chambers for *in tlilli in tlapalli*, the black and the red — the scribes' painted texts, rolled or folded accordion-style into wooden bins and reed chests. A few were history timelines that the tellers used to remember what to say and to work out when a particular song fitted. Most had nothing to do with art. They were business records: boundary decisions, chains of authority, noble lineages, tribute owed. Moctezuma even sent people, often frightened merchants, into places he had not conquered yet, to record what business was done there and what resources were available.[^59]

That is the machinery that produces the last paragraph of the chapter. In 1518 he sent observers to look at some strangers who had turned up more than once on the Maya coast. They lay on the bluffs and watched the newcomers gallop their huge deer up and down the hard sand, wheeling and shouting with laughter, metal glinting. The strangers glanced up, knowing they were being watched. The observers knew they knew, and did not care: their job was not secrecy, it was intelligence. They took notes in glyphs. Then they walked home by the routes they knew, resting when to rest and pushing when to push, and in a matter of days they knelt in front of their king.[^60]

**The shape of time.** Vigilance is continuous, because nothing holds itself up. Governing this arrangement took eternal watching — a finely tuned organism, ferocity and peace side by side, which could not be expected to maintain itself. That was the job description, and the people held him to it. *The ruler used to keep vigil through the night*, they remembered.[^61]

**What is worth having.** Beauty, and the fact that somebody has to pay for it out of sight. The visitors remembered the gardens first — flowers spilling off ordinary people's flat rooftops as well as the king's, trees shaped strangely enough to look enchanted, and big carved wooden cages full of quetzals and parrots and flamingos and parakeets flashing colour as they moved. Then the stars came out, and the priests charted them while everyone else just looked. They looked, the Mexica used to joke, like popcorn scattered across the sky.[^62]

Flamingo Snake grew old inside that. He knew the darker side of Mexica power from the inside, being Chalcan, and he loved what the city had built anyway, because he could watch artists from different altepetls answering each other's work instead of repeating their own. The bill was paid somewhere he would never see. For the valley to have that much peace and room for art, the war and the hunger had to be pushed out to the villages of strangers. The people of a great city almost never see the shattered people who support them. They see them briefly and unreally, as honoured victims in a magnificent ceremony.[^63]

**And what the arrangement costs at the top.** In 1498 daughters of the city's leading families were taken to Texcoco to watch a woman and her lovers and everyone who had covered for them stoned and strangled, as a lesson in obedience. Ladies brought daughters still in the cradle so they would see. People came from towns all around, even Tlaxcalans and Huexotzincans, who were enemies. The old woman who remembered it as a child remembered the feast afterwards better than the executions — the food had made more of an impression.[^64]

A few years later Huexotzincatzin, the presumed heir in Texcoco, was strangled. He and a merchant's daughter from Tula, famous for spinning poems and turning them into songs like any man, had got a reputation for composing works addressed to each other and teasing each other, wittily, in front of an audience. That broke with the convention of taking turns, and in breaking with it they had made something. His father would have handled it privately; Moctezuma wanted a nephew of his own on the Texcocan throne and had been waiting for a reason. The old woman's summary, decades later, was six words: *he was punished just for composing songs to the Lady of Tula.*[^65]

## Ch. 4 — Strangers to Us People Here, 1519

**A girl walking down to the beach.** Twenty enslaved women are led from the Maya town of Potonchan along a winding path to the shore, through ceiba and mahogany and rubber trees, with spearmen alongside in case anyone runs. They are peace offerings. When they come out into the sunlight they see the giant boats with cloth hung from poles to catch the wind, and the bearded men turning from their smoking fires — they are trying to keep the mosquitoes off — to stare.[^66]

She had been born to a Nahua nobleman on the coast at Coatzacoalcos, and her mother, who was nobody, had buried her umbilical cord by the hearth and said the prayer any mother said: *you will be the heart of the home. You will go nowhere. You will not become a wanderer anywhere. You become the banked fire, the hearthstones.*[^67]

**What a person is.** Whatever their mother's standing lets them be. When the Mexica came demanding allegiance, the children of less powerful mothers were the ones who ended up in a canoe. Nobody thought of killing children — they were far too valuable, and could be raised as household dependents or sold.[^68] She was sold at Xicallanco for a weight of cacao or bolts of cotton, the two currencies of that town, and then sold on to Potonchan, and she stopped being anybody's elder sister or youngest child.[^69]

Work is sorted the same way. Weaving was holy, so the honoured wives and daughters did it. The enslaved women ground corn, made tortillas, hauled water and minded children. They also sowed and picked the cotton, beat and carded the fibre for hours, spun it, boiled it in dye until the colour came, and warped the loom. Then the lady of the house could begin.[^70]

**How people should relate.** There is no category she could betray. Mexicans today generally call Malintzin a traitor, and she would have been baffled by the question, because her language had no word meaning Indians. Mesoamerica was the whole known world, and the only available term for people native to the Americas would have been *human beings* — and human beings were plainly not all on one side. The Mexica were her people's enemies; they were the reason she was taken from her family, and their merchants sold her.[^71]

The word came later and it came awkwardly. People began saying *nican titlaca*, we people here, when they needed to distinguish themselves as a whole from the arrivals. Moctezuma's messengers used it about her. The interpreter was not one of the ones from across the sea, they said, she was one of us people here. They meant she came from the eastern lands, not that she was one of theirs. It never occurred to them to expect loyalty from her, any more than from anybody else they had made war on.[^71]

**Nobody knew what to call the strangers.** In this world everybody is named for the place they come from — Tenochca from Tenochtitlan, Tlaxcalteca from Tlaxcala, Culhuaque from Culhuacan. If you do not know where a man is from, you do not know what to call him.[^72]

The one thing that got clear quickly was that these men said they represented their god. So the Nahuas called them *teules*, from *teotl*. A generation later Spanish writers loved that, because *teotl* means god and it let them say they had been worshipped. But the word did other work: in a ceremony a *teotl* was the god's stand-in, the one destined for sacrifice, and in other settings it meant strange power of the kind a sorcerer might have. The Spanish king used it that way himself, writing to Cortés about converting the Indians' lords and their *teules*, meaning their priests.[^72]

**What is real, and the claim they did not make.** They did not believe people became gods, or that gods came to earth in one particular year, or that anybody held a preordained right to conquer them. Quetzalcoatl was not their main god — he was Cholula's — and he was not originally connected to any objection to human sacrifice.[^73]

The story that they were arrived at later, by their own grandchildren, and the chapter says why. The young indigenous writers of the 1560s and 70s came from the elite families that had lost everything forty or fifty years earlier. They knew both their Mexica relatives and their European teachers far too well to believe their own people were simply inferior. They needed an explanation that was not that. Their teachers had one available. So the students wrote down what no indigenous person had said before: pillars of fire, terrifying omens, a trembling king. Those passages look a great deal like the Greek and Latin texts in the school library.[^74] A few pages further on the same students switched to writing down what old men who had been there actually said, and the tone changes completely. It gets specific and practical. *At the first shot the wall did not give way, but the second time it began to crumble.* The pillars of fire are gone.[^74]

**How you know.** Moctezuma sent scouts to every important town between the coast and Tenochtitlan and set up a war room. Messengers arrived as others left; there was no time when they were not listening and no time when reports were not being given. His scouts even brought back a summary of the sermon the Spanish priest kept giving, so that when the Spaniards finally tried to preach at him he cut them off — he had already heard it.[^75]

And the chain the whole conquest ran on was assembled by a slave in about an hour. When two canoes came out to the flagship, Aguilar tried to translate and found himself listening to Nahuatl, which he did not know, and Cortés got angry at the man he had paid to ransom. Nobody expected a young slave girl to step forward. She did, and by the end of that hour her full value had been felt.[^76] She learned Spanish from Aguilar with no blackboard and no grammar, and within a few months did not need him.[^77] The local people called her Malintzin. They had no *r*, so Marina came out Malina, and the honorific *-tzin* went on the end. They called Cortés by her name too, which the Spaniards found disorienting and felt should have been the other way round.[^78]

**The shape of time.** The chapter's own answer to why it went the way it did is measured in millennia rather than in years, and the people living it had no access to it. In the Old World people had farmed full-time for ten thousand years, and Europeans, who were not the first farmers, were the heirs of all of it — the population, the ships, the navigation gear, the flour mills, the barrel-making, the carts, the printing presses. In the New World full-time farming was perhaps three thousand years old. It was almost as if Renaissance Europe had met the ancient Sumerians, who were stunningly impressive and could not have beaten Charles the Fifth working with the Pope. Knowing that would have been a relief to the young writers of the late 1500s, and it was not available to them.[^79]

**What makes things happen.** A hard calculation, made by a man with good information. Moctezuma sent an offer of annual tribute — gold, silver, slaves, textiles, delivered however they liked — on one condition, that they not enter his lands. That was what he would have wanted in their place. He could not afford a confrontation near home. He knew from his own sources that the strangers won their battles, and that even if he raised a great army and destroyed them, the casualties would be beyond anything in his experience, and his kingdom would be gone anyway, because allies do not stand with a power that cannot deliver an easy victory at its own centre. He did not even want them close enough for comparisons to be drawn. Scholars afterwards enjoyed explaining that he did nothing because of something in his culture — man-god communication, an inability to imagine war to the death. He had a pragmatic agenda, as he had had all his adult life.[^80]

The other side ran on a legal theory. Cortés knew Spanish law, and Spanish law held that a leader and his subjects were bound by an organic unity of purpose. Even a king could be set aside by *all good men of the land* if he behaved outrageously. The good men refusing to obey were not traitors; they were acting for the common good. He had left the Caribbean without permission and was technically an outlaw. So he needed a citizenry demanding that he lead them, and he arranged for every Spaniard present to sign a document founding a town and asking him to take them to Tenochtitlan.[^81] Then he had the ships beached — not destroyed, but repairable only over many weeks, which made going home a project rather than a decision.[^82]

**What is worth having.** Not looking weak in front of the people watching. That is what Moctezuma is protecting, and it is what the Chontal lords at Potonchan decided too. They counted their dead after the horses came over the flat ground and found they had lost more than two hundred and twenty warriors in a few hours. Nothing like it existed in anything recorded in stone or in legend. Even if they eventually drove these men off, everybody in their world would hear about the cost, and they would be left weak in front of their enemies. So they sued for peace.[^83]

**And what it looked like when the two sides finally met.** Moctezuma decided to stage it as two brother monarchs meeting. Hundreds of dignitaries gathered at the gate, representatives of every altepetl in the centre, and each one stepped forward in turn, touched the ground and kissed the earth from his hand — the standard Nahua way of showing that a body politic is united. The chiefs were patient about it. Cortés was not: *I stood there waiting for nearly an hour until everyone had performed his ceremony.*[^84]

Then the newcomers looked down a broad straight avenue that put the crooked streets of European cities to shame. A royal company came towards them under a great canopy, its gold and stones catching the light, as though the king were carrying a piece of the sun.[^85] One of them, writing as an old man, remembered thinking the towns rising out of the water were an enchanted vision out of a knight's tale, and that some of the soldiers asked whether it was a dream. Then he flinched at the end of his own paragraph: *today all that I then saw is overthrown and destroyed; nothing is left standing.*[^86]

*Read: lines 886–1079.*

# Below the Line

*Everything above is sourced to the chapters named. Everything below is built rather than found, and is not measured by `assessgate.sh`.*

## Ch. 1 — Roads Not Taken `[SPECULATIVE]`

**A live alternative, with the source's own verdict attached.** Shield Flower's father declared himself *tlatoani* and stopped paying tribute, then taunted the strongest chief in the area to make the point stick. He may have gone as far as asking to marry the man's daughter and sacrificing her when she arrived — though since he was not a madman, the taunt was more likely refusing an order or attacking an ally. Either way it was a significant error of judgement.[^87]

The alternative is documented by what happened next: two generations later the Mexica did the same thing — declared themselves independent under their own king — and it held. What differed was preparation, and specifically that they began *without* a rash implicit declaration of war against their neighbours.[^88] Same move, same people, opposite outcome, and the variable is named.

## Ch. 1 — What Transfers `[SPECULATIVE]`

**Ask for what the holder has already written off.** The Tolteca Chichimeca did not ask to be armed, they asked for the broken shields lying where the ash water gets thrown, and they raised the obvious suspicion out loud before the owner could. *Applies when* the thing you need has a cheap version the holder does not value and will not miss, and when being underestimated costs you nothing you were going to use. *Fails* the moment the cheap version cannot be repaired into the real one — the whole plan runs on night after night of gluing and sewing, and without that the rubbish stays rubbish.
*Decision type:* timing a bold move.

## Ch. 2 — What Transfers `[SPECULATIVE]`

**Pay the rival line for waiting, and the arrangement outlives you.** Alternation between two royal houses is a bribe with a schedule: the family that loses this round is guaranteed the next. *Applies when* the rival is powerful enough to wreck you and permanent enough to still be there in a generation. *Fails* when the turn is too distant to be believed — this version needed three or four generations of kept promise before anyone collected.
*Decision type:* succession.

**A face-saving frame that requires the adversary's participation will keep the adversary in good health.** The Flower Wars were invented so nobody had to say Tlaxcala could not be taken, and they gave Tlaxcala's four kings a permanent shared enemy and a standing reason to keep meeting as one body.
*Decision type:* strategic retreat.

## Ch. 2 — Counsel From Elsewhere `[SPECULATIVE]`

**A Mongol advisor on the book burning.** The Mongol pattern in this vault is a conqueror who leaves the conquered world's memory largely intact and takes its administrators into service, rather than replacing its account of itself — see [[LAB/Worldview Reports/weatherford-genghis-khan-worldview-archaeology|What the Mongols Took For Granted]]. From that seat, Itzcoatl's bonfire is spending something for nothing. He is not burning a rival people's history; he is burning his own people's, and the thing he buys with it — a story in which his succession was always expected — is one his court already knows to be false, since they are the ones saying he owes his power to his nephew's generalship.

What the counsel would predict is exactly what the chapter records. The suppressed version does not die; it goes into the households of Tlacaelel's descendants and comes back out in their annals a century later, still claiming Tlacaelel won the war. A destroyed record leaves a shape where it was, and the people who remember the shape are the ones you did not persuade.

## Ch. 3 — Counsel From Elsewhere `[SPECULATIVE]`

**A Kautilyan advisor on the Chalcan singers.** The *Arthashastra* treats a bonded confederacy as the hardest thing to beat and prescribes *bheda* — find the resentments, cultivate people quietly on each side, let the quarrel do the work. See [[LAB/Worldview Reports/trautmann-arthashastra-worldview-archaeology|What a Mauryan Statecraft Manual Took For Granted]].

Chalco is the inverse case: a polity already destroyed, its royal houses disbanded, whose young men have re-formed a shared grievance anyway and are now voicing it inside the conqueror's own palace. A Kautilyan reading would say the Mexica made the standard error — they broke the institutions and left the *memory* intact, which is the part that reconstitutes. Fifteen years is exactly long enough for a generation with no memory of the war to inherit a memory of the self-government.

What Axayacatl then does is the correction, and it does not look like statecraft at all. He listens to the song, dances, takes the singer to bed, and sends him back out with the king's own clothes on. Parleys follow, and eventually the four royal lines of Chalco are put back and Chalco joins the inner circle. Buying the grievance costs him a suit of clothes and a seat at the table; breaking it a second time would have cost another ten-year war.

## Ch. 3 — What Transfers `[SPECULATIVE]`

**A protest in a borrowed voice is deniable at both ends, which is what makes it usable — and what caps it.** The Chalca Woman's Song says a subject town's case in a captive concubine's voice, so everybody decodes it and nobody has to acknowledge it, and the king can respond by dancing rather than by conceding. *Applies when* the grievance is real, the audience is literate in the convention, and both sides need a way to move without a public climbdown. *Fails* where the ruler wants the protest on the record so he can punish it — the same song performed in the streets in July 1564 got eight poles set up by the market the next morning.
*Decision type:* when to compromise a core value.

## Ch. 4 — Roads Not Taken `[SPECULATIVE]`

**A constructed one, and it is a forecast.** Suppose Moctezuma had refused the meeting and fought at distance, accepting the casualties he was trying to avoid. First order, he loses men in front of the allies he was trying not to look weak in front of — which is the thing he was avoiding, so the cost is real and immediate. Second order, no strangers inside the city means no hostage, no expulsion, and no *Noche Triste*; the war starts on open ground where numbers matter more. Third order — and this is where it thins — the smallpox arrives regardless, because it travelled ahead of armies. **The epidemic is the part no decision touches, which is what makes the whole counterfactual weaker than it first looks.**

## Ch. 5 — A War to End All Wars, 1520–1521

**A dead woman nobody could move.** She had been lying in the palace for days when Moctezuma's daughter woke beside her sisters on the soiled mats. Nobody left in the building was strong enough to carry her out. The girl was about eleven. Her sisters' faces and arms were covered in sores, and the sores were beginning to heal, which meant they were going to live.[^1]

Her name was Tecuichpotzin, Lordly Daughter. Two of her brothers had been killed the night the Spaniards were driven out of the city, and her father had been found strangled. When the singers buried people they called out *are we born twice on this earth?* and the chorus answered *no*.[^2] She understood what they meant now.

**What is real.** Power is made of things you can name. When the old warriors were asked, thirty years later, how a few hundred foreigners had beaten them, they did not say the foreigners were better men. They said *tepoztli* — metal — more often than any other word. *Their war gear was all iron. They clothed their bodies in iron. They put iron on their heads, their swords were iron, their bows were iron.* Then they said the second thing: they wanted to know how word had travelled so fast, to so many people across the sea, about a kingdom nobody there had visited.[^3] They had seen the ships. They had not seen the compasses or the printing presses. They picked the right two questions anyway.

Nothing in that account gives the enemy more merit or a better mind. It gives him better equipment and a faster post, and both of those are objects in the world rather than qualities in a soul.

**What makes things happen.** For the first time in the book, the answers stop working. Priests promised a great victory within eight days and it did not come. In an earlier defeat, priests had promised one on the eightieth day, and the promise cost more lives than the fighting.[^4] The allies who had walked away came back — Spanish writers said it was because the priests had been discredited, and the indigenous account of the earlier failure supports that people did lose faith. But something else happened the same week: messengers arrived from the coast carrying powder and crossbows, which anyone spying on the camp could see.[^5] Two causes stand next to each other and nobody picks.

The smallpox has no cause at all in this chapter. It arrives, rises for about sixty days, takes as much as a third of a town, then recedes because there is nobody unexposed left, and starts again somewhere else.[^6] No god sent it. No mistake invited it. It is the one thing in the whole book that happens without anybody doing anything.

**The shape of time.** Everything gets counted. Cuitlahuac ruled for about eighty days before the pox killed him.[^7] Moctezuma spent about eighty days in irons.[^8] The Mexica went silent for more than twenty days while they widened the canals and walled up the passages between houses.[^9] The Tlaxcalan kings argued for twenty days about whether to finish the Spaniards off.[^10] The fighting lasted three months. These numbers are not decoration — they are how the people involved held the shape of a crisis in mind, the same way the year-count histories held a century.

Against all that counting sits the singers' flat answer. You get one life here and there is no second one. Time on earth is fleeting, and the dead do not come back.[^2]

**What a person is.** Two answers were live in the same city at the same time, and they could not both be acted on.

A ruler exists to keep his people alive. Moctezuma stood on a rooftop and had a younger man with a carrying voice shout it down to the crowd: *We are not their match. May the arrows and shields of war be laid down. The poor old men and women, the common people, the infants who toddle and crawl, who lie in the cradle and know nothing yet, all are suffering.*[^11] The old histories and prayers are consistent about this. A ruler's one paramount duty was to save the lives of his people down to the youngest babies, so the altepetl could go on. A ruler who was stubborn and committed his people to a war he could not win was the lowest of the low — he lacked a chief's wisdom.[^12]

A young warrior exists to fight. It was not their duty to be circumspect. It was their duty to die if that was what defending their honour took, and the long-term consequences were somebody else's department.[^13] Cuitlahuac's messengers put it to Cortés in arithmetic: they had worked out that even if twenty-five thousand of them died for every one Spaniard, they would finish first, because they were many and the Spaniards were few.[^14]

Neither of those is cowardice and neither is recklessness. They are two jobs, and the city had both.

**How people should relate.** The old alternation between royal branches keeps running right through the catastrophe, and it keeps costing lives. Cuauhtemoc came from Itzcoatl's side of the family and had a Tlatelolcan mother, which brought him the big market on the north of the island and the people who used it.[^15] Moctezuma's surviving sons came from the other branch and had been taught by their father that open war with the strangers was futile. They were an argument as much as a faction. So Cuauhtemoc had six of them killed — one of them, some said, with his own hands — and the Tlatelolcan noblemen who held him blameless explained why: *the reason these nobles were killed is that they were favouring the common people in desiring peace, and trying to see to it that shelled white maize, turkey hens, and eggs should be collected so that they could have them submit to the Spaniards.*[^16]

Then he married Tecuichpotzin. Not out of desire — she carried both royal lines in her person, and a new ruler from one branch marrying a close relative of the man he replaced was simply how the thing was done. It also settled a rumour. Out in the countryside people had started pairing her name with Cortés's, or confusing her with Malintzin, and that had to stop.[^17]

**How you know.** Moctezuma built an instrument out of his own daughters. He sent Tecuichpotzin and two sisters to the newcomers as possible brides, and the point was to see what came back. If the strangers treated them as concubines rather than brides, that was bad news, but he would at least know where he stood.[^18] Either answer was information. At the same time he kept a younger daughter and a boy hidden, so the Spaniards did not learn they existed for years.[^19]

The warriors observed the same way. Their description of a crossbow is not awe, it is a report. *He pointed it right at the person he was going to shoot, and when it went off, it went whining, hissing, and humming. And their arrows missed nothing.* Then the guns: *the shot came upon people unawares, giving them no warning when it killed them. Whoever was fired at died if some dangerous part was hit: the forehead, the nape of the neck, the heart, the chest, the stomach or the abdomen.*[^3]

They acted on what they saw, too. They made spears long enough to match Spanish lances. They learned to zigzag canoes fast enough that men on the brigantines could not aim. They took a cannon, worked out that they had neither the ammunition nor the experience to use it, and sank it in the lake so nobody else could.[^20] When the Spaniards built a catapult and the arm threw its stone almost straight down behind the marketplace, the Mexica watched the carpenters jab their fingers in each other's faces and found it funny.[^21]

**What is worth having.** Food, and being allowed to go and look for it. At the end Cuauhtemoc paddled out in a canoe with his advisers and his wife and gave himself up, and asked for one thing: that his people be let out into the countryside to find something to eat.[^22] By then they had eaten deer hides, insects, lizards and softened adobe. The roads had shattered bones and scattered hair on them, and the walls of the houses were slippery.[^23]

And keeping up appearances to the last. Four weeks into the siege the warriors called across a broken bridge for the woman who was one of the people from here, and offered immediate peace if the Spaniards would go home. While the terms were being put, an old man in full view of everybody pulled provisions out of his knapsack, very slowly, and ate them.[^24]

*Read: lines 1080–1269.*

---

## Ch. 6 — Early Days, 1520s–1550s

**A blind man listening to a village burn.** In 1559 riders sent by the Franciscan prior set fire to the little village of Amozoc, and the thatch went up fast and came down onto everything underneath. The people ran out screaming and then stood and watched their belongings crackle. An old chief nearby had gone too blind to see it, but the sound and the smell told him what was happening. He was called Smoking Shield by his people and don Alonso de Castañeda by everyone else, and he had spent two years telling those villagers the Spaniards meant it about moving into the big town.[^25]

He had helped grant them that land himself, twenty-eight years earlier.

**What is real.** The gods are one thing and political power is another, and the second can be taken while the first cannot. In 1524 the friars preached for hours to a room of Mexica lords, and the lords said they were not the right men to answer and would fetch the priests. In the morning the priests came, asked to hear the whole thing again from the beginning, listened to all of it a second time, and then the senior one stood up.

*You have told us that we do not know the One who gives us life and being... This way of speaking is entirely new to us, and very scandalous. We are frightened by this way of speaking, because our forebears who engendered and governed us never said anything like this.*[^26]

He worked his way through the reasons to be grateful to the gods — they give rain, they make the things of the earth grow, through them we live and exist — and then he arrived where he had been going the whole time. *All of us together feel that it is enough to have lost, enough that the reed mats, the thrones have been taken from us. As for our gods, we will die before giving up serving and worshipping them.*[^27]

The reed mats and the thrones mean rule. He is conceding the conquest in one clause and refusing it in the next, and the two halves are about different things.

There is also a hole in the language that shows the same split from the other side. The friars needed a word for the Devil and could not find one. They settled on *tlacatecolotl*, which had meant a malicious shaman who could turn into a horned owl and fly about at night casting spells on people — somebody to avoid, not a rival to God.[^28] There was no Lucifer-shaped gap in the world for the word to drop into.

**What makes things happen.** A thing becomes binding by being said aloud in public, by more than one person, and then painted. When nineteen refugee families arrived in 1531 under two chiefs and the Cuauhtinchan leaders agreed to give them empty land, the agreement was made permanent through formal public statements repeated by several parties, and then a designated man painted it — hills, water, roads, marking the boundaries.[^29]

That year they added something. They brought along a young man who had learned the Roman letters from one of the Christians, and he wrote the statements out. Smoking Shield gave his Nahuatl name and added the Spanish one, plus a title the Spaniards had told him meant nobleman. He came out of the meeting as don Alonso de Castañeda Chimalpopoca.[^29]

**The shape of time.** One of the friars, hearing the priests refuse, muttered that they would just have to wait for these old men to die, because the young ones would be better listeners.[^30] Then that is exactly what the order did. They picked four towns, set up missions, and worked with young people.

The same clock runs everywhere in the chapter. Noblemen were pressured to pick one wife out of several and simply did not, and the pressure could be ignored for a while; in the end only generational change brought them round to monogamy.[^31] The school at Tlatelolco wanted boys of ten to twelve — old enough not to need watching, young enough to shape.[^32] Cristóbal came home a fluent writer with beautiful handwriting who prayed to the Christian god and dressed in Spanish clothes, and walked straight into a quarrel between the families who had sent sons and the families who had not.[^33]

**What a person is.** Someone whose death can be done to them correctly or incorrectly. Smoking Shield's father was invited to a neighbouring village by a messenger who spoke with extreme courtesy, went, and was strangled. His brother reacted badly to the sight and was put on the cutting stone, but not treated as a real sacrifice to the gods — *when they cut his breast, they did not quickly take his heart out. They stopped in the middle. So he went into convulsions before he died.*[^34] A child watched that and was still specifying the pause sixty years later.

Also someone who fights when they give birth. Isabel called it *nomiquizpan*, my moment of death, and her Nahua servants talked her through it the way they had always talked women through it: *exert yourself. Here are your old mothers. Grab hold of the shield. My daughter, young one, be a brave woman. Face it. Imitate the brave goddess Cihuacoatl.*[^35] All her life she had understood a woman in labour as a warrior with a chance to win honour, not as somebody being punished for her sex. This time there was no honour in it, because the baby was taken away as soon as it was born and carried to the house of Cortés's cousin.

And a person can be turned into an animal with a pun. A relative of Cristóbal's wrote in a margin, in Spanish: *well-born noblemen who do not know their letters have no understanding. They are noble beasts.* Tamed animals were called noble beasts and were owed kindness. But *bestia* also meant stupid, so the line reads either as calling them livestock or as calling them stupid noblemen, and it was meant both ways.[^36]

**How people should relate.** Obligations get rotated so nobody carries one forever. Thirty men from Cuauhtinchan had to serve in Spanish households, and the town was free to rotate that duty among themselves however they liked, as long as able bodies turned up at the right place on the right day.[^37] The rest of the tribute was flat and enormous: twenty-four thousand woven blankets every four years, twenty turkeys, six thousand bushels of corn, sixteen baskets of beans, eighty of chilli, sixteen of chia, sixteen of salt.[^38]

Smoking Shield's first act under the new order was to send the messengers back for better terms. Not to refuse — to ask exactly how many, and to fix a basket size for the corn that both sides would recognise as the right amount.[^39] Then he agreed, because it was a number his people could actually meet.

The Spanish side had its own arithmetic of obligation. In 1524 every Spanish man had to own a dagger, sword, lance, shield, helmet and breastplate. A man holding up to five hundred Indians also had to buy a crossbow and bolts, or a musket and enough ammunition for two hundred shots. Between five hundred and a thousand, he had to get a horse. Fail to comply and the whole grant went.[^40]

**How you know.** In 1546, instead of going out at night to burn the Tepeacans off the fallow land, don Alonso sued them. He and his entourage went to Mexico City, found lodgings, spent frightening amounts of money, and turned up at the High Court from May to August. He demanded that particular witnesses appear. He organised his own. After each statement was transcribed he had the court interpreter read it back, and then he nodded.[^41]

That is where the chapter turns. He had spent his life in a world where a decision was made permanent by being spoken publicly with ritual language and then commemorated on paper — which is what happened in the Spanish court too. But the paper was different. Pictographic writing needed priests who spent decades memorising hundreds of symbols and then took much of what they knew into the grave; these new marks encoded the voice, and young men like Cristóbal assured him anybody could learn them. If an epidemic killed every trained man in the High Court tomorrow, somebody else could still read the documents. His own words could be heard, exactly, generations later.[^42]

**What is worth having.** A history, and a joke.

He went home and started a book. Not for sentiment — he could see it being used as evidence about land in a Spanish courtroom, and carried to ceremonies as a sacred object. But the real reason was further out. Once the meaning of the old glyphs had faded and the communities had been pushed into poverty deep enough to narrow everything down to survival, a great forgetting would follow. And if they could not remember their past, how were they going to make demands about their future?[^43]

So Cristóbal picked up a quill and don Alonso started talking, and the first thing out of his mouth was an old story about a man called Huemac. *Then he demanded women of them. He said to the Nonohualca, "You are to give me women. I order that the buttocks be four spans wide."*[^44] Huemac meant Big Gift; he had been a foundling, supposedly a present from the gods. Some gift he turned out to be. The question hanging over the room is whether the boy's Nahuatl was still good enough to get it.

*Read: lines 1270–1473.*

## Ch. 7 — Crisis: The Indians Talk Back, 1560s

**A man on a rack who will not say a name.** On the night of 7 January 1568 the guards came down to the cell under the High Court for don Martín, Malintzin's son by Cortés. They tied him naked to the rack, turned the levers, and dislocated both arms and both legs. He said he had already spoken the truth and had no more to say. They turned it again. He said it again. Then they put his head below his body, held his nose, pushed a horn into his throat and poured. Four times. Between each one he said the same sentence.[^45]

Every other man they had brought in had confessed and given names. They were sons of Spanish noblemen, highborn, proud, used to sunlight and to contests held in public, and they had never had to imagine a world in which they were completely powerless in a dark room with men who were not afraid to kill them.[^46]

**What is real.** A king is, by definition, a man who knows what is best for his people and thinks about their future. That is not an opinion in this chapter; it is what the word means, which is why it can be used as a weapon.

In a prison cell the judge Ceynos told a jailed protester named Pedro Acaçayol to pay one peso and three tomines and a basket of corn, and to stop being difficult. Acaçayol answered: *It will not be possible, O king. Where will I get it from? I have only saved one half-peso and ten cacao grains.* Ceynos asked whether he served only his children. *Whom if not my children? Our Lord gave them to me.* Ceynos said: *Fine, you will be sold to the metal works.* And Acaçayol said: *Fine, you know what to do, for you are the king.*[^47]

He was sold to the metal works. The line was remembered anyway.

**What makes things happen.** In October, after the first collection came in, the four quarters of the city each sent a speaker to the open meeting. Don Martín Ezmallin of Moyotlan, a grandson of Ahuitzotl old enough to remember the days before the conquest, sobbed. He talked about the injustice of asking landless men to produce income as if by magic, and about having to ask the women to earn it by spinning. Then he turned on the men who had rioted. *You elders, you men of experience, you have hurt the altepetl by confronting it and rising up. Did anyone here order this? It came from Spain.*[^48]

That last sentence is the whole fight. The inspector Valderrama had spent the year trying to relocate the cause — he told the king that the people only thought they were poor because their own nobility and their friars were eating the difference, and that ordinary Indians would be delighted to pay a head tax if it freed them of supporting their lords.[^49] When the city exploded anyway he was genuinely bewildered, and wrote that *an animal without reason understands and recognises the good that is done for him, more than a man, even though he has a bit of reason.*[^50] It had not occurred to him that the grandchildren of the men who ruled Mesoamerica forty years earlier might object to becoming tribute-paying plebeians inside one lifetime.

**The shape of time.** Forty years, which is exactly one working generation. The Mexica who were small children at the conquest or born in the decade after it were now at the peak of their adult lives. They knew the world their parents had lived in and they had been raised in a different one, and they could argue with Spaniards in terms Spaniards understood.[^51]

The tax had its own calendar and everyone learned it fast: fourteen thousand pesos a year, three payments, the first due in July, signed into law in January and effective immediately.[^52]

**What a person is.** Honour comes to a man by birth, and it also comes from courage — don Martín had both available and only the second one left. He had grown up at the Spanish court as a half-breed Indian in the eyes of everyone around him, silent and distant, and he had learned early that people could look past him. When the water went in the fourth time he had nothing to trade except the thing he had built himself.[^46]

Standing is carried in a syllable. When the city decided its governor had not fought hard enough against the tax, they started calling don Luis Cipactzin *Nanacacipac*, Mushroom Alligator — up overnight, no substance. And they dropped the *-tzin* from his name, which they still gave to every other royal figure of the recent past.[^53]

The category for made nobility never went away either. The Spaniards liked to appoint Indians they got on with, and the Nahuas filed them under an old word: *quauhpilli*, eagle lord, which had always meant a commoner or an outsider who reached power by merit rather than birth.[^54] The word was already there.

**How people should relate.** The nobility owe the commoners anxiety. When don Luis sent emissaries out to the church painters and scribes, they spoke in the old formal way and reminded the artisans what their governors were doing on their behalf. *They suffer anxiety in the night. They don't eat with tranquility, worrying about how they will care for the wings, the tail.*[^55] Wings and tail meant the ordinary people. He also married doña Magdalena Chichimecacihuatl, the youngest of Tizoc's line, and danced in front of the crowd in traditional feathers with a gold-painted drum — because a king dancing meant something, and everybody watching knew what.[^56]

The judges spent the year trying to break that bond. They encouraged a lawsuit against the governor brought by a baker and a tailor, and the complaints filed in their names were about literacy, feast-day dancing, feathers, polygamists and taverns — not the sort of grievance a baker arrives with. Only at the very end came the one that might have been real, that the nobility squeezed the commoners.[^57] When those two ran off to the countryside and would not come back, the judges released a man from the sentenced rioters and ran the case again through him.[^58]

**How you know.** Truth is necessarily multiple, and one person cannot hold it.

After it was over, men set about writing as full an account of the disaster as they could, and they built it the way a *xiuhpohualli* was performed: different perspectives given voice, one after another. They took statements from men of different neighbourhoods, which still matched the old calpolli groupings, and transcribed them carefully, because no single person could give a full account of an important moment. They filled dozens of pages with dialogue and detail and anger, and they wanted posterity to see the constraints they had been under and why they finally paid.[^59]

The other method in the chapter produces the opposite. Every Spaniard on the rack confessed and named names, and none of the naming was true.

**What is worth having.** Not being forgotten, specifically and by name. Forty-six men were arrested after the riot — thirty-one Tenochca and fifteen Tlatelolca. Their heads were shaved to mark the shame, they were marched through the streets taking two hundred lashes as they went, and then sold into servitude for two or five years, with the town crier announcing it at every corner so nobody in the city could miss it. The man writing it all down made a list of their names, so that posterity should not forget what they suffered.[^60]

The Spaniards understood the counter-move. On the Monday after, they put up eight poles by the indigenous market and announced that anyone criticising the authorities would be tied to them.[^61] The Sunday before that, somebody had performed the Chalca Woman's Song in the streets — the same song Flamingo Snake had sung to Axayacatl's face eighty-five years earlier. *It is infuriating. It is heartrending, here on earth. Sometimes I worry and fret. I consume myself in rage.*[^62] The authorities recognised it, which is why the poles went up.

*Read: lines 1474–1667.*

## Ch. 8 — The Grandchildren, 1570s–1620s

**Straw mats pulled off beds to carry bodies.** At six in the evening on 3 May 1612 the doors of the Royal Accounting Office were unlocked and twenty-nine headless black bodies were lying inside. Their families had been allowed in earlier to spread cloths over them, but the flies were still there. The people who came at the hour passed around by word of mouth — black men and women, Spanish friars, a number of Indians — found there were no biers for so many, so the families brought straw mats taken off beds and floors and walls. As they carried them towards the Hospital of Our Lady of Mercy, the friars began to sing.[^63]

Don Domingo, who worked at a church by the southern gate and whom scholars call Chimalpahin, helped with the burial and then went home and wrote it down.

**What is real.** Every soul is worth exactly the same, and every person alive is descended from Adam and Eve. He said it repeatedly, and he was not saying it to please anyone — he said it about mestizos who belittled him, and about the Africans, and about the Filipinos, whom he called *macehualtin*, the same word he used for his own people.[^64] His favourite book was the *Confessions*, Book 1 best, which ends *the God who made me must be good, and all the good in me is his.*[^65]

Sitting alongside that, without visible strain, is the older thing. His grandparents' religion was built on a careful record of worlds that collapsed and were remade, none of them ever entirely forgotten. He and Tezozomoc were not living in the original world. They lived under a Fifth Sun, and since it began people had been getting through changes in it by reciting everything that came before.[^66]

**What makes things happen.** He wanted a world that was mostly good with some bad men loose in it. When the chaplain Zárate had a sick man stripped, tied to a stone pillar and lashed nearly to death, then preached about him from the pulpit and had him jailed to pay the money back, Chimalpahin's verdict was: *let him alone give an accounting to our lord God.* And: *let him not be talked about* — meaning let him not be honoured or known.[^67]

May 1612 broke that. Thirty-five people were hanged in one day on eight new gallows, denying to the end that there had been any plot at all, shouting *we do not know what we are accused of, what we are being punished for.*[^68] He did not write an argument about it. He wrote down the names and titles of every one of the fourteen Spanish royal officers who had condemned them, in a long vertical column that dominates the page, and finished: *these were the councillors who administered the law upon the thirty-five blacks, so that they were hanged on this day.*[^69]

The problem had stopped being certain evil individuals. It was that a small group had the legal right, born of might, to do this to a great many people, and the disempowered had almost no recourse when they chose to strike. So, as he said about Zárate's parish, *they kept it inside.*[^70]

**The shape of time.** He counted nine generations back to his family's arrival in the region in the 1200s.[^71] He kept a year-count of his own days from the age of eleven, at the level of detail that means a boy is enjoying himself: on Sunday 26 April 1592 two jaguars from the zoo were shipped to Spain, and on another day a horde of grasshoppers arrived at exactly four o'clock.[^72]

The pageant of 1600 gave him the other measurement. Juan Cano de Moctezuma wanted a tableau, and needed somebody to play Moctezuma; the man who took it was Tezozomoc, at least sixty, grandson of Moctezuma through his mother and grandnephew through his father. He rode through the streets on a canopied litter with dancers ahead of him, and the dancers could not do the old dances as well as people had at don Luis Cipac's wedding, so they improvised, and it worked.[^73] But it had been eighty years since the city fell. Almost nobody was left who could remember a celebration from before 1519, or who had heard one described by a parent. Antonio Valeriano, the best of the first generation of the friars' students, was going deaf and a little senile and needed a young man beside him for everything.[^74]

**What a person is.** A condition can now be inherited, and that is new. Before the Spaniards came, a slave's child was never a slave. Now it was settled that children followed the legal condition of the mother, so a woman's disaster reached her descendants forever. Chimalpahin recorded that his people got used to the idea that *in tliltique*, they who were black, were tied to slavery if born to an enslaved mother — living and working alongside them, sometimes resenting them, sometimes loving them, and almost never questioning the arrangement holding all of them.[^75] He notes that this would once have been unthinkable.

He also made up a word. The honorific *-tzin* in ordinary speech was less a mark of rank than of affection, so he wrote *in tliltzitzin*, something like the poor blacks. Strictly he should have written *in tlilticatzitzin*, but he had invented it himself and could do as he liked.[^76]

The colonial machinery worked the other way. *Cimarrón* had meant runaway cattle and other stray farm animals before it was shortened and applied to people.[^77]

**How people should relate.** By what you may wear and how many of you may live in one house. In April 1612 the criers read out that no black man was to carry a sword or wear a Spanish-style collar, no black woman was to wear a veil, and no household was to keep more than two black slaves — so the rest had to be sold. No sitting viceroy would have taken that much money off the richest men in the city; there was no viceroy, and lesser men were in charge. Guards went onto every road into the city in case the maroons came in to free their kin, and Chimalpahin could see them on the southern road from where he lived.[^78]

What made the Spaniards frightened enough to do it was a party. On Christmas Eve 1608 dozens of black residents had crowned a king and queen with paper crowns on decorated thrones and celebrated all night, which is normal in West Africa and normal at European carnival. The investigation could not prove that anyone had ever seriously meant to start an African monarchy.[^79]

**How you know.** Truth is what cannot be said falsely in front of the people who were there.

The best document Chimalpahin ever got hold of came through don Vicente, who had copied part of a book belonging to his father-in-law don Rodrigo, who had been Amaquemecan's scribe in the 1540s. In 1547 the five sections of that town were arguing about which of them should supply the ruler, and a judge was sent to settle it. So the noble elders held a great public meeting and each segment put forward its ancient statements, and don Rodrigo wrote them down. *What the elders sought to present was really a true account, just like it had been, because it was impossible to lie before the others.*[^80] The guarantee is the room.

Tezozomoc worked the same way from the other end. He held dozens of detailed Mexica genealogies in his head and in rolls of paper in boxes and baskets, he knew where the gaps were, and when he could not remember the name of somebody's third daughter or who she married, he said so instead of making something up.[^81] Chimalpahin, for his part, spent the last section of his great work explaining where every document had come from, because — as he put it — a scholar's readers might someday want to know, *so that you the reader, you who are Christian, may not doubt or waver.*[^82]

He also thought about his reader's ignorance. When he mentioned a god called Ome Tochtli, Two Rabbit, he knew a seventeenth-century reader might not know the name even if that reader was indigenous, so he told them to think back to their school days and compared him to Bacchus.[^83]

**What is worth having.** The record, and the promise attached to it. He and Tezozomoc made almost the same vow in almost the same words, both of them reaching for the old formula. *It will never be forgotten. It will always be preserved. We will preserve it, we who are the younger brothers, the children, grandchildren, great grandchildren and great great-grandchildren, we who are the hair, eyebrows, nails — the colour and the blood, we who are the descendants.*[^84]

And the small things, said plainly and without embarrassment: chicken's eggs, cow's milk, wax candles, and boxes with locks.[^85] Also the new music in the streets from Africa and Europe, and the colours on the silks off the Manila galleons.

He started the great history in 1608 and worked on it into the 1620s. He stopped keeping the record of current events in 1615.[^86]

*Read: lines 1668–1859.*
