## Ch. 9 — Epilogue

**Paying a workshop for an old-looking document.** By the second half of the eighteenth century virtually nobody could write a year-count history any more, or read one. When a village needed papers with the flavour of olden times to defend its land, it hired a workshop to produce them. The results were often very beautiful and were certainly indigenous, and they bore almost no resemblance to the histories that had actually been written.[^87]

**How you know.** That is the epilogue's centre, and it runs in two directions. Forged antiquity at one end; at the other, Nahuatl speakers today writing a Nahuatl-to-Nahuatl dictionary, because they do not want translation into a European language to be the only point of working with a Nahuatl text. They would rather do the thinking in the terms their own language allows.[^88]

**How people should relate.** The Crown built two republics — one for creole Spaniards, one for the indigenous, each governing itself, with the second contributing labour to the first.[^89] What eventually damaged indigenous identity was not that system but its abolition. After independence, with everyone suddenly equal before the law, it seemed backward to keep encouraging people to speak their own language. So a native person in court no longer got a translator. A parent could no longer say she preferred to educate her child in the old way. A village could no longer say it preferred to hold its land in common and let the chiefs allocate it — and if it wanted to prove title, it could go to court, in Spanish.[^90]

**What a person is.** Africans and Native Americans intermarried so extensively that the African phenotype was largely lost, and their descendants thought of themselves as largely Indian.[^91]

**What is worth having.** A story everybody wants to be true. Pilgrimages to the Virgin of Guadalupe became a full phenomenon in the mid-1600s, carrying the account that she had first appeared to an Indian called Juan Diego in 1528 on the edge of the city. That the story was recent did not matter to anyone, because rich and poor alike wanted it.[^92] At the end of the same century Sor Juana Inés de la Cruz wrote some of her poetry in Nahuatl. Her grammar was dreadful and she clearly never spoke it well, and her Spanish-speaking readers were delighted with it anyway.[^93]

**The shape of time.** The counting never stopped. Perhaps, say the poets, we have now started life under a Sixth Sun.[^97]

**What is real, and what makes things happen.** Not in the range read (lines 1860–1891). The epilogue is a survey of what became of a people and carries almost nothing on either — what it carries instead is the fate of their way of holding a record, which is where its weight sits.

*Read: lines 1860–1891.*

## Ch. 5 — Roads Not Taken `[SPECULATIVE]`

**A live alternative, argued by people the source names.** In Tlaxcala, with Maxixcatzin dying of smallpox and thousands of his people with him, the four kings' councils argued for twenty days about killing the Spaniards outright. The case for it was made in the room: these strangers were a plague of hungry grasshoppers who had turned up during a sickness, and their appetite for war had already cost hundreds of young Tlaxcalan lives. Against it came two arguments and a piece of intelligence. The first argument was experience — twenty-odd horses and a few hundred men had already done extraordinary damage. The second was doña Luisa's and Malintzin's, and it was about the future rather than the present: these are the advance party, thousands more are coming.[^10]

The road not taken was finishing the job in the twenty days when it was still possible. What makes it a real fork rather than a wish is that the losing side had the numbers and the moment, and lost on a forecast — one that turned out to be right.

## Ch. 5 — Counsel From Elsewhere `[SPECULATIVE]`

**A Stoic advisor on Moctezuma's rooftop speech.** The dichotomy of control divides what is yours from what is not: your judgement, your intention and the quality of your action are yours; your body, your property, your reputation and your command are not. See [[ARCHIVES/concepts/history/stoic-dichotomy-of-control|The Stoic Dichotomy of Control]]. It is not a counsel of withdrawal — Marcus wrote it while running an empire and a frontier war.

Read that way, Moctezuma is doing the thing exactly right and is punished for it precisely where the doctrine predicts. He assesses accurately, acts on the assessment, and loses the one thing the doctrine says was never his: reputation. His own words were pulled out of context for centuries afterwards to prove he was a coward interested in saving himself. A Stoic advisor would have told him that outcome was always outside his control and that the assessment was still correct — which is true, and which would not have kept a single warrior off the roof.

**A Kautilyan advisor on the same moment, and they diverge.** The *Arthashastra* reads a bonded confederacy as the hardest thing to beat and treats the strength of an enemy's internal cohesion as the first variable to attack. See [[LAB/Worldview Reports/trautmann-arthashastra-worldview-archaeology|What a Mauryan Statecraft Manual Took For Granted]]. From that seat, Moctezuma's error is not the assessment but the venue: he made the case for surrender in public, to everybody at once, including the young men whose entire function was to refuse it. The Kautilyan move is to make the same case privately, to the men who can be brought along, and to give the young warriors an errand somewhere else while it happens.

Where the two converge is worth naming. Neither says fight. Both say the war is lost. They split entirely on whether telling the truth in public is a duty or a blunder, and that split is the whole distance between a doctrine of the self and a doctrine of the state.

## Ch. 6 — What Transfers `[SPECULATIVE]`

**Negotiate the unit of measure, not the number.** Smoking Shield's first move under conquest was to send the messengers back to fix a basket size for the corn that both parties would recognise. The headline figure is what everybody argues about; the unit is what actually determines the burden, and it is usually settled by whoever cares enough to raise it. *Applies when* the obligation is recurring and denominated in something physical. *Fails* when the demand is in cash, which has no unit left to negotiate — which is exactly why the 1564 head tax broke Mexico City and this tribute did not break Cuauhtinchan.
*Decision type:* when to compromise a core value.

**A technology that survives its custodians will beat one that doesn't, even when it is worse at the job.** Glyph-writing carried more per mark and needed decades of training, so an epidemic took a generation of readers with it. Alphabetic writing carried less and could be learned in weeks by anybody. Don Alonso worked that out in a courtroom, watching his own words read back. *Applies when* the population holding the skill is itself at risk. *Fails* as a general rule — under stable conditions the expensive craft usually wins, which is why the trade-off is invisible until the crisis arrives.
*Decision type:* timing a bold move.

## Ch. 7 — Roads Not Taken `[SPECULATIVE]`

**A live alternative, proposed and refused in the room.** One protester, still out of jail, asked for a meeting with don Luis Cipac and the cabildo and put a plan to them. Two Mexica — one nobleman and one commoner — would stand up together and loudly refuse to pay. They would probably be executed. But the point would have been made in front of the Spanish authorities that the Mexica could not be pushed past a certain line, and that would give them pause and force them to readjust.[^94]

The council heard it out, looked at each other, and laughed harshly. *You propose that only two will die? When they have died, then you will die.*[^94]

What the proposal assumed is that the authorities were running a calculation about acceptable cost — that a demonstration of resolve is an input they would process. What the council knew, from forty years of watching, is that the calculation was about fear, and that a demonstration of resolve is an input that makes fear go up. The same misreading is why the two-martyr plan and the July riot both ended in the same place.

## Ch. 7 — What Transfers `[SPECULATIVE]`

**When an intermediary is squeezed from both ends, the squeezers will pay to have him blamed.** Valderrama's entire strategy in 1564 was to route the anger of the commoners onto don Luis Cipac rather than onto the tax: sponsor a lawsuit in a baker's name, release a convicted rioter to run the case when the baker vanishes, invite a jailed painter to draw the nobility's abuses. *Applies when* an unpopular demand has to be collected through a local authority who did not set it. *Fails* when the demand's origin is common knowledge — Ezmallin's *did anyone here order this? It came from Spain* is the counter-move, and it works because it is true and everybody already knew it.
*Decision type:* power consolidation.

**Positioning beats planning when you cannot predict the shock.** The strategic point is not to execute a brilliant sequence but to end up somewhere with more options than the other side has — see [[ARCHIVES/concepts/behavioral-mechanics/shih-and-strategic-depth|Shih and Strategic Depth]]. Between 1565 and 1567, with the Spaniards tearing each other apart, don Luis's people did not rebel. They ran a new census designed to show the head-count the tax was based on was too high given the recent epidemic deaths, and they widened the cabildo to let non-royal families sit on it.[^95] Neither is dramatic. Both left them with more places to stand.
*Decision type:* strategic retreat.

## Ch. 8 — Counsel From Elsewhere `[SPECULATIVE]`

**A Nahua archivist's own doctrine, applied to his own decision.** Writing history down is treated here as a form of resistance rather than of scholarship — see [[ARCHIVES/concepts/history/archive-as-resistance|Archive as Resistance]] and [[ARCHIVES/concepts/history/chimalpahin-annals-indigenous-historiography|Chimalpahin's Annals and Indigenous Historiography]]. On that reading, Chimalpahin stopping his record of current events in 1615 while carrying on with the ancient history until at least 1631 is the sharpest decision in the chapter, and the source offers two explanations and settles on neither: perhaps there was not time and energy for both, perhaps the present was depressing and the past was energising.[^86]

A third reading is available from his own practice. His method needed the guarantee he named himself — that a true account is one nobody in the room can contradict. The ancient history had that: elders speaking in turn in front of each other in 1547, transcribed. The current events did not, and by 1612 he had watched the same procedure run in reverse, with thirty-five people confessing to a plot that had not happened because the alternative was more water. A man whose test for truth is the room stops writing when the room is the basement of the High Court.

**An advisor on equanimity, and where it runs out.** Composure under pressure is treated in this vault as an operational asset rather than a temperament — see [[ARCHIVES/concepts/behavioral-mechanics/equanimity-as-operational-advantage|Equanimity as Operational Advantage]]. Chimalpahin had it, visibly: he could watch Spaniards keep vigil all night over a rumour started by a practical joker or some roving pigs, and find it funny that they were being destroyed by their own fear and did not look like such great warriors after all.[^96] That detachment is what let him keep working for thirty years in a church at the city gate.

It is also what the column of fourteen names breaks. The list is the one thing he wrote that has no composure in it, and it is the only sanction he had.

## Ch. 8 — What Transfers `[SPECULATIVE]`

**A record that names the officials outlasts one that describes the injustice.** He did not write an indictment. He wrote down who signed. *Applies when* you have no enforcement and a long time horizon — a name attached to an act is the cheapest durable sanction there is. *Fails* where the record itself can be destroyed, and fails completely where the officials are anonymous by design, which is the countermeasure.
*Decision type:* when to compromise a core value.

# What Runs Through All of It — Fifth Sun

> **Closing pass across all nine chapter runs of Camilla Townsend, *Fifth Sun: A New History of the Aztecs*.** Read from `RAW/books/The Fifth Sun-A New History of the Aztecs.md`, chapters 1–8 and the Epilogue. Written last, out of the finished runs.
>
> **Siblings:** [[LAB/Worldview Reports/camilla-townsend-fifth-sun-worldview-archaeology-part-1|Part 1 — Chapters 1–4]] · [[LAB/Worldview Reports/camilla-townsend-fifth-sun-worldview-archaeology-part-2|Part 2 — Chapters 5–8 and the Epilogue]] · thread map: [[LAB/Threads/camilla-townsend-fifth-sun-threads|The Explanation You Adopt When You Lose]]
>
> ⚠ **Supersedes** [[LAB/Worldview Reports/camilla-townsend-fifth-sun-worldview-archaeology|the original whole-book report]], which was built from vault concept pages rather than from chapters.

*Source ingest: [[ARCHIVES/sources/camilla-townsend-fifth-sun|Camilla Townsend, Fifth Sun: A New History of the Aztecs]]*

---

## What Runs Through All of It

Unpleasant jobs get handed round so that nobody carries one forever. That is the deep structure here, and it turns up in eight chapters out of nine. Tasks were shared so that no one group would have to handle something unpleasant all the time, or hold unlimited power all the time. The chieftainship alternates between lineages. Itzcoatl and Moctezuma turn that into a three-generation schedule. Cuauhtinchan's thirty service workers rotate their duty among themselves however they like, and Mexico City's wards are still rotating the public chores along the old calpolli lines in 1564. When the tax finally has to be collected house by house, the four quarters each send a speaker to the meeting, in turn.

The one place the rotation stops is the head. Tenochtitlan formalised it at scale for everybody else and kept the top of the arrangement for itself, permanently. That exception is what Chalco's young men are complaining about in 1479, and what Tlatelolco goes to war about in 1473.

A person is their mother's child, and that fact carries the political weight all the way to the end. No primogeniture, no word for illegitimate, a slave's son who becomes high king. Then the same fact turned over: half-brothers by different mothers with their mothers' home towns standing behind them, which is how a succession becomes a civil war three separate times. Rearranging your wives is how you make a public announcement, and everybody reads it correctly.

One thing reverses completely across the book, and it is whether a condition can be inherited. Chapter 2 states the old rule and gives the reason with it: a slave's child was never a slave, because if the condition were heritable, towns would fill with slaves in a few generations and come apart. Chapter 8 records the new one — children follow the legal condition of the mother, so a woman's disaster reaches her descendants forever — and notes that this would once have been unthinkable. Nothing else in the book turns over that far.

Honour needs an audience, and every person in this book knows it. Shield Flower waits to start screaming until her own people arrive. The Chalcans sing a protest a king can dance to instead of punishing. Moctezuma cannot afford to look weak in front of the allies, which is the whole reason he lets the strangers in. The Chontal lords sue for peace not because they cannot fight but because everyone in their world will hear what the fight cost them. Don Martín keeps his mouth shut on the rack, and by dawn the whole city is talking about it. The one figure with no audience left is don Luis Cipac, fighting an imaginary enemy on a roof in the middle of the night, and he is the one who breaks.

Truth, in this world, is what several people will say in front of each other. The bards disagreed about Shield Flower and the disagreement was kept. Court performances moved between the perspectives of the different parts of the altepetl, twisting the strands into one. The writers of 1564 took statements from men of different neighbourhoods because no single person could give a full account of an important moment. Don Rodrigo transcribed all five segments of Amaquemecan in 1547, and Chimalpahin's verdict on that document sixty years later is that it had to be true, *because it was impossible to lie before the others.*

Set against that, three chapters running, is the procedure that gets a single confident answer out of one isolated person. Every Spanish nobleman on the rack confessed and named names, and none of it was true. Thirty-five black men and women said yes to whatever their torturers fed them and were hanged for it. The book never lines those two methods up and says so. Read by chapter, they sit four pages apart.

Itzcoatl's bonfire and Chimalpahin's list are the same instrument pointed opposite ways. One man burns the record so that a story he does not want cannot be told. The other writes down fourteen names so that a story nobody will prosecute cannot be lost. Both are betting that what stays on paper decides what people are able to say later, and the book's last movement is the second bet paying off — badly, slowly, and only after three centuries in somebody else's cupboard.

The book's own answer to why they lost arrives twice, from two different heights. The old warriors, asked directly, said metal and the speed of news, and gave away nothing on merit or intelligence. Their grandchildren, forty years on, took the omens and the returning god out of the friars' library because they needed an explanation that was not inferiority and nobody had given them the real one. Chapter 4 supplies what would have relieved them: ten thousand years of full-time farming against three thousand, Renaissance Europe meeting the Sumerians. **The grandfathers had the better answer and the grandchildren wrote the one that stuck.**

## Which dimensions the book never reached

What these people thought was real gets thinner as the book proceeds, and that is a fact about the sources rather than about the people. Chapter 2 says why. Under Spanish rule the Nahuas could write openly about history, and it was dangerous to write about the gods. So the gods reach us as names carrying a range of possible traits, rather than as a world somebody has described from inside it. Four collapsed suns, the fire at Teotihuacan, the debt you pay by bleeding yourself — all of that sits in chapters 1 and 2, and then it goes quiet and stays quiet for six chapters.

Nothing in any chapter reports what an ordinary farming family outside the tribute lists believed about anything. The book is honest about this. The epilogue counts the indigenous who stayed in their villages in the millions, still speaking their own languages and organising their minds at least partly along the old lines, and it makes no claim to know what was in them. Every run above is drawn from people who wrote, sang, ruled, or were killed in front of witnesses. That is a narrow seam, and it is the only one there is.

The epilogue itself reaches almost none of the seven. Not in the range read (lines 1860–1891): what is real, and what makes things happen. It is a survey of what became of a people and of their way of holding a record. That is what it carries, and it carries it well — the workshops selling old-looking documents, the Nahuatl-to-Nahuatl dictionary, the story of Juan Diego that everybody wanted to be true.

## Where two chapters pull against each other

Chapter 5's Moctezuma and chapter 7's don Luis Cipac are the same man in the same trap, and the book treats them differently. Both are rulers who work out accurately that resistance will destroy their people, say so, and are hated for saying it. Moctezuma gets a full defence: the old histories and prayers are clear that a ruler's paramount duty was to save lives, and that a ruler who committed his people to an unwinnable war was the lowest of the low. Cipac gets a nickname, Mushroom Alligator, loses the honorific from his name, and beats an old woman in the street. The doctrine that exonerates the first is never applied to the second by anybody in either chapter.

Chapter 2's Flower Wars and chapter 5's Tlaxcalan council are the same decision at forty years' distance. The Mexica left Tlaxcala standing because taking it would have cost too much, and dressed the retreat up as ceremony. In 1520 the four Tlaxcalan kings spent twenty days deciding whether to finish the Spaniards, and let them live on a forecast that thousands more were coming. Both are a stronger party declining a war it could probably win. Only one of them turned out to be the mistake, and the reason is visible only from the far end.

## What the by-chapter reading recovered

The nine runs surfaced material that a merged reading of this book deletes, because it appears once and does not come back. The calendar's five blank days and the reputation of a year called One Rabbit. The burden bearer paddling water vats round the edge of the town for the rest of his life. The market's canoes of collected urine. The joke that the stars look like popcorn. The pun on *noble beasts*. The basket size negotiated for the corn tribute. The invented word *in tliltzitzin*. The two jaguars shipped to Spain on 26 April 1592, and the grasshoppers that arrived at exactly four o'clock.

None of those recur. Several of them are the sharpest thing in their chapter. A merged reading keeps what a book repeats, and what a book repeats is usually what its author already knew going in.

# What the Buddhist Kingdoms Took For Granted — Chapters I–XIII

> **Chapters I–XIII of Fa-hien, *A Record of Buddhistic Kingdoms*, in James Legge's translation** — Ch'ang-gan to Nagara, across the Gobi, the Onion range and the Indus. Read from `RAW/books/A Record of Buddhist Kingdoms.md`. One full archaeology pass per chapter, sweeping all seven dimensions in every run.
>
> **Siblings:** [[LAB/Worldview Reports/faxian-worldview-archaeology-part-2|Part 2 — Chapters XIV–XXVI]] · [[LAB/Worldview Reports/faxian-worldview-archaeology-part-3|Part 3 — Chapters XXVII–XL]] · [[LAB/Worldview Reports/faxian-worldview-archaeology-synthesis|What Runs Through All of It]]. No sibling thread map exists for this source yet.
>
> ⚠ **Supersedes** [[LAB/Worldview Reports/faxian-worldview-archaeology|the original whole-book report]], which merged the whole journey into one account. What changed: the chapter-by-chapter reading recovers the local rules — three days' hospitality, eight seals, the wheat, the bowl — that a merged reading treats as colour.
>
> **A note on the text**. Everything cited here is Fa-hien's own narrative. Legge's footnotes are a nineteenth-century scholar's commentary and are not the worldview of anybody inside the source; where a note is used it is named as Legge's.

*Source ingest: [[ARCHIVES/sources/faxian-record-of-buddhist-kingdoms|Fa-hien, A Record of Buddhistic Kingdoms]]*

---

## Ch. I — From Ch'ang-gan to the sandy desert

**A man sets out because the rule-book is wrong**. Fa-hien was living in Ch'ang-gan and deploring the mutilated and imperfect state of the collection of the Books of Discipline. So he made an agreement with four other monks that they would go to India and fetch the Disciplinary Rules.[^1] That is the whole motive, stated in one sentence, and nothing else in forty chapters displaces it.

**What is worth having**. An accurate copy of the monastic code, at the price of the rest of your life. Not a teaching, not a vision, not a relic — the rules for how the order runs its internal and external business. Everything he goes on to see is seen by a man who set out for a legal document.

**What is real**. The desert has demons in it, and they are listed alongside the distances. The prefect of T'un-hwang supplied the means of crossing a waste in which there are many evil demons and hot winds, and travellers who meet them perish to a man.[^2] The demons get exactly the same grammar as the wind. Neither is a metaphor and neither needs an argument.

**How you know where you are going**. By the dead. *There is not a bird to be seen in the air above, nor an animal on the ground below. Though you look all round most earnestly to find where you can cross, you know not where to make your choice, the only mark and indication being the dry bones of the dead*.[^2] The route exists because people died on it in a line.

**The shape of time**. The year has a fixed stopping place in it. They stopped for the summer retreat at K'een-kwei, went on when it was over, and passed another retreat with the enlarged company before resuming.[^3] Travel is what happens between retreats, and the calendar of the order, not the season or the road, decides when a journey pauses.

**How people should relate**. A king houses you and it has a name. The king of Chang-yih found the country too disturbed for the roads to be used, kept the party in his capital, and acted the part of their *danapati* — their donor-host, the man who supplies what a monk may not earn.[^4] The relation is not charity and not hospitality in general; it is a defined role with a word for it, and kings take it up.

**What a person is**. Somebody who has quitted their family, and who travels in company. The party keeps growing and splitting by name — Che-yen, Hwuy-keen, Sang-shao, Pao-yun, Sang-king join, and then Fa-hien and four others start ahead in the suite of an envoy while the rest wait.[^3] Nobody in this book travels as an individual until the others are dead or turned back.

**What makes things happen**. Disturbance in a country closes the roads. That is the first causal statement in the book and it is entirely political: the country was so much disturbed that travelling was impossible.[^4] The demons are in the desert; the obstacle in the settled world is other men's wars.

*Read: lines 228–239.*

---

## Ch. II — On to Shen-shen and thence to Khoten

**Seventeen days, about fifteen hundred li, and a country with a thin barren soil**. The clothes of the common people are coarse and like those worn in the land of Han — some felt, some coarse serge or haircloth — and that was the only difference he saw.[^5]

**How people should relate — and what the whole journey turns on**. The rules of India are practised by everybody here, commoners and monks alike, only the monks do it more exactly and the laymen more loosely.[^5] Same rules, different exactness. That is the model he carries all the way to Ceylon, and it means he never once describes a foreign practice as a foreign practice. He describes it as this one done well or done slackly.

**How you know**. A shared book language across kingdoms that cannot speak to each other. Each kingdom had its own peculiar barbarous speech, and the monks, who had given up the worldly life, were all students of Indian books and the Indian language.[^5] A man from Ch'ang-gan can walk fifteen hundred li into a place whose speech is unintelligible to him and be understood by four thousand men there, because they all learned the same texts. That is the infrastructure the whole book runs on, stated once and never remarked upon again.

**What a person is**. Somebody measurable by how strictly they keep the code. At Woo-e the monks were so strict that sramans from Ts'in were all unprepared for their regulations.[^6] Fa-hien does not say the Woo-e monks were wrong or that his own were lax. He records that his party did not know the local standard and could not meet it.

**What is worth having, and what its absence costs**. Propriety and righteousness owed to strangers. The people of Woo-e neglected these duties and treated the travellers so meanly that Che-yen, Hwuy-keen and Hwuy-wei turned back towards Kao-ch'ang, hoping to find the means of continuing from there.[^6] A failure of hospitality is what breaks the party — not the desert, not the mountains.

**What makes things happen**. One man's liberality. Fa-hien and the rest went straight on south-west only through the liberality of Foo Kung-sun, the guest-master, who had already got them two months in the monastery.[^6] The journey proceeds from named individual to named individual, and stalls when one of them fails.

**What is real, and the shape of time**. Nothing on either beyond the counting — seventeen days, fifteen hundred li, more than four thousand monks, a month here, a month and five days of uninhabited country in which the difficulties and sufferings were unparalleled in human experience.[^6] The chapter's whole content is the social gradient above.

*Read: lines 280–285.*

---

## Ch. III — Khoten. Processions of images. The king's new monastery.

**Houses standing apart like separate stars, each with a tope in front of the door**. The smallest of them twenty cubits high or rather more.[^7] That is what devotion looks like from the road: not a temple in the middle of a town but a monument at every doorway, and the smallest one still three times the height of a man.

**How people should relate**. A room is kept ready for a monk who has not arrived. They make rooms in the monasteries for monks from all quarters, and the use of them is given to travelling monks who turn up, who are provided with whatever else they require.[^7] The infrastructure is built for strangers in advance, which is the only reason a journey like this one is possible at all.

**What a person is — and it is audible**. Three thousand monks at Gomati are called to meals by a bell. They enter with a reverent gravity, take their seats in regular order, and keep a perfect silence. No sound comes from the alms-bowls or the other utensils. When one of them wants food he is not allowed to call out for it; he makes signs with his hands.[^8] A trained man is one whose meal makes no noise.

**How people should relate, at the top**. The king takes his crown off in the street. When the image-car is a hundred paces from the gate, he puts off his crown of state, changes into a fresh suit, goes out barefoot with flowers and incense in his hands and two rows of followers behind him, and does homage at the image's feet with his head and face bowed to the ground.[^9] The queen and her ladies are up in the gallery over the gate scattering flowers that float down and land anywhere.

**What is worth having, and where the money goes**. Of whatever things of highest value the kings of the six countries east of the range possess, they contribute the greater portion to the King's New Monastery and use only a small portion themselves.[^10] Not a tithe. The greater portion.

**The shape of time**. The monastery took eighty years to build and ran across three reigns.[^10] Two of the three kings who paid for it never saw it. The procession works the other way — it begins on the first day of the fourth month and ends on the fourteenth, one monastery's car per day, and then the king and queen go back inside.[^9]

**What is real, and what makes things happen**. Not directly in the range read (lines 322–338). What the chapter carries instead is precedence: the Gomati monks, being mahayana students and held in great reverence by the king, took the first day of the procession ahead of all the others.[^9] Which school you belong to decides what day you go.

*Read: lines 322–338.*

---

## Ch. IV — Through the Onion mountains to K'eeh-ch'a

**A man leaves the party to follow a stranger**. Sang-shao, by himself alone, followed a Tartar who was an earnest follower of the Law, and went off towards Kophene.[^11] No discussion is recorded and no objection. Shared observance is enough to travel with somebody, and the party is not a unit anyone is obliged to stay in.

**How people should relate**. A king's standing is quoted in monks. The king of Tsze-hoh was a strenuous follower of the Law and had around him more than a thousand monks, mostly students of the mahayana.[^11] That is the whole description of the man. Across forty chapters this is the standard form: what a ruler is, is a number and a school.

**The shape of time**. The retreat again decides the itinerary. Twenty-five days to Tsze-hoh, fifteen days there, four days south into the Ts'ung-ling mountains, then a halt at Yu-hwuy to keep the retreat, and only when it was over another twenty-five days among the hills to K'eeh-ch'a, where they found Hwuy-king and his two companions waiting.[^11]

**Everything else**. Not in the range read (lines 386–389). The chapter is a stage of a road, and what it carries is the counting and the two facts above.

*Read: lines 386–389.*

---

## Ch. V — The great quinquennial assembly

**A king gives everything away and then buys it back**. The *pancha parishad* falls every five years. The king requests the presence of the sramans from every quarter of his kingdom, and they come as if in clouds. The place of session is grandly decorated: silken streamers and canopies hung out, water-lilies made in gold and silver and fixed up behind the seats of the chief men, clean mats spread. Then the king and his ministers present their offerings according to rule and law.[^12]

Then it goes further. He exhorts the ministers to make other and special offerings, and the doing of this runs one, two, three, five, or even seven days. When that is finished he takes his own riding-horse, saddles and bridles it and waits on it himself, and has the noblest and most important minister in the kingdom mount it. Then he distributes fine white woollen cloth, all sorts of precious things, and the articles the sramans require, uttering vows along with all his ministers as he does it. **And when the distribution has taken place, he again redeems whatever he wishes from the monks**.[^13]

**What is worth having**. The giving, not the goods. The circuit is closed on purpose: the property leaves and comes back, and what stays behind is the vow and the fact that everybody watched. A king who wanted to be poorer could simply stay poorer. This king wants the transfer to have happened.

**What makes things happen**. Monks ripen wheat. The country is high and cold and only the wheat comes on. After the monks have taken their annual portion of it the mornings suddenly show hoar-frost — so the king always begs the monks to make the wheat ripen before they take their share.[^14] The request is made to the men, not to a god, and it is made as a matter of agricultural scheduling.

**How people should relate**. The lay world underwrites the order and gets the harvest for it. That is the exchange the whole system rests on, and here it is stated as a bargain with a deadline.

**What is real**. Buddha's stone spittoon is in the country, the colour of his alms-bowl, and a tooth of his, over which a tope has been reared with more than a thousand monks and disciples attached to it.[^15] A spittoon is listed in the same breath as a tooth and neither is remarked on. The category is *things he touched*, and it has no floor.

**What a person is**. The rules observed by the sramans here are remarkable and too numerous to be mentioned in detail.[^15] That is the one place in the book where Fa-hien, who came for the rules, says there were too many to write down.

**The shape of time, and everything else**. Five years between assemblies; one, two, three, five or seven days of special offering; the assembly in the first, second or third month, mostly in spring.[^12] Nothing in the range read (lines 412–421) on what a person is beyond the line above, or on how you know.

*Read: lines 412–421.*

---

## Ch. VI — On towards North India. Darada. The image of Maitreya.

**Dragons that spit poisonous wind**. The snow rests on the Onion mountains winter and summer. Among them are venomous dragons which, when provoked, spit forth poisonous winds and cause showers of snow and storms of sand and gravel — and not one in ten thousand who meets these dangers escapes with his life. The people of the country call the range the Snow mountains.[^16]

**What is real**. A weather system with a temper. The dragons are provoked, which means the danger is relational rather than random, and the local name for the range records only the snow. Fa-hien reports both the explanation and the plain name and does not choose between them.

**How you know what a being looks like when he is not here**. You go and look, and you go three times. An arhan of that kingdom took a clever artificer up to the Tushita heaven by his supernatural power, to see the height, complexion and appearance of Maitreya Bodhisattva, and then come back and make an image of him in wood. First and last, this was done three times, and then the image was completed — eighty cubits high and eight cubits across at the base, knee to knee.[^17]

Three trips. The craftsman did not get it right the first time or the second, and the fix each time was another journey to check. That is a working method, and it treats a heaven as a place you can return to with a question.

**What is worth having**. An image accurate enough that kings compete over it. On fast-days it emits light, and the kings of the surrounding countries vie with one another in presenting offerings to it. *Here it is — to be seen now as of old*.[^17]

**How people should relate, and what makes things happen**. Not in the range read (lines 442–449) beyond the competition between kings above. The chapter carries the mountains and the image.

**What a person is, and the shape of time**. A month on the way to get across the range; the image standing unchanged from then to now.[^17] The one anthropological fact is the arhan's supernatural power, which is stated as a capacity a man can have and used for transport.

*Read: lines 442–449.*

---

## Ch. VII — Crossing the Indus

**Seven hundred ladders down a wall of rock**. The way ran along a bank exceedingly precipitous, a hill-like wall of rock ten thousand cubits from the base. When you approach the edge your eyes become unsteady, and if you wanted to go forward there was no place to put your foot. Beneath were the waters of the Indus. In former times men had chiselled paths along the rocks and distributed ladders on the face of them, seven hundred of them altogether, and at the bottom a suspension bridge of ropes crossed the river where the banks are eighty paces apart.[^18]

**What makes things happen**. Somebody built it. Fa-hien's account of the crossing is entirely an account of earlier labour, and he checks it against the record: the place and its arrangements are in the Records of the Nine Interpreters, but neither Chang K'een nor Kan Ying had reached the spot.[^19] The two most famous Chinese travellers west did not get this far, and he says so without comment.

**How you know — and this is the chapter's centre**. The monks asked Fa-hien when the Law of Buddha first went east. His answer is a chain of custody, and he names every link in it. *When I asked the people of those countries about it, they all said that it had been handed down by their fathers from of old that, after the setting up of the image of Maitreya Bodhisattva, there were Sramans of India who crossed this river, carrying with them Sutras and Books of Discipline*.[^20]

Then he dates it, and he dates it twice. The image was set up rather more than three hundred years after the nirvana, which may be referred to the reign of king P'ing of the Chow dynasty.[^20] One event, fixed in the Buddhist count and again in the Chinese dynastic count, so that a man from either world can find it.

**Who is the authority**. The Indian monks ask the Chinese one. He is standing at the western edge of the road his own religion came down, and the men who live there put the question to him because he has just walked its whole length.

**What makes things happen, at the largest scale**. Not men. *We know of a truth that the opening of the way for such a mysterious propagation is not the work of man; and so the dream of the emperor Ming of Han had its proper cause*.[^20] He has just given a fully human account — an image, some sramans, a river, some books — and then says the opening of the way was not human work. Both stand.

**What is worth having**. Sutras and Books of Discipline, carried across on foot, which is what the men in his own story were doing and what he is doing now.

**What is real, what a person is, the shape of time**. Not in the range read (lines 468–475), except as the dating above supplies it: three hundred years, a Chinese reign, and a dream.

*Read: lines 468–475.*

---

## Ch. VIII — Woo-chang, or Udyana

**Three days, and then find your own bed**. There are five hundred sangharamas in Woo-chang. When stranger bhikshus arrive at one of them their wants are supplied for three days, after which they are told to find a resting-place for themselves.[^21]

**How people should relate**. Hospitality with a number on it. Nothing in the chapter suggests the limit is resented or apologised for. It is the rule, it is uniform across five hundred houses, and it is exactly the thing a man planning a fifteen-year journey needs to know. Three days is also long enough to rest and short enough that nobody settles.

**What is real**. A footprint that changes size depending on who is looking at it. Buddha left a print of his foot here which is long or short according to the ideas of the beholder — and it exists, and the same thing is true about it, at the present day.[^22] Also the rock where he dried his clothes, fourteen cubits high and more than twenty broad, with one side smooth, and the place where he converted the wicked dragon.

The footprint and the rock are given in the same sentence and the rock is measured. One object behaves according to the viewer and the other has dimensions, and Fa-hien records both the same way. He does not mark the difference, which means he does not think there is one worth marking.

**What a person is**. Somebody who uses the language of Central India and eats and dresses as they do there. That is his entire description of the people, and it is a statement about connection rather than about character.[^21]

**How people relate, when the party splits again**. Hwuy-king, Hwuy-tah and Tao-ching went on ahead towards Buddha's shadow in Nagara; Fa-hien and the others stayed in Woo-chang and kept the summer retreat, and went south afterwards.[^23] Splitting up to cover ground is normal, and the retreat is why they split.

**What makes things happen, how you know, what is worth having, the shape of time**. Not in the range read (lines 508–515), except the retreat setting the schedule again.

*Read: lines 508–515.*

---

## Ch. IX — Soo-ho-to. The legend of Buddha.

**A hawk, a dove, and a man cutting a piece out of himself**. Sakra, ruler of the devas, tried the Bodhisattva in a former age by producing a hawk in pursuit of a dove — and the Bodhisattva cut off a piece of his own flesh and with it ransomed the dove.[^24]

**What is worth having**. A weight of your own flesh, weighed against a bird. The transaction is exact: a ransom, not a rescue. The hawk is owed something and gets it.

**How you know this happened here**. Because he came back and said so. After Buddha had attained to perfect wisdom, travelling about with his disciples, he arrived at this spot and informed them that this was the place where he ransomed the dove with a piece of his own flesh. *In this way the people of the country became aware of the fact, and on the spot reared a tope*, adorned with layers of gold and silver plates.[^24]

That is the mechanism behind hundreds of the sites in this book, stated once and plainly. The place did not remember; a man returned and identified it, and the marker went up afterwards.

**What is real**. A test set by a god who manufactures the situation. Sakra produced the hawk. The dove was not in danger until somebody arranged for it to be, which makes the whole thing an examination with a real cost attached.

**How people should relate, what a person is, what makes things happen, the shape of time**. Not in the range read (lines 534–537). The chapter is one story, and everything in it sits on the two dimensions above.

*Read: lines 534–537.*

---

## Ch. X — Gandhara. Legends of Buddha.

**A man gave his eyes away here**. When Buddha was a Bodhisattva he gave his eyes also for another man in Gandhara, and at the spot they have reared a large tope adorned with layers of gold and silver plates.[^25]

**What is worth having**. The word doing the work is *also*. Flesh in the last chapter, eyes in this one, the head and the whole body in the next. Fa-hien is walking through a landscape organised by what the Bodhisattva gave up at each stop, and the sites come in the order the road takes them rather than in the order the stories happened.

**How people should relate**. The place where Dharmavivardhana, the son of Asoka, ruled.[^25] A kingdom is located by naming who governed it, and the man named is a king's son placed here by his father — which is how Asoka's administration reaches into this book, as geography.

**What a person is**. The people of the country were mostly students of the hinayana.[^25] The census is doctrinal, as it is everywhere.

**What is real, how you know, what makes things happen, the shape of time**. Not in the range read (lines 554–555). Five days east from the last stop, and that is the whole chapter.

*Read: lines 554–555.*

---

## Ch. XI — Takshasila. The four great topes.

**A kingdom named after a decapitation**. Takshasila means "the severed head" in the language of China. Here, when Buddha was a Bodhisattva, he gave away his head to a man, and from this circumstance the kingdom got its name.[^26]

**What is real**. The name of a place is a record of what happened in it. Not a commemoration added afterwards but the name itself, in daily use by people buying and selling. Two days further east is the place where the Bodhisattva threw down his body to feed a starving tigress.[^27]

**What is worth having**. The giving series finishes here — flesh, eyes, head, whole body — and the fourth item is spent on an animal that was going to die anyway.

**How people should relate**. Competitive giving, and it never stops. Large topes have been built at both places, adorned with layers of all the precious substances, and the kings, ministers and peoples of the surrounding kingdoms vie with one another in making offerings at them. *The trains of those who come to scatter flowers and light lamps at them never cease*.[^27]

The verb is the same one used of the kings competing over the Maitreya image. Devotion between rulers is a contest with an audience, and the traffic on the road is continuous. Flowers and lamps are what the contest is scored in, and both burn out, so it has to be paid again tomorrow.

**What makes things happen, how you know, what a person is, the shape of time**. Not in the range read (lines 570–576), beyond the seven days' journey and the two days' journey that place the sites.

*Read: lines 570–576.*

---

## Ch. XII — Purushapura. King Kanishka's tope and Buddha's alms-bowl.

**A herd-boy building a tope in the road**. Buddha told Ananda that after his pari-nirvana there would be a king named Kanishka who would build a tope on this spot. Kanishka was afterwards born into the world, and once, when he had gone out to look about him, Sakra, ruler of the devas, wanting to put the idea into his head, took the appearance of a little herd-boy and made a tope right in the king's way. The king asked what sort of thing he was making. The boy said, *I am making a tope for Buddha*. The king said, *very good* — and immediately reared another one right over the boy's, more than four hundred cubits high and adorned with layers of all the precious substances.[^28]

**What makes things happen**. A prophecy, and then a god arranging for it to come true. Neither is treated as making the other redundant. Kanishka is prophesied, born, prompted by a disguised deity, and then does it himself, and the story keeps all four steps.

**And the joke at the end**. When the king's tope was finished, the little tope of the boy came out from its side on the south, rather more than three cubits in height.[^28] The four-hundred-cubit monument cannot cover the three-cubit one. The small thing extrudes.

**What is worth having, and who is allowed to have it**. Buddha's alms-bowl is in this country. A king of Yueh-she raised a large force, invaded, and subdued the kingdom, wanting to carry the bowl away — and he and his captains were sincere believers, so they made offerings on a great scale first. Then he had a large elephant grandly caparisoned and the bowl placed on it, and the elephant knelt down on the ground and could not go forward. He had a four-wheeled waggon prepared and the bowl put in it, and eight elephants yoked to it dragged with their united strength and could not move it either.[^29]

*The king knew that the time for an association between himself and the bowl had not yet arrived, and was sad and deeply ashamed of himself*. So he built a tope and a monastery at the place and left a guard to watch the bowl, making all sorts of contributions.[^29]

**What is real**. An object with an opinion about who owns it, and a conqueror who accepts the verdict. He had already won the war. Eight elephants is not a failure of force; it is a ruling, and he reads it as one, and his response is shame rather than another attempt.

**How you know a thing's capacity**. By who is filling it. The bowl holds rather more than two pecks, is of various colours with black predominating, has the seams of its fourfold composition distinctly marked, is about a fifth of an inch thick and has a bright glossy lustre.[^30] Then: when poor people throw in a few flowers it becomes immediately full, while very rich people wishing to offer many flowers might not stop till they had thrown in hundreds, thousands and myriads of bushels, and would still not be able to fill it.

The measurements are given first, precisely, and then the rule that overrides them. Both are reported as facts about the same object. A fifth of an inch thick and two pecks deep, and a rich man could pour bushels into it all day.

**The shape of time, daily**. Near midday they bring the bowl out and, along with the common people, make their various offerings to it, and then take their midday meal. In the evening, at the time of incense, they bring it out again.[^30] More than seven hundred monks are attached to it.

**What a person is — and here the party comes apart**. Pao-yun and Sang-king made their offerings to the bowl and then resolved to go back. Hwuy-king, Hwuy-tah and Tao-ching had gone ahead to Nagara; Hwuy-king fell ill there and Tao-ching stayed to look after him, while Hwuy-tah came on alone to Purushapura, saw the others, and turned back to Ts'in with Pao-yun and Sang-king. **Hwuy-king came to his end in the monastery of Buddha's alms-bowl**. And on this Fa-hien went forward alone towards the flat-bone of Buddha's skull.[^31]

Five men leave the story in one paragraph. Three go home, one stays behind to nurse the sick, and one dies in the monastery of the alms-bowl. The sentence that follows is the first in the book with nobody else in it.

**How people should relate**. By staying with the sick man. Tao-ching's decision is recorded in four words and never praised.

*Read: lines 584–593.*

## Ch. XIII — Nagara. The festival of the skull-bone, and the shadow.

**Eight men, eight seals, one door**. The king of Nagara reveres the flat-bone of Buddha's skull and is anxious it might be stolen. So he has selected eight individuals, representing the eight great families in the kingdom, and given each of them a seal, with which he seals the shrine and guards the relic. At early dawn the eight men come, each inspects his own seal, and then they open the door.[^32]

**How people should relate**. Security by splitting the key between the families who would otherwise be the ones to take it. No guard, no wall — eight men who each have to look at their own mark in front of the other seven, every morning, forever. The families' rivalry is the lock.

**What the morning looks like**. They wash their hands with scented water and bring the bone out, and place it outside the vihara on a lofty platform, supported on a round pedestal of the seven precious substances and covered with a bell of lapis lazuli, both adorned with rows of pearls. It is yellowish-white, and forms an imperfect circle twelve inches round, curving upwards to the centre. The keepers climb a high gallery and beat great drums, blow conchs and clash copper cymbals. When the king hears them he comes, and makes his offerings of flowers and incense.[^32]

**What a person is, in the moment**. Each of them in order raises the bone, places it for a moment on the top of their heads, and departs — going out by the west door, having come in by the east.[^32] One-way traffic, so the line does not meet itself.

**The shape of a day, and it is the same shape for everyone**. *The king every morning makes his offerings and performs his worship, and afterwards gives audience on the business of his government*. The chiefs of the Vaisyas also make their offerings before they attend to their family affairs.[^33] Relic first, then government. Relic first, then the shop. The order is identical at the top and in the middle of society, and it is stated as a matter of course.

**What makes things happen**. A robe brings rain. It is a custom of the country, when there is a great drought, for the people to collect in crowds, bring out Buddha's Sanghali, pay worship to it and make offerings — on which there is immediately a great rain from the sky.[^34] No conditions, no failures reported.

There is also his pewter staff in a wooden tube, sixteen or seventeen cubits long, made of Gosirsha Chandana, and though a hundred or a thousand men were to try to lift it they could not move it.[^35] Same rule as the alms-bowl: the object decides.

**How you know — and the one thing in the book that cannot be copied**. South of the city, half a yojana, there is a rock-cavern in a great hill fronting south-west, and here Buddha left his shadow. *Looking at it from a distance of more than ten paces, you seem to see Buddha's real form, with his complexion of gold, and his characteristic marks in their nicety clearly and brightly displayed. The nearer you approach, however, the fainter it becomes, as if it were only in your fancy*.[^36]

Kings from all the regions around have sent skilful artists to take a copy and none of them has been able to. Set that beside chapter VI, where an artificer went up to a heaven three times and came back with an eighty-cubit Maitreya that everybody could see. There the method worked and here it does not, and the same trade is doing the looking both times. The saying current among the people of the country is that *the thousand Buddhas must all leave their shadows here*.[^36]

**What is worth having**. A model. Four hundred paces west of the shadow, Buddha shaved his hair and clipped his nails and built a tope with his disciples, seventy or eighty cubits high, *to be a model for all future topes* — and it is still standing, with a monastery of more than seven hundred monks beside it and as many as a thousand topes of arhans and pratyeka buddhas around it.[^37]

**What is real**. A place that does not move. The vihara stands in a square of thirty paces, and *though heaven should shake and earth be rent, this place would not move*.[^38] Flower and incense sellers set up outside the door every morning, and the kings of various countries are constantly sending messengers with offerings.

*Read: lines 632–649.*

# Below the Line

*Everything above is sourced to the chapters named. Everything below is built rather than found, and is not measured by `assessgate.sh`*.

## Ch. II — Roads Not Taken `[SPECULATIVE]`

**A live alternative, taken by three named men**. Che-yen, Hwuy-keen and Hwuy-wei turned back towards Kao-ch'ang from Woo-e, hoping to find there the means of continuing.[^6] That is the fork stated in the source: go on into uninhabited country on one patron's liberality, or go back to a place with resources and try again from there.

Nothing further is recorded about them. What makes the choice real rather than cowardly is the sentence Fa-hien writes about the road they did not take — a month and five days in which the difficulties and the sufferings were unparalleled in human experience. He does not say the three were wrong, and he does not say they were right.

## Ch. XII — Roads Not Taken `[SPECULATIVE]`

**A constructed one, and it is a forecast**. Suppose Fa-hien had turned back with Pao-yun and Sang-king from the alms-bowl. First order, he has the Maitreya image, the crossing, and the whole northern route, which is already more than Chang K'een or Kan Ying brought back. Second order, he has no Books of Discipline — Patna and the three years of copying are still eleven chapters away — so the journey fails at the only thing it was undertaken for. Third order, and this is where it thins, somebody else goes; the road is open, the monasteries keep rooms for strangers, and the traffic on it never ceases. **What would have been lost is this account, not the transmission**. The route was not fragile. The record of it was.

## Ch. XII — What Transfers `[SPECULATIVE]`

**A refusal that arrives as physics costs the refuser nothing**. The Yueh-she king had won his war and could not be told no by anybody. What told him no was an elephant that would not stand up. He read the kneeling as a verdict on his merit, was ashamed, and built a monastery on the spot instead — which left him with the credit for the shrine and no defeat on the record. *Applies when* a demand cannot be refused by a person without the refusal becoming a fight. *Fails* where the claimant is willing to test the mechanism twice; this one tried the waggon and eight elephants before he stopped, and a third attempt would have made the object look merely heavy.
*Decision type:* when to compromise a core value.

## Ch. XIII — What Transfers `[SPECULATIVE]`

**Split the key among the people most able to steal it, and make them look at each other every morning**. Eight families, eight seals, one door that only opens when all eight marks have been inspected in company. *Applies when* the guards and the likeliest thieves are the same set of people, and when the asset must be used daily rather than merely stored. *Fails* the moment the eight can profit together rather than against each other — the scheme is built on their rivalry, not on their honesty, and nothing in it survives their agreeing.
*Decision type:* power consolidation.

# What the Buddhist Kingdoms Took For Granted — Chapters XIV–XXVI

> **Chapters XIV–XXVI of Fa-hien, *A Record of Buddhistic Kingdoms*, in James Legge's translation** — the Little Snowy mountains to the confluence of the five rivers, across the Middle Kingdom. Read from `RAW/books/A Record of Buddhist Kingdoms.md`. One full archaeology pass per chapter, sweeping all seven dimensions in every run.

## Ch. XIV — The death of Hwuy-king in the Little Snowy mountains

**A man freezing to death tells his friend to leave**. On the north side of the range, in the shade, they met a cold wind that made them shiver and left them unable to speak. Hwuy-king could not go any farther. A white froth came out of his mouth, and he said to Fa-hien: *I cannot live any longer. Do you immediately go away, that we do not all die here*. With those words he died.[^1]

**What a person is**. Somebody whose last calculation is about the other men's chances. He does not ask to be carried, or to be waited with, or to be buried. He gives an instruction with a reason attached, and the reason is arithmetic — one death here, or three.

**What makes things happen**. Fa-hien stroked the corpse and cried out: *Our original plan has failed — it is fate. What can we do?*[^2] Then, in the next clause of the same sentence, *he again exerted himself*, and they got across to the south of the range. Fate is what he names the loss, and it does not stop him for a line. Both attitudes are in one breath and neither is offered as a correction of the other.

**How people should relate**. The two survivors go on. There is no funeral in the text, no marker, and no tope for Hwuy-king — the only man in this book to die on the road and get nothing built over him.

**The shape of time**. They had waited at Nagara until the third month of winter before starting, and at Lo-e they stopped for the summer retreat and went on only when it was over.[^3] The calendar keeps its hold even in the year a companion dies.

**How people should relate, in numbers**. Lo-e had nearly three thousand monks studying both the mahayana and the hinayana; Poh-na also more than three thousand, all hinayana.[^3] Two kingdoms of the same size, one mixed and one not, and no comment on the difference.

**What is real, how you know, what is worth having**. Not in the range read (line 690), beyond the snow that lies on the mountains winter and summer and the level country on both banks of the Indus where they crossed it again.

*Read: lines 690–691.*

---

## Ch. XV — Bhida. The sympathy of the monks.

**Monks who are astonished that anybody came**. In Pe-t'oo, when they saw their fellow-disciples from Ts'in passing along, they were moved with great pity and sympathy, and said: *How is it that these men from a border-land should have learned to become monks, and come for the sake of our doctrines from such a distance in search of the Law of Buddha?*[^4]

**What a person is, seen from the inside of the world Fa-hien came to**. A man from the borders. Not an enemy, not a barbarian to be corrected — somebody they pity for having so far to come. The whole chapter is four sentences and the sentence in the middle of it is the one that tells you where he stands in their eyes.

**How people should relate**. They supplied them with what they needed and treated them in accordance with the rules of the Law.[^4] Not in accordance with their feelings. The pity is in the first half of the paragraph and the procedure is in the second, and it is the procedure that gets him fed.

**What is worth having**. Whatever it is that could make a man from the edge of the world walk here for it. The question is left as a question, and the men asking it are the ones who already have the thing.

**What is real, what makes things happen, how you know, the shape of time**. Not in the range read (line 714). The chapter is one exchange, and both dimensions it carries are social.

*Read: lines 714–715.*

---

## Ch. XVI — On to Mathura. The customs of the Middle Kingdom.

**A king who takes his hat off and sits on the floor**. Everywhere from the Sandy Desert, in all the countries of India, the kings had been firm believers. When they make their offerings to a community of monks they take off their royal caps and, along with their relatives and ministers, supply the food with their own hands. That done, the king has a carpet spread for himself on the ground and sits down in front of the chairman. *They dare not presume to sit on couches in front of the community*.[^5]

**How people should relate**. There is a seat a king may not take, and everybody in the room knows which one. And the reason given is not law or fear — it is precedent: the laws and ways according to which the kings presented their offerings when Buddha was in the world have been handed down to the present day.[^5]

**How the country is run, and this is the most political paragraph in the book**. All south of Mathura is called the Middle Kingdom. The cold and heat are finely tempered and there is neither hoarfrost nor snow. The people are numerous and happy. They do not have to register their households or attend to any magistrates and their rules. Only those who cultivate the royal land pay a portion of the grain from it. **If they want to go, they go; if they want to stay on, they stay**.[^6]

The king governs without decapitation or other corporal punishments. Criminals are simply fined, lightly or heavily, according to the circumstances of each case. Even in cases of repeated attempts at wicked rebellion, they only have their right hands cut off. The king's bodyguards and attendants all have salaries.[^6]

That is a description of a state written by a man from one that registered households and executed people. He does not compare the two. He lists what is absent — the registry, the magistrates, the block — and then names the one tax and the one penalty.

**What is worth having, and what everybody agrees not to do**. Throughout the whole country the people do not kill any living creature, nor drink intoxicating liquor, nor eat onions or garlic. They do not keep pigs and fowls and do not sell live cattle; in the markets there are no butchers' shops and no dealers in drink. In buying and selling they use cowries.[^6]

**And the exception the whole arrangement is built on**. The only exception is that of the Chandalas — the name for those who are held to be wicked men, and live apart from others. When they enter the gate of a city or a market-place they strike a piece of wood to make themselves known, so that men know and avoid them and do not come into contact with them. **Only the Chandalas are fishermen and hunters, and sell flesh meat**.[^6]

A country where nobody kills is a country where a named group does the killing and announces itself with a rattle so the others can step back. The purity of the majority is a job, and somebody holds it. Fa-hien lists the rattle in the same sentence as the empty butchers' shops and the cowrie currency, as one more fact about how the markets there work. He is describing a market with no meat in it and the men who bring the meat, and he does not put those two facts against each other.

**How you make a thing outlast a reign**. Metal. After the pari-nirvana, the kings of the various countries and the heads of the Vaisyas built viharas for the monks and endowed them with fields, houses, gardens and orchards, along with the resident populations and their cattle — *the grants being engraved on plates of metal, so that afterwards they were handed down from king to king, without any daring to annul them, and they remain even to the present time*.[^7]

**What a person is, and how a stranger is received**. When stranger monks arrive, the old residents meet them, carry their clothes and alms-bowl for them, give them water to wash their feet and oil to anoint them, and the liquid food permitted outside the regular hours. When the stranger has had a very brief rest, they ask **the number of years he has been a monk**, and after that he gets a sleeping apartment with its fittings according to his regular order, and everything is done for him that the rules prescribe.[^8]

Seniority is counted in years of ordination, not in age or birth, and the question is asked after the feet are washed and before the bed is assigned. A man's place in a house he has never entered is settled by a number he brings with him. Nobody checks it, and nobody could. The oil and the food come first, unconditionally, and the ranking comes only after the stranger has already been fed.

**What is worth having, sorted by who you are**. The topes are for Sariputtra, Maha-maudgalyayana and Ananda — and also for the Abhidharma, the Vinaya and the Sutras.[^9] Three men and three bodies of text, given the same kind of monument.

Then each class of person offers at its own: the nuns mostly at Ananda's tope, *because it was he who requested the World-honoured one to allow females to quit their families*; the novices mostly to Rahula; the professors of the Abhidharma to the Abhidharma and those of the Vinaya to the Vinaya; the mahayana students to the Prajna-paramita, to Manjusri and to Kwan-she-yin. Every year there is one such offering, and each class has its own day for it.[^10]

**The shape of time**. A month after the annual rest, the families that are looking for blessing stimulate one another to make offerings, and send round the liquid food that may be taken outside the ordinary hours. All the monks come together in a great assembly and preach the Law, and then offerings are made at Sariputtra's tope with all kinds of flowers and incense. **All through the night lamps are kept burning, and skilful musicians are employed to perform**.[^11]

**What is real**. From the crossing of the Indus to Southern India and on to the Southern Sea, forty or fifty thousand li, all is level plain. There are no large hills with streams among them; there are simply the waters of the rivers.[^12]

**How you know the whole thing is intact**. *From the nirvana of Buddha, the forms of ceremony, laws, and rules practised by the sacred communities have been handed down from one generation to another without interruption*.[^10] That is the sentence Fa-hien walked six years to be able to write, and it is the answer to the question he set out with in chapter I.

*Read: lines 724–742.*

## Ch. XVII — Sankasya. The descent from the Trayastrimsas heaven.

**A woman who works out how to be first in the queue**. The kings of eight countries with their ministers and people had collected in clouds, thirstily looking up, waiting for Buddha to come down. The bhikshuni Utpala thought in her heart: *To-day the kings, with their ministers and people, will all be meeting and welcoming Buddha. I am but a woman; how shall I succeed in being the first to see him?*[^13]

Buddha immediately, by his spirit-like power, changed her into the appearance of a holy Chakravartti king, and she was the foremost of all in doing reverence to him.[^13]

**How people should relate**. The obstacle is real and it is not removed. She is not told the crowd will part for a nun, or that being first does not matter. She is issued a temporary king. The system stays exactly as it was and one woman is put through it in disguise, with the disguise supplied from above.

**What is real**. Three flights of steps let down out of the sky — the middle one of the seven precious substances with Buddha on it, a silver flight on the right where the king of Brahma-loka attended with a white chowry, purple gold on the left where Sakra attended with an umbrella. When he had come down, all three disappeared into the ground except seven steps, which stayed visible.[^14]

**How you test a thing like that**. You dig. King Asoka, wishing to know where the ends of the steps rested, sent men down to look. *They went down to the yellow springs without reaching the bottom of the steps, and from this the king received an increase to his reverence and faith*.[^14] He excavated to the water table, found no end, and believed more than before. The investigation is real and the result is read as confirmation.

**How a dispute is settled**. By a lion. Teachers of another doctrine once argued with the sramanas over the right to this place as a residence, and the sramanas were having the worst of the argument — so both sides took an oath that if the place did indeed belong to the sramanas there should be some marvellous attestation of it. When the words had been spoken, the lion on top of Asoka's pillar gave a great roar. Their opponents were frightened, bowed to the decision, and withdrew.[^15]

Both sides agreed the terms first. The losing side of the argument called for the test, and the other side accepted the format. It is a wager on a signal, entered into by mutual consent, and the verdict is honoured.

**What makes things happen**. A dragon farms for them. Where the monks live there is a white-eared dragon which acts the part of *danapati* to the community — causing abundant harvests in the country and the enriching rains to come in season, without any calamity, so that the monks enjoy their repose and ease.[^16] The word is the same one used of the king of Chang-yih in chapter I. A dragon can hold the office of donor.

**And what they owe it back**. In gratitude they have made it a dragon-house with a carpet to sit on, and appointed a diet of blessing which they present for its nourishment. Every day they set apart three of their number to go to its house and eat there.[^16]

**The shape of the year, and how it ends**. Whenever the summer retreat is over, the dragon changes its form and appears as a small snake with white spots at the side of its ears. As soon as the monks recognise it they fill a copper vessel with cream, put the creature into it, and carry it round from the one with the highest seat at their tables to the one with the lowest, when it appears as if saluting them. When it has been taken round it immediately disappears. **Every year it thus comes forth once**.[^16]

The dragon is carried down the seniority order, top to bottom, and greets every man in it. The ranking that decides where a stranger sleeps is the same ranking a snake is carried along. It happens once a year, at the same point in the calendar, and then the creature is gone. Three men eat in its house every day for the rest of the year, and it does not appear to them.

**What is worth having**. The country is very productive, the people prosperous and happy beyond comparison, and when people of other countries come they are exceedingly attentive to them all and supply them with what they need.[^17] Prosperity and hospitality are given as one fact.

**What a person is**. Somebody who can be counted, up to a point. At the Great Heap monastery there are a hundred small topes at which a man may keep counting a whole day without getting to know their exact number. If he is firmly bent on knowing, he will put a man beside each tope — and then, counting the men, whether they are many or few, he will still not get to know the number.[^18]

The workaround is a good one. Put a man on each tope and the topes stop being the thing you have to count. It fails anyway, and Fa-hien records the attempt as well as the failure. He does not say who tried it, or how many men they had, or what number they kept arriving at.

**And a test set by a hostile king**. A good spirit constantly keeps a tope swept and watered without any labour of man. A king of corrupt views said: *since you are able to do this, I will lead a multitude of troops and reside there till the dirt and filth has increased and accumulated, and see whether you can cleanse it away or not*. The spirit raised a great wind, which blew the filth away and made the place pure.[^19]

Two experiments in one chapter, both proposed by sceptics, both run, both settled against the sceptic. Asoka's dig, though, was a man asking a question he wanted answered, and this king is picking a fight. The wind is the only violent thing in the whole chapter, and it is aimed at rubbish. Nobody is hurt and the king is not punished, which is not how the same story would end in most places.

*Read: lines 810–834.*

## Ch. XVIII — Kanyakubja. Buddha's preaching.

**What he actually said, in six words**. Six or seven li west of the city, on the northern bank of the Ganges, is the place where Buddha preached to his disciples. It has been handed down that what he talked about there was *the bitterness and vanity of life as impermanent and uncertain*, and that *the body is as a bubble or foam on the water*.[^20]

**What is real**. A body with the density of foam. It is the one place in twenty-six chapters where the content of a sermon is reported rather than the site of one, and the content is that the thing standing in front of you will not hold.

**How you know**. *It has been handed down*. No text is named and no chain of teachers. The formula is the same one he used at the Indus for the arrival of the Law in the east, and it is doing the same work: this is what the people here say, and I am writing it as that.

**What is worth having**. A place where words were said, marked in stone. At this spot a tope was erected and still exists — and across the Ganges, three yojanas south, a village with places where Buddha preached, sat, and walked, all of them with topes on them.[^21] Preaching, sitting and walking are three separately markable acts.

**How people should relate, what a person is, what makes things happen, the shape of time**. Not in the range read (lines 890–894), beyond the two monasteries of hinayana students in the city and the seven yojanas from the Dragon vihara, which he left after the summer retreat.

*Read: lines 890–894.*

## Ch. XIX — Sha-che. The legend of Buddha's tooth-stick.

**A twig that will not be got rid of**. Buddha chewed his willow branch and stuck it in the ground, and it grew up seven cubits and stayed at that height, neither increasing nor diminishing.[^22]

**What is real**. A living thing that has stopped. A tree that grows is ordinary and a tree that is dead is ordinary; this one is fixed, which is the detail that makes it a marker rather than a plant.

**What makes things happen**. Persistence, against people. *The Brahmans with their contrary doctrines became angry and jealous. Sometimes they cut the tree down, sometimes they plucked it up, and cast it to a distance, but it grew again on the same spot as at first*.[^22]

Not once. Sometimes, and sometimes — a repeated campaign over years, reported without heat and without a name attached to either side. The tree does not punish anybody. It comes back.

**How people should relate**. Two communities in the same town, one of which periodically digs up the other's monument. Fa-hien records this as the local condition and moves on in the next clause to the four Buddhas who walked and sat here and the tope that is still existing.[^22]

**What is worth having, what a person is, how you know, the shape of time**. Not in the range read (line 908), beyond the three yojanas south-east and the fact that the tope still stands.

*Read: lines 908–909.*
