## Ch. XX — Kosala and Sravasti. The Jetavana.

**A great city with two hundred families left in it**. In Sravasti the inhabitants were few and far between, amounting in all to only a few more than two hundred families — the city where king Prasenajit ruled, where the old vihara of Maha-prajapati stood, where the well and walls of Sudatta's house are, and where the Angulimalya became an arhat.[^23]

**What is worth having, and what it cost**. Sudatta bought the park by covering it with gold coins.[^24] The measure of the purchase is the surface area of the ground, paid in a single layer, and that is how the transaction is remembered rather than as a sum.

**What is real — the first image, and it moves**. When Buddha had gone up to the heaven to preach for his mother, Prasenajit, longing to see him, had an image carved in sandalwood and put in the place where he usually sat. When Buddha came back into the vihara, he said to it: *Return to your seat. After I have attained to pari-nirvana, you will serve as a pattern to the four classes of my disciples*. And on this the image returned to its seat. **This was the very first of all the images, and the one that men subsequently copied**.[^25]

Then Buddha moved out and lived in a small vihara twenty paces away, on the south side, in a different place from the one with the image in it. He gives it his seat and goes elsewhere.

**What makes things happen**. A rat with a lamp-wick in its mouth. The Jetavana was originally of seven storeys, and the kings and people of the countries around vied with one another in their offerings — silken streamers and canopies hung about it, flowers scattered, incense burnt, lamps lit so as to make the night as bright as the day, day after day without ceasing. A rat carrying a lamp-wick set one of the streamers on fire, which caught the vihara, and all seven storeys were consumed.[^26]

The devotion is the fuel. Making the night as bright as the day means several hundred open flames in a wooden building hung with silk, kept going every night without a break. Nothing in the chapter is blamed and no lesson is drawn. The practice that honours the place burns it down, and the two facts sit in consecutive sentences.

The kings and their officers and people were all very sad, supposing the sandalwood image had gone. But after four or five days, when the door of a small vihara on the east was opened, the original image was seen. They were all greatly rejoiced and co-operated in restoring the building — and when they had got two storeys up, they moved the image back to its former place.[^26]

**What a person is, and the moment the book turns inward**. When Fa-hien and Tao-ching first arrived at the Jetavana and thought how the World-honoured one had formerly lived there for twenty-five years, painful reflections arose in their minds. Born in a border-land, they had travelled through so many kingdoms with their like-minded friends; some of those friends had returned home, and some had died, *proving the impermanence and uncertainty of life*; and today they saw the place where Buddha had lived, now unoccupied by him. They were melancholy through their pain of heart.[^27]

He uses the doctrine of chapter XVIII to describe his own dead companions, in the same words. It is the only place in the book where he applies a teaching to himself. Twenty-five years of Buddha's residence is what he came to stand in, and what he finds is an empty room. The friends who set out with him are accounted for in one clause — some went home, some died — and then he goes on.

**How people should relate**. The monks came out and asked what kingdom they were from. *We are come from the land of Han*. And the monks sighed: *Strange that men of a border country should be able to come here in search of our Law!* Then they said to one another: *During all the time that we, preceptors and monks, have succeeded to one another, we have never seen men of Han, followers of our system, arrive here*.[^28]

The same astonishment as in chapter XV, said by different men eight yojanas further on, and now with a length of time attached to it. Nobody in the succession has seen this before.

**How you know who won an argument**. By where the lamps end up. Opposite the vihara built on the site of Buddha's great debate stood a rival temple of the same height, called "The Shadow Covered" — because when the sun was in the west the shadow of Buddha's vihara fell across it, and when the sun was in the east that building's shadow was diverted north and never fell on Buddha's.[^29]

The rival believers employed men to watch their temple, sweep and water it, burn incense, light the lamps and present offerings — and in the morning the lamps were found to have been removed to the vihara of Buddha. The Brahmans were indignant and said: *Those Sramanas take out lamps and use them for their own service of Buddha, but we will not stop our service for you!* So that night they kept watch themselves, and saw the deva spirits they served take the lamps and go three times round the vihara of Buddha and present offerings, and then disappear. On which they left their families and became monks.[^29]

They suspected theft, set a watch, and caught their own gods doing it.

**How people should relate, across a doctrinal line**. In the Middle Kingdom there are ninety-six sorts of views erroneous and different from our system, all of which recognise this world and the future world and the connexion between them. Each has its multitude of followers, and they all beg their food — only they do not carry the alms-bowl. They also seek to acquire the blessing of good deeds on unfrequented ways, setting up houses of charity by the road where rooms, couches, beds, food and drink are supplied to travellers and to monks coming and going as guests, *the only difference being in the time for which those parties remain*.[^30]

Ninety-six rival systems, all running free hostels on the empty stretches of road, taking in each other's travellers, and the sole distinction Fa-hien records is the length of stay. He has just walked those roads. He notes one other difference and it is a small one: they beg their food like his own men do, only without carrying the bowl. That is his whole account of ninety-six ways of being wrong, and it is a description of their catering.

**The shape of time**. Around the Jetavana there were once ninety-eight monasteries, all with monks in them except one place that was vacant.[^30] And the followers of Devadatta are still existing, making offerings to the three previous Buddhas but not to Sakyamuni.[^31] A schism from the founder's lifetime is still keeping its own calendar of offerings nine hundred years later.

*Read: lines 924–952.*

## Ch. XXI — The three predecessors of Sakyamuni.

**Three men, and for each of them the same two places**. Kasyapa Buddha was born at Too-wei; topes were erected at the place where he and his father met, and at the place where he attained pari-nirvana. Krakuchanda Buddha was born at Na-pei-kea; topes at the place where he and his father met, and where he attained pari-nirvana. Kanakamuni Buddha at a town less than a yojana north; topes at the place where he and his father met, and where he attained pari-nirvana.[^32]

**The shape of time**. A life has a fixed set of markable points, and the set does not change between Buddhas. Three of them, three times the identical pair, in three consecutive sentences — this is what a career looks like, and the previous holders of the post left the same marks in different fields.

**What a person is**. Somebody who leaves his father and meets him again. Of everything in a Buddha's life, the moment chosen for a monument alongside the death is the reunion with the man whose household he walked out of. Chapter XXII will say it again about Sakyamuni: *where, after he had attained to Wisdom, Buddha returned and saw the king, his father*.

**What is real**. Over the entire relic of the whole body of Kasyapa Tathagata a great tope was erected.[^32] The whole body, not a portion — which sets up chapter XXIV, where eight kings divide one.

**How people should relate, what makes things happen, how you know, what is worth having**. Not in the range read (lines 1018–1022). The chapter is a list of six sites and its content is the pattern they make.

*Read: lines 1018–1022.*

## Ch. XXII — Kapilavastu, and its desolation.

**The town he was born in has nobody in it**. In Kapilavastu there was neither king nor people. All was mound and desolation. Of inhabitants there were only some monks and a score or two of families of the common people.[^33]

**What is real**. A place that is entirely a list of things that happened in it. Where the old palace stood, images of the prince and his mother. Where he entered his mother's womb on a white elephant. Where he turned his carriage round on seeing the sick man, having gone out by the eastern gate. Where the rishi inspected the marks of Buddhaship on him as an infant. Where he tossed the struck-down elephant aside. Where five hundred Sakyas quitted their families and did reverence to Upali while the earth shook and moved in six different ways. Where he sat under a nyagrodha tree, which is still standing.[^34]

**And one that is still in use**. Where he shot an arrow to the south-east, and it went thirty li, then entered the ground and made a spring come forth — *which men subsequently fashioned into a well from which travellers might drink*.[^34] The miracle got plumbed. It is the only site in this chapter that anybody does anything with.

**How people should relate**. Where Buddha preached his Law to the devas, and the four deva kings and others kept the four doors of the hall, *so that even the king, his father, could not enter*.[^34] The one man in the world with a claim on him is the one kept out.

**What a person is, and what a lineage is worth**. Where king Vaidurya slew the seed of Sakya, and they all in dying became Srotapannas. A tope was erected at this last place, which is still existing.[^34] The family is exterminated and the deaths are counted as entries onto the path. Both halves of that sentence are given in the same tone as the arrow and the tree.

**The shape of a life, stated as a rule**. *There are four places of regular and fixed occurrence in the history of all Buddhas* — first, where they attained perfect Wisdom; second, where they turned the wheel of the Law; third, where they preached, argued for righteousness, and defeated the advocates of erroneous doctrines; fourth, where they came down after going up to the Trayastrimsas heaven to preach for the benefit of their mothers. Other places became remarkable according to the manifestations made at them at particular times.[^35]

Four fixed points and an open list. Chapter XXI showed the pattern and here it is written out as a specification. Every Buddha, past and future, leaves those four marks in whatever country he happens to be born in. The rest of a life makes sites only where something happened to happen.

**What is worth having**. The water. At Lumbini the queen came out of the pond, walked twenty paces, lifted her hand, took hold of a branch of a tree, and with her face to the east gave birth. When he fell to the ground he immediately walked seven paces. Two dragon-kings appeared and washed his body, and at the place where they did so a well was immediately formed — and *from it, as well as from the pond where the queen bathed, the monks even now constantly take the water, and drink it*.[^36]

**What makes things happen, and how you know**. Not in the range read (lines 1036–1048), except that the sites are pointed out rather than found. What the chapter closes on is practical: the country is a great scene of empty desolation, the inhabitants are few and far between, and on the roads people have to be on their guard against white elephants and lions, and should not travel incautiously.[^37]

*Read: lines 1036–1048.*

## Ch. XXIII — Rama, and its tope.

**A dragon that outbids a king**. The king of Rama got one portion of the relics of Buddha's body and built a tope over it. Beside it was a pool, and in the pool a dragon, which constantly kept watch over the tope and presented offerings to it day and night.[^38]

When Asoka came into the world he wished to destroy the eight original topes and build eighty-four thousand instead. He had thrown down seven of them and meant to destroy this one too. Then the dragon showed itself and took the king into its palace — and when he had seen all the things provided there for offerings, it said: *If you are able with your offerings to exceed these, you can destroy the tope, and take it all away. I will not contend with you*.[^38]

The king knew that such appliances for offerings were not to be had anywhere in the world, and thereupon returned without carrying out his purpose.

**How a conflict gets settled**. By showing the other party the accounts and inviting him to beat them. No force is used and no refusal is issued. The dragon proposes a standard, opens its books, and states in advance that it will not fight. Asoka does his own valuation and withdraws.

This is the second time in the book a king with a sufficient army stops on a non-military ground. In chapter XII the elephants would not stand up; here the arithmetic does not work. Neither king is beaten and both give up.

**What makes things happen, when nobody is doing the job**. The ground about the tope became overgrown and there was nobody to sprinkle and sweep it — but a herd of elephants came regularly, bringing water in their trunks to water the ground, and various kinds of flowers and incense, which they presented at the tope.[^39]

**What a person is, and the one career move in the book**. A devotee came from another kingdom to worship at the tope. When he met the elephants he was greatly alarmed and hid among the trees. But when he saw them go through the offerings in the most proper manner, the thought filled him with great sadness — that there should be no monastery here whose inmates might serve the tope, and that the elephants have to do the watering and the sweeping.[^40]

*Forthwith he gave up the great prohibitions by which he was bound, and resumed the status of a Sramanera*. With his own hands he cleared away the grass and trees, put the place in good order, and made it pure and clean. By the power of his exhortations he prevailed on the king of the country to form a residence for monks, and when that was done he became head of the monastery.[^40]

He demoted himself. A fully ordained monk gives up the higher rule and goes back to being a novice, because a novice may do the physical work of clearing ground that his own vows forbade. And then he runs the house he built. *At the present day there are monks residing in it, and in all the succession from that time till now, there has always been a Sramanera head of the establishment*.[^40]

The exception became the constitution. Every head of that monastery since has held the junior rank on purpose, because the founder did. Nobody has been promoted into the job and nobody has restored the older arrangement. A house whose whole reason for existing is that the elephants should not have to sweep is run, permanently, by a novice.

**What is worth having**. Somebody to do the sweeping. The elephants were doing it properly — Fa-hien says so — and it was still not right, because it is a thing men owe.

**What is real, how you know, the shape of time**. Not in the range read (lines 1100–1104), beyond the eight original portions and the eighty-four thousand that Asoka meant to replace them with. *This event is of recent occurrence*, he adds of the devotee, which is the only place in the book he dates something to his own century.[^40]

*Read: lines 1100–1104.*

## Ch. XXIV — Where Buddha renounced the world, and where he died.

**A body divided eight ways**. At Kusanagara, between two trees on the river bank, is the place where the World-honoured one, with his head to the north, attained pari-nirvana. Also the place where Subhadra, the last of his converts, became an arhat; where they made offerings to him in his coffin of gold for seven days; where the Vajrapani laid aside his golden club; and where the eight kings divided the relics of the burnt body. At all of these, topes and monasteries were built and all are now existing.[^41]

**What is real**. A death that is also a distribution. Chapter XXI had a whole body under one tope; here the body is portioned and each portion is a claim, and the place where the portioning happened is itself marked.

**What a person is**. Somebody who sends back his horse. Four yojanas east is the place where the heir-apparent sent back Chandaka with the white horse, and a tope was erected there too.[^42] The renunciation is marked at the point where he dismissed the servant, not where he took the robe.

**How people should relate, when somebody will not let you go**. Twelve yojanas south-east is the place where the Lichchhavis wished to follow Buddha to his pari-nirvana. When he would not listen to them, and they kept cleaving to him, unwilling to go away, *he made to appear a large and deep ditch which they could not cross over, and gave them his alms-bowl, as a pledge of his regard, thus sending them back to their families*. A stone pillar was erected there with an account of the event engraved on it.[^43]

The refusal and the gift are the same act. He makes the ground itself say no, and then hands over the one object he uses every day so that the no cannot be read as rejection. The alms-bowl is the same class of object as the one eight elephants could not move in chapter XII.

**What is worth having, and who is left**. In the city the inhabitants are few and far between, comprising only the families belonging to the different societies of monks.[^44] A second town, after Kapilavastu, whose whole remaining population is the support staff of its own memorials.

**What makes things happen, how you know, the shape of time**. Not in the range read (lines 1124–1132), beyond the seven days of offerings and the yojana counts between sites.

*Read: lines 1124–1132.*

## Ch. XXV — Vaisali. The tope called "Weapons Laid Down."

**A woman on a wall, feeding a thousand soldiers**. The inferior wife of a king on the Ganges brought forth a ball of flesh. The superior wife, jealous, said *you have brought forth a thing of evil omen*, and it was immediately put into a wooden box and thrown into the river.[^45]

Downstream another king saw the box floating, had it brought to him, opened it, and found a thousand little boys, upright and complete, and each one different from the others. He brought them up. They grew tall and large and very daring and strong, crushing all opposition in every expedition they undertook — and by and by they attacked the kingdom of their real father.

He became greatly distressed. His inferior wife asked what was making him so, and he told her: that king has a thousand sons, daring and strong beyond compare, and he wishes to attack my kingdom. She said: *you need not be sad and sorrowful. Only make a high gallery on the wall of the city on the east; and when the thieves come, I shall be able to make them retire*.[^46]

When the enemies came she called down from the tower: *you are my sons; why are you acting so unnaturally and rebelliously?* And when they did not believe her: *look, all of you, towards me, and open your mouths*. She pressed her breasts with her two hands and each sent forth five hundred jets of milk, which fell into the mouths of the thousand sons. **The thieves thus knew that she was their mother, and laid down their bows and weapons**.[^46]

**How you prove a claim**. With the body, in public, at range. She does not produce a token or a witness. She makes the demonstration herself from a structure she asked to have built for the purpose, and it works on a thousand men at once because every one of them receives his own portion of the evidence.

**What makes things happen**. Both fathers then fell into reflection and both got to be Pratyeka Buddhas, and the tope of the two of them is still existing.[^46] The two kings who were about to fight each other end up in the same category, and the woman who stopped the war is not said to have gained anything by it.

**The shape of time**. The thousand little boys were the thousand Buddhas of this Bhadra-kalpa.[^47] And in a subsequent age, when the World-honoured one had become Buddha, he said to his disciples: *this is the place where I in a former age laid down my bow and weapons*. It was thus that men subsequently got to know the fact and raised the tope, which in this way received its name.[^47]

Same mechanism as chapter IX: he returns and identifies the ground, and the marker goes up afterwards. But here he is identifying a spot where he himself surrendered, as one of a thousand brothers, before he was anybody. The tope is named for the weapons rather than for the man, and the men who built it were told what had happened by the one who put the weapons down. It is a monument to somebody backing off.

**What a person is — the failure at Vaisali**. By the side of that same tope, Buddha, having given up the idea of living longer, told Ananda that in three months he would attain pari-nirvana. *And king Mara had so fascinated and stupefied Ananda that he was not able to ask Buddha to remain longer in this world*.[^48]

There was a moment when it could have gone otherwise and the man in the room was not able to speak. It is the only place in the book where somebody's silence changes the outcome. Ananda is not blamed for it and no fault of his is named. A king fascinated and stupefied him, and the three months ran.

**How you know — and this is what he came for**. Three or four li east there is a tope commemorating this: a hundred years after the pari-nirvana, some bhikshus of Vaisali went wrong in the matter of the disciplinary rules in ten particulars, and appealed for their justification to what they said were the words of Buddha. On which the arhats and the bhikshus observant of the rules, seven hundred monks in all, **examined afresh and collated the collection of disciplinary books**.[^49]

That is the procedure. A dispute over ten points of the rule, a claim on both sides to have the founder's words, and the answer is seven hundred men sitting down together and going through the texts again. It is the same operation Fa-hien is performing with his own feet, nine hundred years later and four thousand miles from home.

**What is worth having**. Ambapali built a vihara in the city in honour of Buddha, which is standing now as it was at first, and gave him a garden three li south of the city to reside in.[^50] And when he was leaving by the west gate he turned round, looked at the city on his right, and said: *here I have taken my last walk*. Men subsequently built a tope at that spot.[^50]

**What is real**. A place marked because somebody looked back at it.

*Read: lines 1160–1172.*

---

## Ch. XXVI — The remarkable death of Ananda.

**A man caught between two armies who splits himself in half**. When Ananda was going from Magadha to Vaisali, wishing his pari-nirvana to take place there, the devas informed king Ajatasatru, who immediately pursued him in his own grand carriage with a body of soldiers and reached the river. The Lichchhavis of Vaisali had heard he was coming to their city and came out to meet him. In this way they all arrived together at the river.[^51]

**What makes things happen — the calculation, and it is a social one**. Ananda considered that if he went forward king Ajatasatru would be very angry, and if he went back the Lichchhavis would resent his conduct.[^52] That is the whole reasoning given. Not doctrine, not a vision, not an instruction. Two parties on two banks, each with a claim on his body, and no third bank.

**What he did**. In the very middle of the river he burnt his body in a fiery ecstasy of Samadhi, and his pari-nirvana was attained. *He divided his body also into two, leaving the half of it on each bank; so that each of the two kings got one half as a relic, and took it back to his own capital, and there raised a tope over it*.[^52]

**What a person is**. Divisible, and worth fighting over. Chapter XXIV had eight kings dividing a body after a death; here a man performs the division himself, in advance, to prevent the fight. He does not choose a side, refuse both, or slip away. He arranges for both claims to be satisfied exactly.

**What is worth having**. Half a corpse, and a tope to put it in. Both kings go home content, which is the outcome he engineered.

**How people should relate**. Two rulers who would have gone to war over a relic instead build one monument each, and the man they were competing for made that the only available result.

**What is real, how you know, the shape of time**. Not in the range read (line 1206), beyond the four yojanas east and the confluence of the five rivers where it happens.

*Read: lines 1206–1207.*

---

# Below the Line

*Everything above is sourced to the chapters named. Everything below is built rather than found, and is not measured by `assessgate.sh`*.

## Ch. XIV — Roads Not Taken `[SPECULATIVE]`

**A live alternative, and the dying man named it**. *Do you immediately go away, that we do not all die here*.[^1] The other course is stated in his refusal of it: stay, try to warm him, carry him down. Hwuy-king rules it out on the grounds that it kills everybody, and Fa-hien accepts the ruling without argument.

What makes this a real fork rather than a formality is chapter XII, four pages earlier, where Tao-ching stayed behind with the same man when he first fell ill at Nagara and nursed him back onto the road. The precedent existed and had worked once. It is refused on a mountainside because the conditions are different, and the man who refuses it is the one it would have been done for.

## Ch. XVI — What Transfers `[SPECULATIVE]`

**Engrave the grant on metal and the next king cannot quietly stop honouring it**. Fields, houses, gardens, orchards, and the resident populations with their cattle, cut into plates and handed from reign to reign, *without any daring to annul them*. *Applies when* the beneficiary cannot defend the endowment by force and the succession is frequent — a durable, public, unforgeable record shifts the cost of revocation from the holder to the revoker, who now has to be seen destroying something. *Fails* against a ruler who wants the fight, and against dynastic breaks where the new house owes nothing to the old plates.
*Decision type:* succession.

**Ask the number of years, not the name**. A stranger monk gets his feet washed first and his rank assigned second, from a single number he carries with him. *Applies when* people arrive from unconnected places and must be slotted into a hierarchy immediately, with no shared registry to check them against. *Fails* where the number can be inflated and there is no way to test it — which is exactly the hole the Vaisali council of chapter XXV had to convene over, when men appealed to what they said were the words of Buddha.
*Decision type:* alliance formation.

## Ch. XVI — Counsel From Elsewhere `[SPECULATIVE]`

**A Kautilyan advisor on the Middle Kingdom's arrangements**. The *Arthashastra* takes the visible reach of the state as the thing to be maximised — registration, informers, revenue, the ruler's knowledge of who is where. See [[LAB/Worldview Reports/trautmann-arthashastra-worldview-archaeology|What a Mauryan Statecraft Manual Took For Granted]]. Fa-hien is standing in the same country a few centuries later and reporting the opposite: no household registration, no magistrates to attend, one tax on royal land, and if a man wants to go he goes.

The counsel would be that this cannot be what it looks like, and it would be worth listening to. What Fa-hien is describing is a state that has moved its record-keeping and its coercion off the population and onto two other things — the metal plates that fix the endowments, and the Chandalas who do the killing and announce themselves with a rattle. **Nothing softened. The register moved from the people to the land, and the enforcement moved from the magistrate to a caste**. A Kautilyan reader would find the machinery immediately and would not call it lighter.

## Ch. XXIII — What Transfers `[SPECULATIVE]`

**Open your books and invite the stronger party to beat them**. The dragon did not refuse Asoka, threaten him, or bargain. It showed him the standing offerings, set exceeding them as the price of demolition, and said in advance that it would not contend. *Applies when* your position is genuinely unmatchable and the other party is capable of checking — the concession has to be real, or the invitation is a bluff and gets called. *Fails* against somebody who does not care about the standard you named. Asoka stopped because he wanted the relic housed better, not merely moved; a king who only wanted it moved would have knocked the tope down.
*Decision type:* when to compromise a core value.

## Ch. XXIII — Roads Not Taken `[SPECULATIVE]`

**A constructed one**. Suppose the devotee had done the obvious thing and petitioned the king for a monastery without giving up his own standing first. First order, he is one more visiting monk with a request, and the request costs the king money for a site nobody local is attending. Second order, the elephants keep sweeping, because the thing that actually moved the king was a man already on his knees in the grass having demoted himself to do it. Third order, and this is where it thins — somebody else eventually founds the house anyway, since the relic is real and the traffic exists. **What would not have survived is the rule that every head of that monastery holds the junior rank**. That is a constitution, and it came from one man's decision about his own status rather than from the founding grant.

## Ch. XXVI — What Transfers `[SPECULATIVE]`

**When two claimants cannot both be satisfied, divide the thing they want rather than choosing between them**. Ananda's answer to a river with an army on one bank and a delegation on the other was to make himself into two relics. *Applies when* the asset is divisible without being destroyed, and when the claimants want possession rather than exclusivity — both kings wanted a tope, and two topes are not worth less than one. *Fails* completely where the point of the claim is that the other side does not have it, which is the ordinary case and the reason this looks stranger than it is.
*Decision type:* when to compromise a core value.

# What the Buddhist Kingdoms Took For Granted — Chapters XXVII–XL

> **Chapters XXVII–XL of Fa-hien, *A Record of Buddhistic Kingdoms*, in James Legge's translation** — Patna and Rajagriha, Gaya, Benares, Ceylon, and the voyage home. Read from `RAW/books/A Record of Buddhist Kingdoms.md`. One full archaeology pass per chapter, sweeping all seven dimensions in every run.

## Ch. XXVII — Pataliputtra. Asoka's palace, and the charity houses.

Fa-hien walks into Patna and reports that the palace was not built by men. The royal halls in the middle of the city, which exist now as of old, were all made by spirits Asoka employed. They piled the stones, reared the walls and gates, and did the carving and inlaid work — *in a way which no human hands of this world could accomplish*.[^1] That is his account of the most famous building he has seen so far, given flatly and in the same breath as the distances. What is real, here, includes a labour force you cannot hire.

The hill inside the city is the sharper story, and it turns on a king who cannot get what he wants. Asoka's younger brother had become an arhat and lived on Gridhra-kuta, finding his delight in solitude and quiet. The king wanted him in the family compound, where all his wants could be supplied. The brother would not come, because of his delight in the stillness of the mountain. So the king said: *only accept my invitation, and I will make a hill for you inside the city*.[^2]

He then did it by a trick that is worth following. He provided the materials of a feast, called the spirits, and announced that they would all receive his invitation tomorrow — but that as there were no mats for them to sit on, each one should bring his own seat. Next day they came, each bringing a great rock like a wall, four or five paces square. When the sitting was over the king had them pile the stones into a hill, and at the foot of it he made an apartment out of five large square stones, more than thirty cubits long and twenty wide.[^2] **He got a mountain built by inviting his guests to dinner and telling them to bring a chair**.

What a person is, here, is somebody a king may not sit beside. The great Brahman Radha-sami lived by himself in spotless purity, and the king honoured him and served him as his teacher. When the king went to greet him he did not presume to sit down alongside him. And if in his love and reverence he took hold of the Brahman's hand, then as soon as he let go the Brahman made haste to pour water on it and wash it.[^3] The king accepts this, repeatedly. Radha-sami might be over fifty years old, and all the kingdom looked up to him.

The consequence of that one man is stated as a political fact:

> By means of this one man, the Law of Buddha was widely made known, and the followers of other doctrines did not find it in their power to persecute the body of monks in any way.[^3]

One teacher stands high enough that a king washes his hand after touching him. That is what keeps the rival schools off the monasteries. The protection is real and it does not go through a law.

How you know, in this city, is by resorting to it. Shamans of the highest virtue come from all quarters. So do students, and inquirers wishing to find out truth and the grounds of it. They all go to these two monasteries — one mahayana and one hinayana, six or seven hundred monks between them.[^4] The rules of demeanour and the scholastic arrangements in them are worth watching, he says. A resident Brahman teacher also called Manjusri is honoured by the most virtuous shamans in the kingdom and by the mahayana monks alike.

How people should relate, in this country, has an address you can walk to. The heads of the Vaisya families establish in the cities houses for dispensing charity and medicines. All the poor and destitute in the country go to those houses — orphans, widowers and childless men, maimed people and cripples, and everyone who is diseased. They are provided with every kind of help, and doctors examine their diseases. They get the food and medicines their cases require and are made to feel at ease — *and when they are better, they go away of themselves*.[^5]

Nobody discharges them and nobody counts the days. The clause that closes the description is the one that tells you what the house is for: it is not a place people are kept, it is a place people leave when the leaving is possible.

The shape of the year is a two-night visit. On the eighth day of the second month they hold a procession of images. They build four-storey structures on four-wheeled cars, twenty cubits high and shaped like a tope, wrapped in white cloth of hair and painted. Figures of devas go on them in gold, silver and lapis lazuli, and a niche on each of the four sides holds a seated Buddha with a Bodhisattva standing in attendance. There may be twenty cars, all imposing and each one different. **The Brahmans come and invite the Buddhas to enter the city**. They do so in order and remain two nights in it, with lamps burning all night and skilful music and offerings.[^6]

What is worth having gets an inscription and a number on it, and the number is three. On the pillar in front of the great tope there is a text saying that Asoka gave the jambudvipa — the whole inhabited world — to the general body of all the monks, and then redeemed it from them with money. *This he did three times*.[^7] The same transaction as the quinquennial assembly of chapter V, run at the scale of a continent, by a king who evidently found it worth doing again twice.

What makes things happen is not addressed in the range read (lines 1222–1240) beyond the spirits and the one Brahman. The other pillar, at Ne-le, carries an inscription recording the things that led to the building of the city, with the number of the year, the day and the month.[^8] A date to the day, cut in stone, which is the one piece of record-keeping in the book that would satisfy a modern archivist.

*Read: lines 1222–1240.*

---

## Ch. XXVIII — Rajagriha, new and old.

Sakra brought a musician to entertain the Buddha and then asked him forty-two questions, tracing them out with his finger one by one on the rock. The prints of his tracing are still there, and there is a monastery at the spot.[^9] What is real here is a conversation that left marks, and the marks are of the questions rather than the answers.

How you know something happened at a place, in this book, is by what it left on the ground. This chapter packs a list of such traces into a few hundred paces. The old city of Bimbisara is a circular space formed by five hills standing round it like a suburban wall, and inside it:

> Sariputtra and Maudgalyayana first saw Upasena; the Nirgrantha made a pit of fire and poisoned the rice, and then invited Buddha to eat with him; king Ajatasatru made a black elephant intoxicated with liquor, wishing him to injure Buddha; and at the north-east corner of the city Jivaka built a vihara in the garden of Ambapali, and invited Buddha with his 1250 disciples to it, that he might there make his offerings to support them.[^10]

Two assassination attempts and a dinner party are listed in one sentence, in the order of their position in the town. What a person is, in that list, is somebody with enemies who used food and animals. Neither the poisoner nor the king is condemned in the text and neither is given a consequence.

The shape of time, here, is a city that emptied. These places are still there as of old, *but inside the city all is emptiness and desolation; no man dwells in it*.[^10] New Rajagriha stands a few li away with two monasteries and a tope Ajatasatru built over his portion of the relics. The old city has nobody. It is the third town in the book, after Kapilavastu and Kusanagara, whose sites outlasted its people.

How people should relate is carried by one detail: at Nala, a yojana south-west, Sariputtra was born, and to it he also returned, and there he attained his pari-nirvana. A tope was built over the spot where his body was burned, and it is still in existence.[^11] The same shape as the three predecessor Buddhas in chapter XXI, who each have a monument where they met their fathers again. Going out and coming back is the pattern a life is expected to make.

What is worth having and what makes things happen are not in the range read (lines 1272–1277). What the chapter carries instead is a map: nine yojanas south-east, then a yojana south-west, then a yojana west, then four li south through a valley, and every turn of it lands on something that happened.

*Read: lines 1272–1277.*

---

## Ch. XXIX — Gridhra-kuta hill. Fa-hien passes a night on it.

A frightened man gets a hand through a wall. Ananda was sitting in meditation in a cavern when the deva Mara Pisuna took the form of a large vulture and settled in front of the opening to frighten him. Buddha, by his supernatural power, made a cleft in the rock, put his hand through it, and stroked Ananda's shoulder, so that his fear immediately passed away.[^12] The footprints of the bird and the cleft for the hand are both still there, and the hill is named after the vulture rather than the hand.

What a person is, in that account, is somebody who can be badly frightened while meditating and needs touching to stop it. Nothing is said to him. The remedy is physical, it comes through a wall that had to be opened for it, and the man who supplies it does not enter the room.

What is real is a hillside covered in the evidence of other people's practice. In front of the cavern are the places where the four Buddhas sat. Along the hill there are caverns of the arhats, one where each sat and meditated, amounting to several hundred in all.[^13] There is also the rock Devadatta threw down from the cliffs on the north, which hurt Buddha's toes. It is still there. The hall where he preached has been destroyed and only the foundations of the brick walls remain.

Then the book stops being a survey. In the New City Fa-hien bought incense-sticks, flowers, oil and lamps, and hired two bhikshus who had lived there a long time to carry them up to the peak. When he got there himself he made his offerings with the flowers and incense, and lit the lamps as the darkness began to come on.[^14]

**He felt melancholy, but restrained his tears and said: *Here Buddha delivered the Surangama Sutra. I, Fa-hien, was born when I could not meet with Buddha; and now I only see the footprints which he has left, and the place where he lived, and nothing more.***[^14]

That is what is worth having, said plainly by the man who spent fifteen years getting to it: the footprints, the place, and nothing more. He has walked from Ch'ang-gan to a rock in Magadha to stand where a sermon was given, and the sentence he produces is an accounting of what is missing.

What he does about it is the shape of time in this chapter. With this, in front of the rock cavern, he chanted the Surangama Sutra, remained there over the night, and then returned towards the New City.[^14] He recites the text that was delivered on the spot, in the dark, on the ground where it happened, and stays till morning. The gap between his birth and the Buddha's life is not closed and the recitation is what he has instead.

How people should relate, in the practical sense, appears as a transaction: he bought the supplies in town and hired two long-resident monks to carry them. Pilgrimage has porters, and the porters are local men who know the path.

What makes things happen and how you know are not in the range read (lines 1306–1314) beyond the supernatural power that opened the rock.

*Read: lines 1306–1314.*

---

## Ch. XXX — The cave of the first council. The suicide of a bhikshu.

Five hundred arhats collected the Sutras in a cavern on the north of the hill, in the shade, after the nirvana. Three lofty seats had been prepared and grandly ornamented — Sariputtra on the left, Maudgalyayana on the right, Mahakasyapa president on the middle seat. *Of the number of five hundred one was wanting. Ananda was then outside the door, and could not get in*.[^15]

That is how you know, at the origin: five hundred men in a room, three of them raised, and one man short because the man who had heard the most was locked out. Fa-hien reports the shortfall without explaining it. The same Ananda who could not speak at Vaisali in chapter XXV cannot get through the door here.

What is real is a hillside honeycombed with the same activity. Along the sides of the hill there are a very great many cells among the rocks where the various arhats sat and meditated. Near the road is the Karanda Bamboo garden, where the old vihara still stands with a company of monks who keep the ground about it swept and watered.[^16] Two or three li north of it is the Smasanam, the field of graves into which the dead are thrown.

Then the chapter's real subject, and it is a man arguing himself into cutting his own throat on a large black rock. He walked backwards and forwards on it thinking: *this body is impermanent, a thing of bitterness and vanity, and which cannot be looked on as pure. I am weary of this body, and troubled by it as an evil*.[^17] He grasped a knife and was about to kill himself.

Then he thought again — *the World-honoured one laid down a prohibition against one's killing himself*. And then a third time: *yes, he did; but I now only wish to kill three poisonous thieves*.[^17] Immediately, with the knife, he cut his throat.

**What a person is, in that reasoning, is a container with an infestation in it**. He does not deny the rule. He accepts it and then reclassifies the act, so that what is being killed is not himself but the three poisons living in him. The doctrine of chapter XVIII — the body as bubble and foam — supplies the first move, and the loophole supplies the second.

The verdict is delivered in the wound. With the first gash into the flesh he attained the state of a Srotapanna; when he had gone half through, he was an Anagamin; and when he had cut right through, he was an arhat and attained pari-nirvana, and died.[^18] Three ranks in one stroke, graded by depth. What makes things happen here is the cut itself, doing the work of years of practice, and Fa-hien records the promotion at each stage without comment on the argument that produced it.

How people should relate and what is worth having are not in the range read (lines 1334–1344), except that the man was alone on the rock and nobody stopped him.

*Read: lines 1334–1344.*

---

## Ch. XXXI — Gaya. The attaining of Buddhahood.

A man sits down in a cave and asks for a sign, gets one, and is told he is in the wrong place. He entered a cavern half a yojana north-east of Gaya and sat cross-legged with his face to the west. Then he said to himself: *if I am to attain to perfect wisdom and become Buddha, let there be a supernatural attestation of it*. On the wall of the rock there immediately appeared the shadow of a Buddha, rather more than three feet long. It is still bright at the present day.[^19]

At that moment heaven and earth were greatly moved, and devas in the air spoke plainly:

> This is not the place where any Buddha of the past, or he that is to come, has attained, or will attain, to perfect Wisdom. Less than half a yojana from this to the south-west will bring you to the patra tree, where all past Buddhas have attained, and all to come must attain, to perfect Wisdom.[^19]

**The site is fixed and the man is not consulted about it**. What is real here is a geography that runs across all the Buddhas there have ever been and all there will be, in which one particular tree is the only place the thing can happen. The sign he asked for was granted in full — the shadow is still there — and it was granted at the wrong address.

Then they led the way forward, singing as they went, and he got up and walked after them. Thirty paces from the tree a deva gave him the grass of lucky omen, which he received and carried on. After fifteen paces five hundred green birds came flying towards him, went round him three times, and disappeared. He went forward to the patra tree, put the kusa grass at the foot of it, and sat down facing east.[^20]

King Mara then sent three beautiful young ladies from the north to tempt him and came himself from the south to do the same. The Bodhisattva put his toes down on the ground, and the demon soldiers retired and dispersed, and the three young ladies were changed into old grandmothers.[^20] The whole assault is answered by putting a foot flat. What makes things happen, in the crisis of the story, is a gesture too small to see.

The shape of time in this chapter is seven days, counted over and over. Seven days contemplating the tree and experiencing the joy of release. Seven walking back and forth from west to east under it. Seven while the devas made a hall of the seven precious substances appear and presented offerings. Seven while the blind dragon Muchilinda encircled him. Then the nyagrodha tree, the square rock facing east, Brahma-deva's request, the four deva kings bringing their alms-bowls, the five hundred merchants with roasted flour and honey, and the conversion of the Kasyapa brothers with their thousand disciples. Topes at every one of them.[^21]

What is worth having, in the three monasteries at the place, is a settled arrangement nobody has to renegotiate. The families of the people around supply the communities with all they require, *so that there is no lack or stint*. The disciplinary rules are strictly observed. The laws regulating their demeanour in sitting, rising and entering when the others are assembled are the ones practised by all the saints since Buddha was in the world.[^22]

How you know the map is right: **the places of the four great topes have been fixed, and handed down without break, since Buddha attained to nirvana**.[^22] Born, attained Wisdom, began to move the wheel of the Law, attained pari-nirvana. Chapter XXII gave the four points as a rule about all Buddhas; here they are given as four addresses whose identification has never been interrupted.

Where the trees themselves come in is a small aside with a large claim in it. In Central India the cold and heat are so equally tempered that trees will live for several thousand and even for ten thousand years.[^23] That is why the rock and the tree where he ate the milk-gruel *are there at the present day*, and it is a natural explanation offered in the middle of a chapter full of devas.

*Read: lines 1384–1400.*

---

## Ch. XXXII — Asoka's hell, and the tree his queen cut down.

A boy playing in the road gave a Buddha a handful of earth. Kasyapa Buddha was walking past and begged food, and the boy pleasantly took a handful of earth and gave it to him. The Buddha took the earth and returned it to the ground he was walking on — and because of this the boy received the recompense of becoming a king of the iron wheel, to rule over the whole inhabited world.[^24]

**The gift was worthless and the return was an empire**. What makes things happen, in this account of merit, has nothing to do with the value of what changes hands. The Buddha did not even keep it. He put it back on the path, and the transaction still counted.

What is real is a hell you can build with contractors. Making a tour of inspection, Asoka saw between the iron circuit of two hills a naraka for punishing wicked men. He asked his ministers what it was, and they said it belonged to Yama, king of demons. The king then thought within himself:

> Even the king of demons is able to make a naraka in which to deal with wicked men; why should not I, who am the lord of men, make a naraka in which to deal with wicked men?[^25]

They told him only a man of extreme wickedness could make it. So officers went out to look for one, and found him by a pond: tall and strong, with a black face, yellow hair and green eyes. He was hooking up fish with his feet, and calling birds and beasts to him, and shooting them as they came, *so that not one escaped*. What a person is, for this job, is measured by that last clause. The man's distinction is that nothing gets away from him.

The instructions he gave the man secretly turn on their last clause:

> Make a square enclosure with high walls. Plant in it all kinds of flowers and fruits; make good ponds in it for bathing; make it grand and imposing in every way, so that men shall look to it with thirsting desire; make its gates strong and sure; and when any one enters, instantly seize him and punish him as a sinner, not allowing him to get out. **Even if I should enter, punish me as a sinner in the same way, and do not let me go**. I now appoint you master of that naraka.[^25]

He built a trap that was beautiful on the outside and wrote himself into it. How people should relate, under that rule, is by a law with no exception at the top — which is exactly the thing Fa-hien reports of nowhere else in the book, and it is a hell.

Then a bhikshu begging his food walked in through the gate. The lictors were about to torture him and he asked, frightened, for a moment to eat his midday meal. While he waited, another man was thrust into a mortar and pounded until a red froth overflowed. As the bhikshu watched, the thought came to him of the impermanence and the painful suffering and insanity of this body, and how it is but as a bubble and as foam. Instantly he attained arhatship.[^26]

That is the same sentence as chapter XVIII and the same one the man on the black rock used before cutting his throat. Here it arrives by watching somebody else be destroyed, and it arrives in the seconds before the same thing is done to him.

They threw him into a cauldron of boiling water and there was a look of joyful satisfaction on his face. The fire went out, the water went cold, and in the middle of the cauldron a lotus rose with the bhikshu sitting on it.[^26] The lictors went to fetch the king, who said: *I formerly made such an agreement that now I dare not go to the place*. They told him this was not a small matter and that his former agreement should be altered. He followed them in, the bhikshu preached to him, and he believed and was made free — then demolished the hell and repented of everything he had done.

**The rule with no exception lasted exactly until the king wanted an exception**. His own officers argued him out of it in two sentences. What is worth having, from that point, is a tree: he constantly went to a patra tree and repented under it with self-reproach, accepting the eight rules of abstinence.

The queen asked where he kept going. The ministers told her, and she waited for a time when he was not there and sent men to cut the tree down.[^27] When the king came and saw what had been done he swooned with sorrow and fell to the ground, and his ministers sprinkled water on his face, and after a considerable time he revived.

Then he built all round the stump with bricks and poured a hundred pitchers of cows' milk on the roots. He lay down with his four limbs spread out on the ground and took an oath: *if the tree do not live, I will never rise from this*. When he had said it the tree immediately began to grow from the roots. It has continued to grow till now, when it is nearly a hundred cubits high.[^27]

The shape of time in this chapter runs from a handful of dirt to a hundred-cubit tree, through a hell and a queen's jealousy, and every stage of it turns on somebody making a binding statement and then being held to it or not.

*Read: lines 1434–1444.*

## Ch. XXXIII — Mount Gurupada, where Kasyapa's skeleton is.

A man went down into a mountain through a cleft that would no longer admit a body. Mahakasyapa is inside Gurupada even now: he made a cleft and went down into it, though the place where he entered would not now let a man through. Having gone down very far, there was a hole on one side, and there the complete body of Kasyapa still abides.[^28]

What is real, in that description, is a door that has closed behind somebody who is still in there. Chapter XXI reported the whole body of Kasyapa Tathagata under a great tope. Here the whole body is in a hole in a hill and the entrance has narrowed, and both are given as present-tense facts.

What is worth having is the dirt outside the entrance. It is the earth with which he washed his hands — and if the people living thereabouts have a sore on their heads, they plaster some of it on and feel immediately easier.[^29] A national relic and a local remedy, in consecutive clauses, and the remedy is the one with a use.

How you know, on that mountain, is by staying the night with a strong enough heart. Arhats abide there now as of old. Devotees of the Law from the various countries in that quarter go year by year to present offerings to Kasyapa:

> And to those whose hearts are strong in faith there come Arhats at night, and talk with them, discussing and explaining their doubts, and disappearing suddenly afterwards.[^29]

The visit is annual, the arhats come only at night, they come only to some people, and what they do is answer questions. Then they vanish. It is the one place in the book where the dead are available for consultation, and the terms are unambiguous about who gets the appointment.

How people should relate, what a person is, what makes things happen and the shape of time are not in the range read (lines 1464–1468), beyond the yearly cycle of offerings. The chapter closes on the practical warning it shares with Kapilavastu: on this hill hazels grow luxuriantly, and there are many lions, tigers and wolves, so that people should not travel incautiously.[^30]

*Read: lines 1464–1468.*

## Ch. XXXIV — Benares. The first turning of the wheel.

Five men agree in advance not to talk to him. Buddha wished to convert Kaundinya and his four companions, and they, aware of his intention, settled on a policy:

> This Sramana Gotama for six years continued in the practice of painful austerities, eating daily only a single hemp-seed, and one grain of rice, without attaining to the Path of Wisdom; how much less will he do so now that he has entered again among men, and is giving the reins to the indulgence of his body, his speech, and his thoughts! What has he to do with the Path of Wisdom? To-day, when he comes to us, let us be on our guard not to speak with him.[^31]

**They then all rose up and respectfully saluted him when he came**, and there is a tope at the place where they did it. Fa-hien records the agreement and the collapse of the agreement, and gives the site of each. What a person is, in that account, is somebody whose stated resolve does not survive the other man walking in.

Their reasoning is worth having intact, because it is the ordinary reasoning of the ascetic world he had just left. Six years of extreme austerity produced nothing; going back to eating is therefore a retreat; a man who has given up the hard method has given up. It is a coherent position, held by five serious men, and the whole of what happens next is that they stand up.

What is real, in that park, is a place named after an animal's habit. A Pratyeka Buddha had lived there and the deer were regularly in the habit of stopping with him for the night. When the devas sang in the sky that the son of king Suddhodana would become Buddha in seven days, the Pratyeka Buddha heard them and immediately attained nirvana — and hence the place was named the Park of the rishi's Deer-wild.[^32]

He got out of the way. What makes things happen there is an announcement, overheard by somebody it was not addressed to, who draws the correct conclusion about his own position and leaves before the new man arrives.

The shape of time is measured in paces from the spot where the wheel first turned. Sixty paces north from where the five saluted him, he sat facing east and first turned the wheel of the Law. Twenty paces further north he delivered his prophecy about Maitreya. Fifty paces to the south the dragon Elapattra asked him: *when shall I get free from this naga body?*[^33] Topes at all of them, all still existing.

That question from the dragon is the only thing anybody asks in the chapter, and it is a request for a date. How people should relate and what is worth having are not in the range read (lines 1490–1494), beyond the two monasteries in the park with monks residing in both.

*Read: lines 1490–1498.*

## Ch. XXXV — Dakshina, and the pigeon monastery.

A monastery cut into a hill in five storeys, each shaped like a different animal. The lowest has the form of an elephant with five hundred apartments in the rock, the second a lion with four hundred, the third a horse with three hundred, the fourth an ox with two hundred, the fifth a pigeon with a hundred. At the very top there is a spring, and its water runs in front of the apartments, circling and curving down through the rooms, following the shape of the structure until it reaches the lowest storey and flows out at the door.[^34]

What is real, in that building, is plumbing. Every room in fifteen hundred has running water arriving by gravity from the summit, and the rock has been pierced to make windows so that all of them are bright, with no room left in darkness. Steps have been hewn at the four corners of each tier to get to the top.

The shape of time is a complaint about the present. The men of the present day are of small size, so they go up step by step and manage to reach the top. *But in a former age, they did so at one step*.[^35] The stairs exist because people got shorter, or weaker. The monastery is named Paravata, the pigeon, after its topmost storey.

How people should relate, out there, is the chapter's oddest exchange. The country about is uncultivated hillocks without inhabitants, and the villages are a very long way from the hill. Their people all have bad and erroneous views. They do not know the shamans of the Law of Buddha, or Brahmans, or devotees of any of the other schools.[^36] They are outside every system Fa-hien has a name for.

But they are constantly seeing men on the wing coming and entering this monastery. When devotees from various countries came to worship at it, the villagers asked them: *why do you not fly? The devotees whom we have seen hereabouts all fly*. And the strangers answered, on the spur of the moment: *our wings are not yet fully formed*.[^36]

**The pilgrims made a joke to get out of it, and the villagers had the better information**. How you know, in this chapter, is a real problem for Fa-hien and he says so. The kingdom of Dakshina is out of the way and perilous to traverse, with difficulties on the roads. Those who know how to manage such difficulties should bring money and various articles and give them to the king, who will then send men to escort them, and these will pass them on at stages to others who show them the shortest routes.[^37]

Then comes the line that makes this chapter different from every other one in the book. *Fa-hien, however, was after all unable to go there; but having received the above accounts from men of the country, he has narrated them*.[^37] He has just given several paragraphs of architectural detail about a place he never saw. He marks it once, plainly, at the end, and does not withdraw any of it.

What a person is, what makes things happen and what is worth having are not in the range read (lines 1538–1544) beyond the arhats always residing there and the escort system that would have got him in.

*Read: lines 1538–1544.*

## Ch. XXXVI — In Patna. The three years of copying.

He came for a book and there were no books. Fa-hien's original object had been to search for copies of the Vinaya, and in the various kingdoms of North India he had found one master transmitting the rules orally to another, but no written copies he could transcribe.[^38] That is why he had gone on to Central India, and it is the reason the second half of the journey happened at all.

**How you know, across the whole northern route, was a man's memory and another man's ear**. He walked through kingdom after kingdom of four thousand monks apiece, all of them keeping the rules he came for, and none of them holding a copy. In Patna, in the mahayana monastery, he found one: the Mahasanghika rules, those observed in the first Great Council while Buddha was still in the world, the original of which was handed down in the Jetavana vihara.[^39]

What the other schools have is described exactly and without heat. As to the other eighteen schools, each one has the views and decisions of its own masters. Those agree with this in the general meaning, but they have small and trivial differences, *as when one opens and another shuts*. This copy, however, is the most complete, with the fullest explanations.[^39]

Eighteen versions, agreeing on the sense and differing on the operations, and he takes the fullest one. That is a scholar's judgement, made by a man qualified to make it, and it is the whole answer to the question he set out with in chapter I.

He then got a transcript of the sarvastivadah rules in six or seven thousand verses. Those are the ones observed by the communities of monks in the land of Ts'in — *which also have all been handed down orally from master to master without being committed to writing*.[^40] His own tradition's rules were being kept at home by memory. The text of them existed four thousand miles away, and nobody at home had ever seen it.

The shape of time is three years at a desk. He stayed there learning Sanskrit books and the Sanskrit speech, and writing out the Vinaya rules. He also picked up an Abhidharma treatise of six or seven thousand verses, a Sutra of twenty-five hundred, a chapter of the Parinirvana-vaipulya Sutra of about five thousand, and the Mahasanghikah Abhidharma.[^41]

Then the party ends. Tao-ching arrived in the Central Kingdom and saw the rules the shamans observed there, and the dignified demeanour in their societies under all occurring circumstances. He sadly called to mind what a mutilated and imperfect condition the same rules were in at home. Then he made an aspiration: *from this time forth till I come to the state of Buddha, let me not be born in a frontier land*.[^42]

**He remained in India and did not return**. What is worth having, for Tao-ching, is to be born somewhere else next time. He says so in the form of a vow about all his future lives. The two men saw the same monasteries and drew opposite conclusions from them. One decided this is where a person should be; the other, that this is what has to be carried home.

What a person is, for Fa-hien, is settled in the next clause. *Fa-hien, however, whose original purpose had been to secure the introduction of the complete Vinaya rules into the land of Han, returned there alone*.[^42] The word is the same one he used after Hwuy-king died on the mountain, and this time nobody has died. His last companion has simply decided that the frontier is not worth going back to.

What is real, how people should relate, and what makes things happen are not in the range read (lines 1556–1564) beyond the transmission itself, which is the chapter's whole subject.

*Read: lines 1556–1564.*

## Ch. XXXVII — To Champa and Tamalipti, and by sea to Ceylon.

Two more years at a desk, and then a boat. At Tamalipti, a seaport with twenty-two monasteries, Fa-hien stayed two years writing out his Sutras and drawing pictures of images.[^43] The drawing is new. He has spent seventeen chapters describing things nobody at home has seen, and here he starts producing copies to carry.

Then he embarked in a large merchant vessel and went floating over the sea to the south-west. *It was the beginning of winter, and the wind was favourable; and, after fourteen days, sailing day and night, they came to the country of Singhala*.[^44] The people said it was about seven hundred yojanas from Tamalipti.

How you know a distance at sea is by asking when you arrive. He gives the number of days he sailed and then the local figure for the distance, and does not reconcile them. The same method as the whole overland journey, where his own count of days runs alongside whatever the people of each country tell him.

What is real, in the kingdom, is an island with a hundred smaller ones round it, ten or twenty or even two hundred li apart, all subject to the large one, and most of them producing pearls and precious stones.[^45] One island of about ten li square produces the pure and brilliant pearl.

How people should relate is set out as a tax rate. *The king employs men to watch and protect it, and requires three out of every ten such pearls, which the collectors find*.[^45] Thirty per cent, on a pearl fishery, with a guard force paid for out of it. It is the only rate of tax Fa-hien records anywhere in the book except the grain from the royal land in chapter XVI.

What a person is, what makes things happen, what is worth having and the shape of time are not in the range read (lines 1596–1602), beyond the two years of copying and the fourteen days of favourable wind.

*Read: lines 1596–1602.*

## Ch. XXXVIII — Ceylon. The tooth festival, and a fan of white silk.

The island began with a shop nobody staffed. It originally had no human inhabitants but was occupied only by spirits and nagas, with which merchants of various countries carried on a trade. When the trafficking took place, the spirits did not show themselves. **They simply set forth their precious commodities, with labels of the price attached to them, while the merchants made their purchases according to the price and took the things away**.[^46]

How people should relate, at the founding of this country, is a transaction with nobody present and a fixed price on the label. Neither side sees the other and neither side haggles. Then, through the coming and going of the merchants, the people of their various countries heard how pleasant the land was and flocked to it until it became a great nation.

The shape of time there is that there isn't much of one. The climate is temperate and attractive, without any difference of summer and winter, and the vegetation is always luxuriant. *Cultivation proceeds whenever men think fit: there are no fixed seasons for it*.[^47] Every other country in this book has been organised around the summer retreat and the ripening of a crop. This one has no agricultural calendar at all.

What is worth having is stated in silver and monks. Over the footprint north of the royal city the king built a tope four hundred cubits high, and beside it the Abhayagiri monastery, where there are now five thousand monks. Its hall of Buddha holds an image in green jade more than twenty cubits high, glittering all over, with a priceless pearl in the palm of its right hand.[^48] In the city there are sixty thousand monks getting their food from common stores. The king prepares a further supply for five or six thousand more, who come with their great bowls and take as much as the vessels will hold.

Then, standing in front of that jade image, the book breaks:

> Several years had now elapsed since Fa-hien left the land of Han; the men with whom he had been in intercourse had all been of regions strange to him; his eyes had not rested on an old and familiar hill or river, plant or tree; his fellow-travellers, moreover, had been separated from him, some by death, and others flowing off in different directions; no face or shadow was now with him but his own, and a constant sadness was in his heart.[^49]

**Then he saw a merchant present, as his offering, a fan of white silk — and the tears of sorrow involuntarily filled his eyes and fell down**.[^49] Not the jade image, not the pearl, not the five thousand monks. A trade good from home, in a stranger's hand, in a temple on an island.

What makes things happen, in this kingdom's constitution, is a king who caught himself. One of them once entered a monastic treasury and looked round at the priceless pearls. His covetous greed was excited and he wished to take them by force. In three days, however, he came to himself. He went and bowed his head to the ground in the midst of the monks to show his repentance of the evil thought, told them what had been in his mind, and asked for a rule:

> That from that day forth the king should not be allowed to enter the treasury and see what it contained, and that no bhikshu should enter it till after he had been in orders for a period of full forty years.[^50]

He legislated against his own future self, and against every future king, and set a forty-year qualification for anybody else who goes in. That is the same instinct as Asoka's *even if I should enter, punish me* in chapter XXXII. Unlike Asoka's, this one was not overturned in an afternoon. The man who made it made it a rule of the house, rather than a promise he could be argued out of.

What a person is, in the tooth procession, is a life read out as a list of amputations. Ten days beforehand the king caparisons a large elephant and mounts on it a man who can speak distinctly, dressed in royal robes, to beat a drum and proclaim:

> He gave up kingdom, city, wife, and son; he plucked out his eyes and gave them to another; he cut off a piece of his own flesh to ransom the life of a dove; he cut off his head and gave it as an alms; he gave his body to feed a starving tigress; he grudged not his marrow and his brains. In many such ways as these did he undergo pain for the sake of all living.[^51]

Every one of those is a place Fa-hien walked past on the way here — Gandhara for the eyes, Soo-ho-to for the dove, Takshasila for the head and for the tigress. The proclamation is his itinerary, read out to a crowd on an island two thousand miles further on, as a single life.

**And the count is exact: *since that event, for 1497 years, the light of the world has gone out, and all living beings have had long-continued sadness.***[^51] Then the practical instruction — let all who wish to amass merit make the roads smooth and in good condition, adorn the lanes and by-ways, and provide abundant store of flowers and incense.

How you know what the Bodhisattva looked like at each stage is answered by lining the road with him. The king exhibits the five hundred different bodily forms in which he has appeared. Here as Sudana, there as Sama, now as the king of elephants, then as a stag or a horse. All of them are brightly coloured and grandly executed, *looking as if they were alive*.[^52] Then the tooth is carried down the middle of the road between them, to ninety days of continuous services at the Abhayagiri.

What is real, at the end of the chapter, is a man in a stone room with the animals. Dharma-gupta is a shaman of great virtue on the Chaitya hill, honoured and looked up to by all the kingdom. He has lived for more than forty years in an apartment of stone, *constantly showing such gentleness of heart, that he has brought snakes and rats to stop together in the same room, without doing one another any harm*.[^53]

*Read: lines 1620–1644.*

## Ch. XXXIX — The cremation of an arhat, and a sermon that is nobody's scripture.

Before you can bury a man as an arhat, somebody has to certify that he was one. When a shaman of the Maha-vihara drew near his end, the people all surmised he had attained it, and the king came to examine into the point. He assembled the monks according to rule and asked whether the bhikshu had attained to the full degree of Wisdom, and they answered in the affirmative. *The king accordingly, when he died, buried him after the fashion of an Arhat, as the regular rules prescribe*.[^54]

**How you know is by convening the community and putting the question**. Not by a sign, not by a test, and not by the king's own judgement. He asks the assembled monks and takes their answer, and the answer determines the funeral. It is the same procedure as the Vaisali council in chapter XXV, run on a man instead of a rule.

What the funeral is, is a pile more than thirty cubits square and the same in height, with sandal and aloe and other fragrant woods near the top, and steps up all four sides. They wrapped the body round and round in clean white hair-cloth, almost like silk, and made a large carriage-frame like a funeral car but without the dragons and fishes.[^55]

How people should relate, at the burning, is by throwing their own clothes on it. The king and the people collected in multitudes from all quarters and presented flowers and incense. The king himself presented them while they followed the car to the ground. Then the car was lifted onto the pile, oil of sweet basil was poured over it, and a light applied:

> Every one, with a reverent heart, pulled off his upper garment, and threw it, with his feather-fan and umbrella, from a distance into the midst of the flames, to assist the burning.[^56]

Fa-hien had not arrived in time to see the man alive, and only saw his burial. That is the second time in three chapters he records arriving after the thing he came for, and he states it without complaint both times.

What makes a grant permanent gets demonstrated in the next paragraph, and it is chapter XVI's metal plates again. The king wanted to build a new vihara, so he convoked a great assembly, gave the monks a meal of rice and presented his offerings, then selected a pair of first-rate oxen with their horns decorated in gold and silver and the precious substances. A golden plough had been provided, and *the king himself turned up a furrow on the four sides of the ground* within which the building was to stand.[^57]

Then he endowed the community with the population, fields and houses, writing the grant on plates of metal, to the effect that from that time onwards, from generation to generation, no one should venture to annul or alter it. The king cuts the boundary himself with his own hands, in front of everybody, and then the boundary goes into metal so that his successors cannot move it.

What is worth having, and this is the strangest thing in the chapter, is a doctrine its own author disowns. Fa-hien heard an Indian devotee reciting from a pulpit a long account of where the alms-bowl will go next. Vaisali, then Gandhara, then Western Tukhara, Khoten, Kharachar, the land of Han, Sinhala, back to Central India. Then up to the Tushita heaven, where Maitreya will sigh over it, then back down into the naga palace, then splitting into four bowls again and returning to the mountain they came from.[^58]

The whole future of the world is hung on where that object is. *When the bowl has disappeared, the Law of Buddha will go on gradually to be extinguished*. After that the life of man shortens to five years. Rice and butter and oil vanish, men become exceedingly wicked, and the grass and trees they lay hold of turn into swords and clubs. Those on whom there is blessing withdraw among the hills. Then the recovery runs the same machinery backwards: men unite in the practice of what is good, cherishing a gentle and sympathising heart, and *life will go on to double its length till it reaches 80,000 years*.[^59]

**Fa-hien wished to write it down as a portion of doctrine, and the man said: *this is taken from no Sutra, it is only the utterance of my own mind.***[^60]

That refusal is the sharpest thing in the last quarter of the book. A man who has spent fifteen years distinguishing what is written from what is remembered asks to record a sermon, and the preacher tells him it does not qualify. He wrote it down anyway, and labelled it.

*Read: lines 1704–1720.*
