*Source ingest: [[ARCHIVES/sources/faxian-record-of-buddhist-kingdoms|Faxian, A Record of Buddhist Kingdoms (Legge translation)]]*
*Built from the vault's Faxian concept pages. The observer here is also a figure with decisions to autopsy — see Evidence.*

---

## He Sorts Every Claim Into Three Boxes and Never Mixes Them

Start with the most useful thing in the whole chronicle, and it isn't a fact about India. It's a habit. Faxian spends a full chapter on a five-storey rock monastery at Dakshina. Elephant on the ground floor with five hundred apartments, lion floor with four hundred, horse with three hundred, ox with two hundred, pigeon on top with one hundred. A spring at the summit whose water runs in spirals through every room. Villagers who watch monks fly into the building, because "our wings are not yet fully formed."[^1]

Then, at the end, he tells you he never saw any of it. He couldn't get there. People who had been told him, and he is writing down what they told him.[^2]

That's the whole method in one move, and he runs it consistently. **What he saw** is most of the book, and he marks the line precisely — three or four *le* from the city, because he walked it; the vihara stands in a square of thirty paces, because he paced it; he did not arrive in time to see the famous monk alive and saw only the burial. At Nagara he even reports the Buddha-shadow from the angle he stood at: from more than ten paces you seem to see the real form, and the nearer you get the fainter it becomes, as if it were only in your fancy.[^3]

**What he heard on site** is the second box — the miracle stories, the legends attached to particular places, the flying monks. These go down in the same reverent register, and the chronicle doesn't commit to their being true. It commits to this being what the local sangha was teaching at that site in 405 CE.[^4]

**What he was told about places he couldn't reach** is the third, and it gets flagged. There's a moment where an Indian devotee preaches a long prophecy about the Buddha's alms-bowl travelling from Vaisali to Gandhara to Khotan to the land of Han and on. Faxian wants to write it down as doctrine. The preacher stops him: this is taken from no sutra, it is only the utterance of my own mind. Faxian records the disclaimer along with the prophecy.[^5]

## A Man Who Has to Make a Noise So You Can Avoid Him

Walk into Mathura in the early fifth century. The streets are quiet. Nobody is eating meat or drinking liquor. There are no butchers in the market and no live cattle being sold. The whole texture of the place is a Buddhist moral curriculum running as background.[^6]

Then you hear it at the gate. A wooden knock. It's a man striking a piece of wood so that people know he's coming and can avoid him before anyone makes eye contact. He can't enter the market quietly. He can't come through the gate without announcing himself.[^7]

Faxian's own sentence: they are held to be wicked men and live apart from others; when they enter the gate of a city or a market they strike a piece of wood to make themselves known, so that men know and avoid them and do not come into contact with them.[^8] And then the detail that closes the circuit. In that country they don't keep pigs or fowl or sell live cattle, there are no butchers and no drink-sellers — and only the Chandalas are fishermen and hunters, and sell flesh meat.[^9]

So the moral consensus doesn't abolish the work it forbids. It concentrates it in the people it has already placed outside, and then treats their doing it as further evidence of what they are.

## Sick and Poor Is the Only Qualification

Pataliputra, 405 CE, the old Mauryan capital. At certain houses in the city, sick people are walking in off the street — orphans, widowers, the destitute, people with nobody left, the maimed, anyone diseased. Doctors examine them. They get the food and the medicine their cases need. They stay until they're better, and then, in Faxian's phrase, "when they are better, they go away of themselves."[^10]

No charge, no intake process, no test beyond being ill and poor. The houses are funded by the heads of the Vaisya families — the merchant elite — as a standing institution of the city rather than as occasional charity.[^11]

He gives it eight sentences and no commentary at all. It goes in beside the cowrie currency and the salaried bodyguards, as a feature of the polity that doesn't call for remark.[^12]

That lack of remark is the finding. A man who flags his hearsay carefully, who tells you when he stood ten paces off, does not think a free public hospital is worth a sentence of surprise.

## The Only Question at the Gate Is How Long You've Been a Monk

You've been walking for fourteen days. Your feet hurt, your robe is filthy, you don't speak the language, and the monastery you've reached runs a different Vinaya from your own. You knock.[^13]

What follows is the same at Khotan, at Sankasya, at Mathura, at Anuradhapura. They come out. They take your clothes off your shoulders and your alms-bowl out of your hand. They bring water for your feet, oil for your skin, and whatever the rules permit you to eat outside the regular hours. They wait while you rest.[^14]

Then one question, and it isn't your name or your country or your school. How many years have you been a monk?

You answer, and you're given a sleeping apartment with its fittings according to your regular order — senior place if you're senior, junior if you're junior. You are now a placed member of that house, ranked by years since ordination and by nothing else.[^15]

## Tensions Within the Subject

**The careful witness reports the untouchability without comment too.** The same discipline that flags a hearsay chapter and quotes a preacher's disclaimer records the wood-block at the gate as flatly as the cowries. Whether that's the discipline working correctly — report what is there, don't editorialise — or the limit of what he could see as remarkable is not something the pages settle.

**And two ranking systems run in the same country.** At the monastery gate, seniority in the robe is the only thing that counts and a foreigner with no language is placed by it within the hour. At the city gate, birth decides everything and the man announces himself with a stick. Both are operating in Mathura on the same day.

## Not in the Range Read

Built from the vault's Faxian concept pages, not a fresh read of the Legge translation. Anything the ingest folded is invisible here.

Nothing was read on: the Central Asian legs of the journey in any detail, the Ceylon material beyond the shipwreck, the doctrinal content of the Vinaya texts he was collecting, or the return voyage past the typhoon. No claim is made either way about what the chronicle contains there.

## Evidence

Two things about this source make it unusually good for the method and one makes it fragile. Good first. This is a primary text — a first-person account by a man who walked the ground in 399–414 CE — rather than a modern reconstruction, so the assumptions in it are the assumptions of somebody living inside them rather than a historian's account of them. And the writer supplies his own reliability marking, which almost no ancient source does. The three-tier sorting means a reader can tell which sentences he stands behind.

The fragile part is translation. Everything above comes through James Legge's 1886 English, and the vault holds a page on inter-translator disagreements for exactly this reason. Where a phrase does work in this report — "when they are better, they go away of themselves," or the wording of the Chandala passage — it is Legge's English carrying it, and nothing here should rest on the connotations of a single English word. The substance is in the reported practices, which are concrete enough to survive a translator.

The figure, for the biography half, is Faxian himself, and he's a genuine case. He is fifteen years into collecting manuscripts when the ship starts going down.

# Below the Line

*Everything above is sourced to the vault pages cited. Everything below is built rather than found, and is not measured by `assessgate.sh`.*

## Roads Not Taken `[SPECULATIVE]`

**A live alternative, and it's the sharpest single decision in the chronicle.** Three days out from Ceylon the ship springs a leak. The merchants start throwing cargo overboard to keep it afloat. The tethered lifeboat has already been cut loose by its own crew, who were afraid of being swamped, so there are two hundred men aboard with a leak and no escape vessel.[^16]

Faxian throws his pitcher and washing-basin into the sea — his personal monastic kit, the standard equipment every monk carries — and keeps the books and images.[^17] Then, because he can't stop the merchants doing what he just did to his own belongings, he prays.

That's a real fork with both roads visible. He could lighten the ship with the manuscripts, which is what the merchants were doing with everything else and what any of them would have called sensible. Fifteen years of hand-copied texts against a share of the weight keeping two hundred men alive. He chose the cargo and threw away the equipment that makes a monk a monk day to day.

**And a second one, attested and permanent.** His companion Tao-ching reached the middle country, found the monastic discipline there so complete by comparison with China's that he vowed never to go back, and stayed.[^18] Same journey, same evidence, opposite conclusion. One man decided the books had to be carried home and the other decided home was the wrong place to carry them to.

**A constructed one, briefly, and it's weak.** Suppose he had lost the manuscripts. The obvious forecast is that the Chinese Vinaya tradition develops later or differently. But the transmission had many channels and other pilgrims followed, so the chain runs out fast. **Stated and left alone.**

## Counsel From Elsewhere `[SPECULATIVE]`

**A Kautilyan advisor on the three-tier register, and the compliment is real.** The *Arthashastra*'s central worry is that a ruler's information gets bent by whoever delivers it, and its remedy is structural — a second channel that owes nothing to the first. See [[LAB/Worldview Reports/trautmann-arthashastra-worldview-archaeology|What a Mauryan Statecraft Manual Took For Granted]].

Faxian solves the same problem the other way and does it alone. Instead of building a second reporting network, he tags every claim with where it came from and lets the reader do the discounting. **That's cheaper than a spy service and it survives him**, which the spy service doesn't — a network of agents dies with the king who runs it, and a marked text keeps working sixteen centuries later. A Kautilyan advisor would recognise it as the same job done by disclosure rather than by redundancy, and would note that it only works if the reader bothers to read the tags.

Worth putting beside the Rasputin case. There the parallel channel existed and failed, because the receiver's frame converted every input into confirmation — see [[LAB/Worldview Reports/rasputin-worldview-archaeology|What Late Romanov Russia Took For Granted]]. Faxian's method has the same weakness and admits it: marking a chapter as hearsay does nothing if the reader wants the flying monks to be true.

**An Ashokan advisor on the hospitals, and they are looking at the same country seven hundred years apart.** Ashoka's edicts run the king's relationship to his subjects as a debt to be discharged — wells dug, trees planted, medical provision for humans and animals, all of it the king paying what he owes. See [[LAB/Worldview Reports/ashoka-worldview-archaeology|What a Mauryan King Took For Granted]].

By 405 CE the same city has the provision and the payer has changed. It's merchant families funding it, as a standing institution, with no king in the sentence at all.[^19] An Ashokan advisor would find that both reassuring and alarming: the practice outlived the doctrine that justified it, which means the doctrine wasn't load-bearing — and also means nobody is now obliged to keep it up. **A debt has a debtor you can name. A custom doesn't.**

**And the two ranking systems are worth one line of counsel from the steppe.** Genghis abolished inherited title so that office could be given on merit; the monasteries achieved something narrower and more durable by ranking on one measurable fact that nobody can inherit — years since ordination. See [[LAB/Worldview Reports/weatherford-genghis-khan-worldview-archaeology|What the Steppe Took For Granted]]. It works internationally, across languages and rival Vinayas, because it needs no shared politics, only a shared count.

## What Transfers `[SPECULATIVE]`

**1. Say where each claim came from and you can report anything.**
Faxian writes down flying monks, dragons and a bowl-prophecy without damaging his own reliability, because each is marked. *Applies whenever* you need to preserve material you don't endorse — local belief, rumour, a claim you couldn't check. *Fails* when the tags are inconsistent, since one unmarked hearsay passage retroactively puts the whole register in doubt.
*Decision type:* post-failure narrative.

**2. A moral consensus that forbids a necessary trade doesn't abolish it — it assigns it, and then blames the assignee.**
No butchers in the market, and the only butchers are the people already placed outside. *Applies wherever* a prohibition is general and the underlying need isn't. *Fails* where the trade genuinely stops, which is rarer than the prohibition's supporters believe.
*Decision type:* when to compromise a core value.

**3. Rank on one countable fact and your hierarchy crosses borders.**
Years since ordination places a foreigner with no shared language inside an hour. *Applies when* you need a status order to work between groups with nothing else in common — the fact has to be countable, unfalsifiable and un-inheritable. *Fails* the moment the count can be gamed or the groups start disputing what counts as the start date.
*Decision type:* alliance formation.

**4. An unremarked detail is evidence about the observer's normal, not about the thing.**
The free hospital gets eight sentences and no surprise, from a man who is meticulous about surprise elsewhere.
*Applies when* reading any careful witness: what they explain tells you what they expected you not to know, and what they don't explain tells you what they took for granted.
*Fails* where the omission is editorial rather than perceptual, which is why it only works on writers whose habits you can otherwise measure.
*Decision type:* post-failure narrative.

**5. Throw away the equipment, keep the cargo — but only if you know which is which before the storm.**
The pitcher and basin are what make daily monastic life possible and are replaceable anywhere. The manuscripts are fifteen years old and exist nowhere else.
*Applies* to any forced jettison under time pressure: the test is not what is essential to functioning, it's what can be reacquired.
*Fails* when the "irreplaceable" thing turns out to be duplicated elsewhere, which he had no way to know and which was in fact partly true.
*Decision type:* strategic retreat.

# What Carthage and Rome Each Took For Granted — Worldview Archaeology

> **Which file is this?** This is a **Worldview Archaeology** report — what the people inside the source took for granted, and what those assumptions let them do or stopped them doing. Below a `# Below the Line` divider it turns speculative on purpose. No sibling thread map exists for this source yet.

*Source ingest: [[ARCHIVES/sources/ben-wilson-hannibal-parts-1-2-how-to-take-over-the-world|Ben Wilson, Hannibal — How to Take Over the World, Parts 1–2]]*
*A podcast transcript, and that matters — see Evidence, where the trust calibration goes. Built from the vault's Hannibal concept pages.*

---

## Two Ways of Being Reasonable, and They Can't Share a War

This one is unusual because the report has two worldviews in it, not one, and the whole thing is about what happens when they meet. Hannibal thinks like this: here is the goal, what's the best route to it? His tactics are precise, his positioning is exact, his intelligence work is sophisticated. Rome thinks like this: we have decided that accepting Carthaginian dominance is not acceptable, whatever it costs.[^1]

Neither of those is the irrational one. Both are internally coherent. He's being entirely reasonable about military strategy, and Rome is being entirely reasonable about staying the kind of thing it is. The trouble is that the two forms can't occupy the same war — one of them has to win, and it isn't the one with the better generalship.[^2]

Underneath his whole campaign sits an assumption so ordinary that it's easy to miss. Opponents optimise for survival. Beat them badly enough and they'll negotiate, because worse terms now beat annihilation later.[^3]

That assumption is correct about almost everybody. It is wrong about Rome after Cannae, and the source puts the asymmetry plainly: he is trying to win, and Rome is trying not to die as a civilisation.[^4]

## An Oath Sworn at Nine

The altar is slick with the blood of a freshly killed bull. A nine-year-old boy stands in front of it with his father and the army watching, goes through the ritual, and comes to the part that matters. In the deepest voice he can manage he swears eternal hatred to Rome.[^5]

That isn't decoration in the record. It's a limit on what he's able to think.

He can reason freely about tactics and he cannot reason at all about the goal. Negotiating with Rome would break the oath. Accepting terms would break the oath. Pulling back to Spain and consolidating what he holds would break it too, because the oath doesn't ask for consolidation, it asks for destruction.[^6]

So he's brilliant at every problem the oath permits him to work on, and helpless in front of the only one that matters — Rome won't be solved, and he has no move that isn't a form of solving. The wording varies between accounts and the content doesn't: perpetual enmity. Not revenge, not hostility that could be traded away later. Perpetual, across time and circumstance, for life.[^7]

## One Mind Against a Machine

He's a genius by any measure. Cannae is still the standard. His grasp of terrain, logistics and positioning beats any Roman general's, and he keeps winning against consistently larger forces.[^8]

And he loses — not by being beaten in the field, since he wins most of the engagements, but because Rome isn't trying to match him. Rome is trying to outlast him.[^9]

The mismatch is one of scale, not of quality. Everything on his side runs through one head, which is what makes him fast: rapid adaptation, precise positioning, immediate response to an opening. It's also a single point of failure, and it means the force is exactly as good as the man is on the day.[^10]

Rome has distributed command, political processes that keep producing new consuls, a resource base that keeps generating armies, and a cultural commitment to not stopping. He can beat Rome in any battle. He can't beat it as a system.[^11]

## Tensions Within the Subject

**The oath is both the engine and the cage, and nothing separates them.** Without it there's no Alpine crossing and no Cannae — nobody attempts that campaign on a cost-benefit basis. With it there's no exit, no negotiated settlement, no consolidation of a real Carthaginian position in Italy. The same thing that got him there is the reason he couldn't leave.

**And both sides are the irrational one, depending where you stand.** From inside his framework, Rome refusing terms after Cannae is madness. From inside Rome's, a man who thinks a civilisation can be talked out of existing has misunderstood what he's fighting. The source frames Rome's commitment as *selective* irrationality — a decision to take one option permanently off the table — and that's the whole mechanism, but it's worth noting that a decision like that is only visible as strength afterwards. The same commitment in a state that then loses is just a state that refused to stop.

## Not in the Range Read

Built from the vault's Hannibal concept pages, which cover parts 1 and 2 of the podcast series. Nothing was read on: Carthage's own politics and why it under-supported him, the Roman social and religious world in any depth, Scipio beyond the existence of a page, or the Third Punic War. The Carthaginian side of this report is thin as a result — the source is much more interested in the man than in his city, and this report inherits that.

## Evidence

The classification is `transcript`, and the source-format rules require a trust calibration before anything gets filed. Here it is.

The host is a podcaster working from Polybius and Livy plus modern secondary scholarship, so the reasoning is at second and third hand and the vivid scenes are reconstructions. The nine-year-old at the altar comes down through Polybius and Livy, and the specific wording differs between them — which the vault page notes, and which is the honest form.

The bigger caution is the frame. This is a show called *How to Take Over the World*, and its interest is in extractable lessons about power. That produces exactly the material this report's below-the-line sections want, and it also means the analysis arrives pre-shaped into principles. The rationality-versus-commitment framing above is the host's thesis, stated as such on the source stub, and several of the vault's pages here are that thesis worked out rather than events reported.

Where's the weakest link? It's that the frame is unfalsifiable in the direction it's pointed. Rome won, so Rome's commitment reads as civilisational strength. Had Rome fallen, the same senate decisions would read as fanaticism that destroyed a republic, and nothing in the analysis distinguishes the two in advance. Treat the mechanism as real and the verdict on it as retrospective.

---

# Below the Line

*Everything above is sourced to the vault pages cited. Everything below is built rather than found, and is not measured by `assessgate.sh`.*

## Roads Not Taken `[SPECULATIVE]`

**A live alternative, and it's the one the oath forbade.** Consolidation in Spain was a real strategic option, not a modern invention — his father had built a Carthaginian power base there, and holding it was a coherent programme with a coherent outcome.[^12] The source's argument is precisely that he could not take it, because the oath specified destruction rather than position. So the alternative existed, was available, and was closed by something sworn at nine.

**A constructed one, and this is where the counterfactual gets interesting rather than idle.** Suppose he marches on Rome after Cannae. First order, the field army is intact and Rome is undefended in the way that matters — this is the classic charge against him. Second order, he has no siege train and no logistics for one, and the source's own account of his supply position makes a sustained siege the thing he was least equipped for. Third order, and this is the part the classic charge misses: taking the city gets him the surrender that Rome had already decided not to give, which means the win condition he needed wasn't military in the first place. **A forecast, and one built on the source's own frame rather than on the record.**

## Counsel From Elsewhere `[SPECULATIVE]`

**A Kautilyan advisor, and this is the cleanest match in the folder — the manual is written for exactly this problem.** The *Arthashastra* is a science for a king inside a field of rivals, and its whole method is positional: relations are structural, alliances are instruments, and a campaign is judged by what it leaves you holding. See [[LAB/Worldview Reports/trautmann-arthashastra-worldview-archaeology|What a Mauryan Statecraft Manual Took For Granted]].

Two pieces of counsel follow, and they're specific. First, on the sacred commitment: the manual's four tests treat *dharma* — a claim about what's righteous — as one of the four levers by which a man can be moved off his interest, which is to say the tradition already knows that a sworn moral commitment is a strategic vulnerability. See [[ARCHIVES/concepts/history/four-tests-of-trustworthiness|Four Tests of Trustworthiness]]. Hannibal fails his own dharma test permanently, on purpose, from the age of nine. A Kautilyan advisor would identify the oath as the single largest exploitable feature of the opposing commander and be surprised nobody used it.

Second, on the confederacy. Rome after Cannae holds together because its Italian allies mostly don't defect, and Book Eleven's answer to a bonded polity is *bheda* — find the resentments and let the quarrel do the work — not more battles. See [[ARCHIVES/concepts/history/kautilya-buddha-on-breaking-a-sangha-confederacy|Kautilya and the Buddha on Breaking a Sangha]]. He did attempt this, which is what the post-Cannae Italian campaign largely was. The Kautilyan objection would be to the sequencing: he spent his decisive military advantage first and then went looking for defections, when the manual's logic runs the other way — buy the split while your army is still a threat rather than a stalemate.

**A Roman advisor to Hannibal, using the folder's own material on installed explanations.** After a defeat too large to absorb, a population reaches for the account that preserves its honour, and whoever supplies it first tends to win — that's the stab-in-the-back finding and the Fifth Sun finding both. See [[LAB/Worldview Reports/kershaw-hitler-hubris-worldview-archaeology|What Weimar Germany Took For Granted]]. Rome after Cannae is the same situation with the opposite outcome: a catastrophic defeat, and no myth of betrayal, because the senate supplied the meaning immediately and the meaning was *we do not stop*.

**So here's the convergence, and it's a genuinely new one for this folder.** In every other case here, a defeated people took an explanation from an interested party because it let them keep their dignity. Rome wrote its own on the same day. **The variable isn't the size of the defeat, it's whether the losing side had a story ready before the news arrived.** Germany in 1918 had four years of triumphalist propaganda and nothing else; the Nahua elite in the 1560s had a friar's library; Rome had a self-description it had been rehearsing for centuries. That is now four instances of one mechanism, with one case running the other way, which is what makes the mechanism testable rather than decorative.

## What Transfers `[SPECULATIVE]`

**1. A commitment you cannot revise is a capability and a ceiling in the same object.**
The oath produces the Alps and forecloses the settlement. *Applies* to any goal placed beyond review — a founding promise, a mission statement treated as sacred, a public position that cannot be walked back. The gain is real: it makes possible things a cost-benefit reading would never authorise. *Fails* the moment the situation calls for the one move the commitment forbids, and the failure is invisible until then.
*Decision type:* when to compromise a core value.

**2. Check whether your opponent is optimising or refusing.**
The whole campaign rests on an assumption about how opponents behave under pressure, and it's correct about almost everybody. *Applies* whenever you're modelling the other side as rational — the question isn't whether they're rational, it's what they've taken off the table. *Fails as a diagnosis* if you use it after the fact, since anybody who didn't fold looks like a refuser in hindsight. The tell to look for beforehand is what they've *already* absorbed without folding.
*Decision type:* strategic retreat.

**3. One mind is fast and a system is durable, and the trade is not close over a long horizon.**
Everything through one head means rapid adaptation and a single point of failure. *Applies* when the contest has no fixed end date — the longer it runs, the more the system's replacement rate matters and the less any single brilliant decision does. *Fails* where the contest is short or decided in one engagement, which is exactly where individual genius does win.
*Decision type:* power consolidation.

**4. Winning the battles is not the same as holding the win condition, and the two can be unrelated.**
He won nearly everything and needed a surrender that had already been ruled out. *Applies whenever* your victory is defined by the other side conceding something. If the concession is what they've decided not to give, more victories don't move you closer.
*Watch for:* a campaign where each success requires the next one, with no state of the world in which you stop.
*Decision type:* timing a bold move.

**5. Whether a refusal reads as strength or as fanaticism is decided by the outcome, not by the refusal.**
This is a caution rather than a lesson. The same senate votes look like civilisational nerve or suicidal pride depending on how the war ended, and nothing available at the time separates them.
*Applies as a check* on any argument that recommends commitment by pointing at a case that worked.
*Decision type:* post-failure narrative.

# What Weimar Germany Took For Granted — Worldview Archaeology

> **Which file is this?** This is a **Worldview Archaeology** report — what the people inside the source took for granted, and what those assumptions let them do or stopped them doing. Below a `# Below the Line` divider it turns speculative on purpose. No sibling thread map exists for this source yet.

*Source ingest: [[ARCHIVES/sources/kershaw-hitler-hubris-1889-1936|Kershaw, Hitler 1889–1936: Hubris]]*
*Built from the vault's Kershaw concept pages, which carry the footnotes to the book. **Most of those pages file to behavioral-mechanics and cross-domain rather than history** — this is the case the widened trigger exists for, and under the old rule this report would never have been written.*

---

## A Defeated Army Needed a Culprit

October 1918. The German army on the Western Front has been bleeding for four months. The last offensive collapsed in July. About 1.75 million soldiers fell ill in the spring influenza epidemic and 750,000 were wounded in the same period. Deliberate shirking in the final months is estimated at close to a million men. At home the ration is under a thousand calories a day, less than half what a working person needs. The navy is mutinying at Kiel and Wilhelmshaven.[^1]

Every serious general knows the war is lost and has known for months.

What they do next is the founding act of the next twenty years. The High Command starts seeding a different story: the army was never beaten in the field, Germany was stabbed in the back — by the home front, by Jews, by socialists, by the politicians who went to the armistice talks.[^2]

It's a lie, and the causation runs the other way. Unrest at home was a consequence of military failure, not a cause of it. The army collapsed first and the home front broke under the strain.[^3]

But it wins, for three reasons worth separating. The generals planted it before the truth could settle. Nobody the population trusted was in a position to contradict generals on military matters. And the public had been fed triumphalist propaganda by those same generals as late as October, so they had no way to absorb the size of the defeat when it came.[^4]

A population told for four years that victory was certain, then handed a surrender, will take any explanation that doesn't require them to accept the war was unwinnable. *Betrayed* lets you keep your honour. *Defeated* makes you bury it.

## Nobody Stormed Anything

Quarter past eleven on the morning of 30 January 1933. The new cabinet is walking through the ministerial gardens to where Hindenburg is waiting. Hitler is still unhappy about the limits on his powers and is pressing again for new elections. Hugenberg is against it. The two of them are arguing in an anteroom while the President of Germany waits next door.[^5]

An official warns them the President can't be kept much longer. Papen begs Hugenberg to respect the word of a German man. The minute hand keeps going. Papen gets one last concession out of Hitler — that he'll consult the Catholic Centre about widening the coalition — which both of them know is worthless. Just before noon they go in. Hindenburg, annoyed, gives a short welcome. The oath is sworn. The President closes with one sentence: "And now, gentlemen, forwards with God."[^6]

That's the event. No march on Berlin, no storming of anything, no putsch — an antechamber argument that nearly stopped the swearing-in, ended by an old man's impatience.

The mechanics were ordinary. Hindenburg used the same procedure he'd used for Brüning in 1930, Papen in June 1932, Schleicher that December. Of eleven ministerial posts, three went to Nazis. The other eight went to conservatives who believed they'd bought a useful frontman cheap.[^7]

The regime's own spokesmen avoided *seizure of power* and preferred *takeover of power*, precisely to underline that it was legal.[^8] They were right, and that word is where the whole history starts.

## The Country Worshipped a Second Man

Here's the strange part. The man in the photographs — awkward, unable to run a cabinet meeting, avoiding his own ministers for weeks — was not what Germany worshipped. There was a second one, painted by propaganda and built out of a defeated nation's wishes, running in parallel and getting steadily more popular than the original.[^9]

*If only the Führer knew* was a phrase on people's lips by 1934. Whatever was wrong was the fault of subordinates, of little Hitlers in the party. The real one was incorruptible, statesmanlike, working tirelessly, gradually fixing everything.[^10]

The word *myth* is doing specific work there and it doesn't mean a lie that fools idiots. It means a wall of belief with a building resting on it — manufactured by propaganda, then absorbed and amplified by a society that needed it to be true, and distilled out of the audience's own hopes: national recovery after Versailles, an end to Weimar's squabbling, order restored, the dignity of work, the little man protected. The myth did the integrating work the actual regime couldn't do.[^11]

And it came first. On 3 November 1922 in the Munich Hofbräuhaus, five days after Mussolini's March on Rome, Hermann Esser told a packed room that "Germany's Mussolini is called Adolf Hitler." At that point Hitler still called himself the drummer, and went on doing so for another eighteen months. By 1924 a book had him kitted out with chapter headings — The Prophetic Person, The Genius, The Awakener, The Liberator — before he had any concrete claim to greatness at all.[^12]

So the cult was invented *for* him, by followers who were ahead of him, and was in place waiting when he arrived.

## There Was Nobody There When the Role Came Off

Speer's later verdict, backed by everyone who knew him closely, is that outside the role the man was "tantamount to an 'unperson'."[^13] No real friendships. No personal interests separable from the political performance. No inner life running independently of the public function.

The reading is directed at what's absent. Through the whole 1933–45 period there were no close friends in the ordinary sense — the people nearest him worked inside his official structures. Eva Braun was kept from the German public until 1945 and excluded from political meetings. Reading was "no end in itself, but a means to an end." The art collecting was state aesthetics; the architecture was regime monuments. The line between personal interest and Führer project didn't exist.[^14]

What that configuration makes impossible is the thing worth having. A person whose whole substance is inside a public role cannot retreat to a private one when things go wrong, because there isn't one. Any threat to the role is a threat to the self. In the bunker in 1945 this was not a leader losing a war.[^15]

It also changes what a biography of him can be. If there's no self to write, the attention has to go to the power instead — which is the methodological move the book makes explicitly, and it's why this material is so unusually good for the purpose of this report.[^16]

## Nobody Had to Give the Order

Historians looking for the signed document that starts the Holocaust have never found it. There's no directive. The Wannsee Conference in January 1942 was mid-tier officials working on logistics, and the killing had begun months earlier. The escalation from harassment in 1933 to ghettoisation in 1939 to mass shooting in 1941 to gassing in 1942 happened without explicit central direction at almost every step.[^17]

The phrase that resolves it is *working toward the Führer*. He issued remarkably few explicit orders. His subordinates — the SA, the SS, the Gestapo, the army, the regional Gauleiters, the state governments — competed to anticipate what he wanted and act on it. They radicalised without being told to, because they were competing for favour and the measure of favour was who was doing most to advance the cause as the Führer was understood to see it.[^18]

Two conditions make that machine run. **A signal that's intense but vague** — Germany must be cleansed, the East must be Germanised — strong enough to mobilise and loose enough to interpret. Had the instruction been *deport them, do not kill them*, the structure would not have produced extermination. It wasn't specified, so it got interpreted.[^19] And **many power centres with overlapping authority and no final arbiter**, each competing to be seen as the most effective servant of a goal nobody had defined.[^20]

The result is a system that produced its most extreme outcomes through a leadership that never issued the extreme orders.

## Tensions Within the Subject

**The myth and the man never matched, and only one was visible.** At the cabinet table in March 1933 the actual man was cautious, well-briefed, open to advice, taking notes during financial briefings. The Day of Potsdam that same month was staged theatre welding the myth to Prussian tradition.[^21] Both were happening in the same fortnight.

**Legality is the regime's own claim and it's true.** They preferred *takeover* to *seizure* because it was accurate, and the accuracy is what made the eight conservative ministers think they were safe.

**And the unperson finding is a structural move, stated as one.** It isn't a psychological diagnosis of a man; it's a biographer explaining why he's writing about power instead of personality. That's the honest form of it and it should be kept in that form.

## Not in the Range Read

Built from the vault's Kershaw concept pages, not a fresh read. This volume covers 1889–1936; the second volume is not in the vault, so nothing here speaks to the war years, and the working-toward-the-Führer material is a mechanism described in these pages rather than a period this report has read.

Nothing was read on: the economics beyond the Mefo-bills page, the churches beyond the Concordat, everyday life in the Reich, or the resistance. No claim is made either way about what the book contains there.

## Evidence

The classification is scholarly and this is the standard biography of its subject, which removes the hagiography problem that dominates the Genghis and Rasputin reports in this folder — and replaces it with an opposite one worth naming: with material like this, the pull is toward reading every outcome backwards as intention.

The book's own method cuts against that, which is why it suits this report so well. It works structurally throughout — the power rather than the personality, the myth built by an audience rather than by a man, radicalisation produced by competition rather than by command. Everything above is drawn from that structural layer. Where an intention is attributed, it is attributed to a named person on a named date.

Two things this report is deliberately not doing. It is not treating the outcomes as evidence of personal genius, which is the specific error the source exists to correct. And it is not treating the structures as an account that removes anyone's responsibility — *working toward the Führer* describes how thousands of people chose to act, and a mechanism that explains a choice is not an excuse for it.

---

# Below the Line

*Everything above is sourced to the vault pages cited. Everything below is built rather than found, and is not measured by `assessgate.sh`.*

## Roads Not Taken `[SPECULATIVE]`

**Live alternatives, and this case is unusual because the alternative was the plan.**

The containment strategy was somebody's actual argued position, not a road not taken but a road actively driven. Three of eleven posts, a coalition cabinet, Papen as Vice-Chancellor, conservatives holding Foreign Affairs, Finance, Economics, Labour and Defence.[^22] The men who did that believed they had bought a useful frontman on cheap terms, and they were experienced politicians, not fools. And in the anteroom on the morning itself, Hugenberg was still arguing against the new elections — the last recorded moment where the arrangement was being contested by someone inside it.[^23]

So the counterfactual doesn't need constructing. It was tried, by the people best placed to try it, with a majority of the cabinet, and it failed inside six months.

**A constructed one, and it's a forecast.** Suppose the signal from the top had been specific rather than vague — an explicit written policy with a stated limit. First order, the competing power centres lose the thing they were competing over, because you can't outbid a rival on a metric that's been defined. Second order, responsibility becomes attributable, which is precisely what vagueness prevents: a written limit creates a document somebody can be held against. Third order, the escalation either stops at the stated line or requires a new explicit order to pass it, and each explicit order is a decision point where refusal becomes possible. **That is an inference from how the mechanism is described to work, not a claim about what would have happened. Systems route around specificity too.**

## Counsel From Elsewhere `[SPECULATIVE]`

**A Kautilyan advisor, and the interesting result is that the tradition doesn't cover this.** The *Arthashastra*'s theory of the corrupted state is entirely about information travelling *upward* — ministers tell kings what they want to hear, so the king needs channels outside the hierarchy and officials rotated so they can't nest. See [[ARCHIVES/concepts/history/arthashastra-kingship-and-rajarshi|Arthashastra Kingship and the Rajarshi]].

Working toward the Führer is the same pathology running the other way. The distortion is in what travels *downward*: a signal deliberately left unspecified, interpreted competitively by people whose careers depend on guessing generously. Kautilya's remedies are all diagnostic — better information for the ruler — and none of them touch a system where the ruler's ambiguity is the productive ingredient rather than a defect. **Marking that as a hole in the tradition rather than a failure of the case.** The Kautilyan king is assumed to want accurate compliance. This one benefited from not getting it.

**An Ashokan advisor, and this is the pairing that matters.** Ashoka spent twenty-seven years building the most elaborate compliance machine of the ancient world and then wrote, in his last inscription, that external restrictions are of little consequence and that internal conversion does the real work. See [[LAB/Worldview Reports/ashoka-worldview-archaeology|What a Mauryan King Took For Granted]] and [[ARCHIVES/concepts/history/pillar-edict-vii-the-autocrats-retraction|Pillar Edict VII — The Autocrat's Retraction]].

He is describing the same mechanism. People who have internalised a direction outperform people following orders, because they act when nobody is watching and they act in situations the order never anticipated. Ashoka's evidence for it is the *dharma-mahamatras*; the German evidence for it is the Holocaust.

**So the mechanism is neutral and the content is everything, and this is the hardest thing in this folder.** An advisor from either tradition would recognise the machine immediately. Neither tradition's account of it contains anything that distinguishes the two outcomes, because the distinguishing thing isn't in the mechanism — it's in what got internalised. The vault has met this before, in a different register: the Greene build's central unresolved finding was that a method can be genuinely neutral and that neutrality is not a defence. See [[LAB/Threads/greene-33-strategies-of-war-threads|The Method That Cannot See Its Own Aim]]. This is the same problem, arriving from an unrelated corpus, and it is now the strongest convergence in the folder.

**And one convergence with the Fifth Sun report that's structurally exact.** After the conquest of Mexico, elite indigenous students adopted an explanation of their grandfathers' defeat — that they'd been paralysed by prophecy — which had been supplied by the friars who had beaten them, because the available alternative was that their own people were simply inferior. See [[LAB/Worldview Reports/camilla-townsend-fifth-sun-worldview-archaeology|What the Nahuas Took For Granted]]. The stab-in-the-back is the same move made by an interested party in advance rather than adopted afterwards, but the demand it meets is identical: *betrayed* preserves what *defeated* destroys. **Third instance of this pattern in the vault now**, counting the Greene build's finding that an ambiguous record resolves toward whichever reading yields a usable story.

## What Transfers `[SPECULATIVE]`

These are written as things to recognise, not things to do. The material doesn't support the other register, and the source's own argument is that treating these outcomes as a repeatable playbook is the error.

**1. When a defeat is too large to absorb, the explanation that preserves honour will beat the one that's true, and whoever supplies it first usually wins.**
*Applies when* the population has been told for a long time that the outcome was certain — the prior confidence is what creates the gap the myth fills. *Fails* where expectations were managed honestly, or where a trusted party can contradict the interested one, which is the specific thing October 1918 lacked.
*Decision type:* post-failure narrative.

**2. A vague high-intensity signal plus competing power centres produces escalation that nobody ordered.**
This is the diagnostic. Both conditions are required: intensity without ambiguity gives you orders, and ambiguity without competition gives you drift. *Applies* to any structure where subordinates are rewarded for anticipated rather than instructed performance and no one body has final say. *Fails* where jurisdiction is clear, or where the signal is specific enough to be met and therefore capped.
*The counter-move is specificity*, because a stated limit is the thing a person can later be held against — and its absence is what makes responsibility unattributable afterwards.
*Decision type:* power consolidation.

**3. A myth about a leader is built by the audience out of what the audience needs, and it can precede the leader.**
The cult was named in a beer hall while the man still called himself the drummer. *Applies when* a population has a specific unmet want and someone is available to be cast — the casting is done by the crowd, not the actor. *Fails as a read* where the figure demonstrably built their own image, which is the more common case and the one that makes this one easy to miss.
*Watch for:* the "if only he knew" formula, which is the load-bearing sentence — it lets a believer absorb unlimited evidence of failure without touching the belief.
*Decision type:* alliance formation.

**4. A person with no life outside a role cannot concede, because conceding is annihilation.**
*Applies when* someone's entire substance sits inside a public function — and the diagnostic is absence, not intensity: no friendships outside the structure, no interests separable from the work, nowhere to go on a Sunday. *Fails* where a private domain genuinely exists, however small, because then retreat remains available and defeat stays survivable.
*Decision type:* strategic retreat — this predicts who is structurally unable to make one.

**5. Internalised direction outperforms explicit instruction, and that is true regardless of the direction.**
Ashoka concluded it after twenty-seven years of enforcement; the German case demonstrates it at the opposite moral pole. *Applies* to any system choosing between compliance and conversion. *Fails as guidance* in exactly the way it matters most: the mechanism contains nothing that tells you whether the content is worth internalising, and no amount of study of the mechanism supplies that.
*Decision type:* when to compromise a core value.

# What the Deccan Plateau Took For Granted — Worldview Archaeology

> **Which file is this?** This is a **Worldview Archaeology** report — what the people inside the source took for granted, and what those assumptions let them do or stopped them doing. Below a `# Below the Line` divider it turns speculative on purpose. No sibling thread map exists for this source yet. Its closest neighbour in this folder is [[LAB/Worldview Reports/shivaji-worldview-archaeology|What the Deccan Took For Granted]], which covers the same plateau one generation later.

*Source ingest: [[ARCHIVES/sources/pillai-rebel-sultans|Pillai, Rebel Sultans]]*
*Built from the vault's Rebel Sultans concept pages, which carry the footnotes to the book.*

---

## A Mirror of the World, Not a Frontier

Most accounts of this plateau start with Shivaji. This one puts him at the end, and the three and a half centuries the standard story skips are the point.[^1]

Here's what was already on the ground when he was born in 1630. The daughter of an African slave had become queen to a local king and was busy scheming to murder a more favoured Persian wife. A Brahmin minister was sending Aurangzeb cartloads of mangoes to flatter him while quietly wrecking the emperor's plans. A Muslim prince was fending off his own outraged clergy because he kept putting Hindu gods above the teachings of the Prophet. Shiva worshippers walked to a celebrated Muslim shrine every year. Horses bred in Iraq were on the roads, the elite dressed to the fashions of Iran, travellers arrived from Burma and from France, and European doctors walked into Deccan harems and were astonished to find begums with skin as pale as their own.[^2]

The line the whole book turns on is one sentence: to the world the Deccan was uniquely Indian, and to India it was a mirror of the world.[^3] So the frame to drop before reading anything else is that this was a religious frontier. It wasn't a backwater, it wasn't a battlefield, and it wasn't a border between two civilisations. It was a centre, and the later habit of reducing it to the backdrop for one famous duel is what made it look like an edge.[^4]

## A King Who Called Himself Saraswati's Son

A Sunni Muslim king sat on a golden throne in a painting he'd commissioned, and beside him on another golden throne sat Saraswati — the Hindu goddess of learning, with her peacock and her conch and her veena. The inscription around her, in his own hand, calls him the man whose father is guru Ganapati and whose mother is the pure Saraswati.[^5]

Ibrahim Adil Shah II ruled Bijapur for nearly forty years. He opened official decrees by invoking Saraswati. He minted coins calling himself Friend of the Weak, in Sanskrit. He wore rudraksha beads, the seed rosaries of Hindu ascetics. He renamed his own capital from City of Victory to City of Learning.[^6]

And when he died his epitaph insisted, defensively, that he was a Muslim and pure of faith, and certainly never one of the idolators.[^7] That denial is the useful part. Nobody carves a rebuttal into a tombstone unless the charge was loud enough to need answering — so the fluidity was real, and it was also contested at the time by people who found it intolerable.

He wasn't vague about his own faith either, which is what makes him hard to file. Raised Sunni by his regent, he was expected to revert to his uncle's Shiism when he came of age, and courtiers fell over each other converting in advance. He stayed Sunni and mocked them ever afterwards as "political Sheeas."[^8] The same man endowed Hindu temples, protected pilgrims' rights, called himself Adil Shah Sufi, and wrote fifty-nine devotional songs whose dedication brings Islamic and Hindu divines together and which feature Shiva and Parvati inside an Islamic frame.[^9]

The categories weren't being reconciled by anybody. They simply weren't experienced as contradicting.

## A Slave Could Own a Throne

Around 1600 an African general handed a nervous prince one of his own daughters in marriage to stiffen the boy's nerve for a war he wasn't sure he could win. The general had been born in Ethiopia, sold as a boy, shipped across the Arabian Sea, and bought and resold more than once before he ever held a sword. He gave the daughter away the way a banker pledges collateral. It worked — the prince agreed to fight, the Nizam Shah of Ahmadnagar took a black queen, and the man who put her on the bridal cushion became the real ruler of the kingdom.[^10]

Malik Ambar died around 1626, near eighty, of old age, in great comfort, in a mausoleum he'd designed for himself.[^11] Two things about him matter beyond the arc. He held the Deccan against the full weight of the Mughal empire for decades — not by winning pitched battles, which he often lost, but by refusing to ever stop fighting.[^12] And he originated *bargi-giri*: mobile light cavalry, hit and run, never give the enemy a target. That's the system the Marathas inherited and perfected into the doctrine that wore the Mughals down.[^13]

Under him the Nizam Shahi state became, in one scholar's phrase, a joint Habshi-Maratha enterprise — an Ethiopian regent running Muslim sultans' armies staffed by a Maratha Hindu nobility.[^14] Hold that next to the tombstone in the previous section. The same plateau that produced an epitaph denying idolatry also produced a state nobody in it seems to have found strange.

## Forty Days of Ganges Water Poured on a Rock

1327. A column of porters carries water from the Ganges roughly fifteen hundred kilometres south, walking for forty days, so that it can be poured over a fortress in the Deccan to make it holy.[^15]

The fortress was Devagiri, just renamed Daulatabad, Abode of Fortune. Muhammad bin Tughluq had decided the entire capital of the Delhi Sultanate would move there — not the court, not the army, everyone. Virtually all of Delhi was to be transplanted south.[^16]

The reasoning wasn't stupid. The Sultanate had pushed as far as the Tamil coast, and he'd concluded that no empire could hold the south from a northern seat — that this was the lesson the ancient emperors had failed to learn. Rather than govern through governors he couldn't trust, he'd sit in the middle of his own dominions.[^17]

Within a decade he'd abandoned it. The move broke his treasury and gutted his greatest city, and — without anyone intending it — created exactly the power vacuum in the Deccan that the local nobles filled by rebelling and founding a kingdom of their own.[^18]

So the whole three centuries above start with a logistics decision that went wrong. The blessed water dried on the stone of a citadel its blesser walked away from.

## Tensions Within the Subject

**Fluid and contested at the same time.** The plateau's mixing was real and so was the outrage about it — Ibrahim II's clergy, and the epitaph that answers a charge. A world can be genuinely porous and still contain people who spend their lives objecting to the porousness.

**The guerrilla doctrine has two fathers and only one is remembered.** *Bargi-giri* is Malik Ambar's, and it became the thing that made a Maratha state possible. The later story runs it the other way round.

**And a sensible plan can be the whole cause.** Nothing in the range read suggests Tughluq's reasoning about distance was wrong. The empire really was too big to run from Delhi. The plan was defensible and the execution destroyed the thing it was meant to save, and the Deccan's independent history is the residue.

## Not in the Range Read

Built from the vault's Rebel Sultans concept pages, not a fresh read. Anything the ingest folded is invisible here.

Nothing was read on: Vijayanagar's internal workings beyond the pages on Krishnadevaraya and Ramaraya, the Portuguese presence beyond one page, the diamond economy, or the position of ordinary cultivators anywhere on the plateau. No claim is made either way about what the book contains there.

## Evidence

A popular history by a scholarly writer, with a stated thesis it argues throughout — that the Deccan was the neglected centre rather than a frontier — and everything above sits inside that argument rather than outside it. The concrete details are what this report rests on: the Saraswati painting and its inscription, the coins, the renamed capital, the defensive epitaph, the forty-day water column, the dates of Malik Ambar's life and the composition of the Nizam Shahi state. Those are checkable and specific.

The framing claim — that later communal history has flattened a fluid world into a rigid one — is the book's own and is treated here as its position rather than as established fact. It is worth marking that this thesis and the material happen to support each other very neatly, which is what a thesis is for and also what makes a reader's caution appropriate.

---

# Below the Line

*Everything above is sourced to the vault pages cited. Everything below is built rather than found, and is not measured by `assessgate.sh`.*

## Roads Not Taken `[SPECULATIVE]`

**A live alternative, attested and unusually clean.** Tughluq's own reasoning names the alternative he rejected: govern the Deccan through governors. He decided he couldn't trust them and moved himself instead.[^19] So the fork is stated, with the reason for taking it, by the person taking it — which is rare, and it means the counterfactual has a documented shape rather than an invented one.

**A second live one.** Ibrahim II's courtiers acted on a prediction and got it wrong, converting to Shiism in advance of a reversion that never came, and he mocked them for the rest of his life.[^20] Their reading of what he'd do was a real position held by people close to him. Worth noting because it shows the fluidity wasn't obvious even from inside the court.

**A constructed one.** Suppose the capital had stayed in Delhi and the Deccan had been run through governors. First order, the treasury survives and Delhi isn't gutted. Second order, the local nobles who founded the Bahmani state have a functioning imperial structure above them rather than a vacuum, so rebellion is a harder and later proposition. Third order — and this is where it stops being useful — the whole plateau's three centuries of independent sultanates rest on that vacuum, so the counterfactual doesn't produce a different Deccan, it produces no Deccan history at all as this book tells it, which is a sign the chain has been pushed further than it can carry. **Stated as a forecast and a weak one.**

## Counsel From Elsewhere `[SPECULATIVE]`

**A Kautilyan advisor on Daulatabad, and the manual addresses this directly.** The *Arthashastra*'s worry is that a ruler's information is bent by the people delivering it, and its remedies are structural — rotate officials so they cannot build local nests, keep a channel outside the formal hierarchy, attend personally to what cannot be delegated without loss. See [[ARCHIVES/concepts/history/arthashastra-kingship-and-rajarshi|Arthashastra Kingship and the Rajarshi]].

Tughluq diagnosed the right problem — governors he could not trust — and reached for the most expensive instrument available. A Kautilyan advisor would say the distrust was correct and the response was a category error: you answer an information problem with a second channel, not by relocating your body. Moving the king moves exactly one pair of eyes. Rotation and parallel reporting move the whole map, cost a fraction, and don't require anybody to carry water for forty days.

**A Mongol advisor on the Habshi-Maratha state.** Genghis abolished inherited aristocratic title at the ceremony confirming him and made every office the state's to give, which is the structural condition under which a man's origins stop determining his ceiling — see [[LAB/Worldview Reports/weatherford-genghis-khan-worldview-archaeology|What the Steppe Took For Granted]]. The Deccan reached a similar place by an entirely different route: not by abolishing the categories but by having so many of them in play at once that none could be decisive. An Ethiopian slave, a Maratha nobility, Persian courtiers and a Muslim sultan in one state is not a system without hierarchy — it's a system with several incompatible hierarchies, which turns out to work the same way from the point of view of a talented outsider.

**So two routes to the same opening, and it's worth stating as a pair.** Abolish the ladder, or run so many ladders that no one of them ranks you. The second is cheaper, needs nobody's permission, and is what a cosmopolitan trading plateau produces on its own. It's also less stable, because nothing prevents one ladder becoming decisive later — which is roughly what the next two centuries did to it.

## What Transfers `[SPECULATIVE]`

**1. A defensive epitaph is evidence about the accusation, not about the man.**
Nobody denies a charge nobody made. *Applies* wherever a record contains an unprompted denial — the denial dates and locates the pressure. *Fails* where denials are formulaic in the genre, which is common in funerary writing, so check whether the same line appears on the neighbours' tombs.
*Decision type:* post-failure narrative.

**2. Many competing hierarchies open the same doors as no hierarchy, at a fraction of the cost and with less stability.**
*Applies when* several status systems overlap and none can override the others — trading centres, frontier courts, coalition institutions. *Fails* as soon as one system becomes able to rank the others, at which point the opening closes without anyone announcing it.
*Decision type:* alliance formation.

**3. Answer an information problem with a channel, not with your body.**
Tughluq's diagnosis was right and his instrument moved one observer at enormous cost. *Applies whenever* the temptation is to go and see for yourself. Going yourself is a fix for one place at one time and buys nothing structural. *Fails* where the thing genuinely cannot be reported — where your own judgement in the room is the irreplaceable input.
*Decision type:* strategic retreat.

**4. The innovation gets attributed to whoever used it last.**
*Bargi-giri* was Malik Ambar's and is remembered as Maratha. *Applies when* a method passes from a smaller or less-storied actor to a larger one — attribution follows fame, not chronology. *Fails as a correction* if the later user genuinely transformed it, which the Marathas partly did; the honest version is two inventors, not a theft.
*Decision type:* power consolidation.

**5. A sensible plan executed at full scale can be worse than a bad plan executed partially.**
The reasoning about distance was sound. Moving one court is a manageable error; moving a population is not. *Applies when* a correct diagnosis suggests an intervention whose cost scales with the whole system. *Fails* where partial execution is meaningless — some moves genuinely only work whole, and knowing which kind you have is the actual decision.
*Decision type:* timing a bold move.
